The verse also illustrates how envy can blind individuals to moral truth, leading them to believe that eliminating a perceived rival will solve their problems and restore their standing, when in reality it only compounds their wrongdoing. It serves as a warning against the false logic that one can deliberately commit grave sins with the expectation of simply repenting later.

translation: One of them said, 'Do not kill Joseph, but throw him into the bottom of the well; some caravan will pick him up, if you must do something.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates that even in the midst of collective wrongdoing, God's mercy can manifest through a single voice of relative compassion. The speaker, while still participating in the crime against Joseph, represents a moderating influence that prevents the greater evil of murder. This teaches us that when preventing injustice entirely is beyond our capacity, we are obligated to minimize harm to whatever extent possible. It also reveals God's subtle intervention in human affairs - using even the limited conscience of one brother to preserve Joseph's life for the divine plan that would later unfold. The verse illustrates that moral choices exist on a spectrum, and choosing a lesser evil when unable to prevent all wrongdoing is still a meaningful ethical act that can have profound consequences in God's greater design.

translation: They said, 'O our father, why do you not trust us with Joseph while indeed we are to him sincere counselors?'
interpretation: This verse reveals the brothers' attempt to manipulate their father Jacob through feigned innocence and protestations of trustworthiness. Their question itself is ironic, as they are plotting harm against Joseph even as they claim to be his well-wishers. This demonstrates how deception often cloaks itself in the language of sincerity and wounded feelings. The brothers exploit their father's protective instinct by presenting it as unreasonable suspicion, when in fact his paternal intuition correctly senses danger. This verse teaches that evil schemes frequently begin with manipulative speech designed to disarm natural caution, and that those harboring ill intent will often be the first to loudly proclaim their good intentions.

translation: Send him with us tomorrow to play and enjoy himself, and indeed we will be his guardians.
interpretation: This verse reflects the deceptive plea of Prophet Yusuf's brothers to their father Ya'qub, requesting to take Yusuf with them under the false pretense of recreation and promising his safety. It demonstrates how evil intentions can be masked with seemingly innocent proposals and false assurances. The verse teaches believers to be discerning about trusting others with their loved ones, especially when intuition or circumstances suggest potential harm. It also illustrates how familial jealousy and envy can lead individuals to craft elaborate deceptions, even against their own family members. The brothers' promise of being 'guardians' proved hollow, as they intended the opposite - to harm Yusuf. This serves as a warning against making false oaths and breaking trusts, particularly when vulnerable individuals are involved.

translation: He said, 'Indeed, it saddens me that you should take him, and I fear that a wolf would eat him while you are of him unaware.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the protective nature of parental love and the prophetic foresight that comes through divine inspiration. Prophet Ya'qub's (Jacob's) expressed fear is both a natural paternal concern and a veiled warning informed by spiritual intuition. His specific mention of the wolf is deeply ironic, as it foreshadows the very excuse his sons will later use to deceive him. This demonstrates how truth often manifests in unexpected ways - Ya'qub's genuine fear became the instrument of his sons' lie. The verse teaches that divine wisdom sometimes plants awareness of future trials in the hearts of the righteous, not necessarily to prevent them, but to prepare the soul for tests that serve a greater purpose in Allah's plan. Ya'qub's anxiety reflects the tension between human love and submission to divine decree, showing that even prophets experience the full spectrum of human emotion while remaining surrendered to God's will.

translation: They said: 'If the wolf should eat him while we are a [strong] group, indeed, we would then be losers.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the brothers' response to their father Jacob's concern about sending Joseph with them, revealing their false confidence and deceptive reassurance. Their statement ironically foreshadows the very excuse they would later use when they returned without Joseph. The verse demonstrates how they manipulated their father's trust by emphasizing their collective strength and capability as a group, making it seem impossible that any harm could befall Joseph under their watch. This highlights the depth of their premeditated deception, as they were already planning to abandon Joseph while appearing sincere in their promise to protect him. The verse teaches about the nature of betrayal disguised as concern, and how false oaths and assurances can mask evil intentions.

translation: So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the bottom of the well, We inspired to him, 'You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs while they do not perceive [you].'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates God's divine reassurance to the innocent in their darkest moments. When Yusuf was at his most vulnerable—betrayed by his brothers and cast into a well—God immediately consoled him with a revelation promising future vindication. The interpretation here is that divine wisdom often allows trials not as abandonment, but as preparation for eventual triumph. God's promise that Yusuf would one day confront his brothers from a position they could not imagine teaches us that apparent defeats may be preludes to greater victories, and that God's knowledge encompasses both our present suffering and future elevation. The phrase 'while they do not perceive' suggests that divine plans unfold in ways beyond human comprehension, and that those who wrong others remain blind to the consequences that await them.

translation: And they came to their father at night, weeping.
interpretation: This verse describes the moment when the brothers of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) returned to their father Ya'qub (Jacob) after throwing Yusuf into the well. Their weeping was a deliberate act of deception, meant to cover their crime and convince their father that a tragedy had befallen Yusuf beyond their control. The timing of their arrival at night ('isha) was strategic, as darkness could help conceal any signs of their guilt and make their fabricated story more believable. This verse teaches us about the nature of deception and how wrongdoers often resort to false displays of emotion to mask their sins, while also highlighting that such deceptions, though they may temporarily succeed with people, cannot hide the truth from Allah who knows what is concealed in hearts.

translation: They said, 'O our father, indeed we went racing one another and left Joseph with our possessions, and a wolf ate him. But you would not believe us, even if we were truthful.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the moral consequence of habitual dishonesty and broken trust in relationships. The brothers' own acknowledgment that their father would not believe them 'even if we were truthful' demonstrates how previous deceptions or unreliability destroy credibility to the point where truth itself becomes unrecognizable. It teaches that trustworthiness must be cultivated consistently, for once lost, even genuine honesty may be met with justified skepticism. The verse also highlights the spiritual tragedy of those who fabricate lies—they implicitly confess their own guilt through defensive statements, and they become trapped in a web where their words carry no weight, illustrating how sin corrupts not only one's actions but one's very standing before others and before God.

translation: And they brought upon his shirt false blood. He said, 'Rather, your souls have enticed you to something, so patience is most fitting. And Allah is the one sought for help against that which you describe.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the response of Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob) to his sons' deception regarding Yusuf (Joseph). His statement demonstrates profound spiritual wisdom in recognizing falsehood without concrete proof - he intuitively perceived their fabrication despite the presented evidence. The verse teaches that true insight comes from spiritual discernment rather than mere external signs. Ya'qub's response of 'beautiful patience' represents a higher spiritual station where one maintains composure and dignity while facing injustice, neither denying one's pain nor succumbing to despair. His reliance on Allah as 'the one sought for help' establishes that ultimate recourse is to divine justice rather than human vindication, showing that when human systems fail or deceive, the believer's refuge remains in Allah's perfect knowledge and eventual justice.

translation: And there came a caravan, and they sent their water drawer, and he let down his bucket. He said, 'Good news! Here is a boy.' And they concealed him as merchandise. But Allah was Knowing of what they did.
interpretation: This verse illustrates divine providence working through seemingly chance events, as Joseph's rescue from the well appears as a fortunate discovery to the caravan but is actually part of God's predetermined plan. The tension between human schemes—the brothers' plot, the caravan's deception in treating Joseph as contraband to avoid sharing profits—and divine omniscience demonstrates that while humans may act according to their limited knowledge and self-interest, Allah's perfect awareness encompasses all actions and intentions, ensuring that His ultimate purpose prevails regardless of human manipulation or concealment.

translation: And they sold him for a reduced price - a few dirhams - and they were, concerning him, of those content to give him up.
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound irony of human shortsightedness in recognizing true value. The brothers of Joseph sold him for a trivial sum, viewing him as worthless, yet he would later become a figure of immense importance and authority. This teaches that worldly assessments of worth are often severely mistaken, and what people discard or undervalue may possess tremendous significance in Allah's plan. It also illustrates how human greed and haste can lead to decisions that grossly underestimate the divine worth embedded in every soul, and how those who act with such spiritual blindness ultimately harm themselves more than their intended victims.

translation: And the one who bought him from Egypt said to his wife, 'Make his stay comfortable. Perhaps he will benefit us, or we will adopt him as a son.' And thus We established Joseph in the land that We might teach him the interpretation of events. And Allah is predominant over His affair, but most of the people do not know.
interpretation: This verse reveals the paradox of divine will operating through human choice: the Egyptian official's decision to honor Joseph, motivated by pragmatic self-interest and perhaps compassion, becomes the very instrument through which God fulfills His greater plan. The official could not have known that his simple act of kindness would position Joseph for future greatness, demonstrating that God's purposes prevail even when humans act according to their own limited understanding and intentions. The closing statement emphasizes that while humans make plans based on visible circumstances, God's overarching control ensures outcomes that transcend human awareness, reminding us that apparent coincidences and human decisions are often the hidden mechanisms of divine providence working toward purposes beyond our immediate comprehension.

translation: And when he reached maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge. And thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine principle that spiritual and moral excellence in one's formative years is rewarded with wisdom and deeper understanding upon reaching maturity. It establishes that God's bestowal of discernment and knowledge is not arbitrary but rather a recompense for those who conduct themselves with excellence and righteousness. The verse suggests that moral development and intellectual capacity are interconnected in God's system of justice, and that the cultivation of good character naturally prepares one to receive and properly utilize divine gifts of wisdom and understanding.

translation: And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him. She closed the doors and said, 'Come, you.' He said, 'I seek the refuge of Allah. Indeed, he is my master, who has made good my residence. Indeed, wrongdoers will not succeed.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the profound moral strength required to resist temptation when placed in positions of trust and vulnerability. Joseph's refuge in God demonstrates that true integrity is maintained not through external enforcement but through internal conviction and consciousness of divine accountability. His reference to his master's kindness reveals an ethical principle: betrayal of trust compounds moral transgression, as it violates both divine law and human decency. The verse teaches that those who exploit power imbalances or abuse hospitality—the 'wrongdoers'—ultimately fail because they corrode the moral foundations upon which lasting success is built, while those who maintain righteousness despite immediate cost preserve their spiritual dignity and eventual triumph.

translation: And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus it was that We might turn away from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was of Our chosen servants.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the divine protection granted to sincere servants of God, showing that when confronted with temptation, spiritual insight and consciousness of God's presence serve as an internal barrier against sin. The 'proof of his Lord' represents the manifestation of divine wisdom that strengthens the believer's resolve in moments of trial, reminding us that God actively aids those who are devoted to Him by fortifying their hearts against transgression, not merely through external constraints but through internal spiritual awakening.

translation: And they both raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from the back, and they found her husband at the door. She said, 'What is the recompense of one who intended evil for your wife but that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment?'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates how those who commit wrongdoing often resort to false accusations and deception when confronted with exposure, prioritizing self-preservation over truth. It illustrates the human tendency to deflect blame and reverse victim and perpetrator roles when caught in transgression, revealing the depths to which moral corruption can drive a person to compound sin upon sin through slander rather than accepting accountability.

translation: He said, 'It was she who sought to seduce me.' And a witness from her household testified: 'If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has spoken the truth, and he is of the liars.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of divine justice manifesting through human wisdom and observation of physical evidence. The witness's logical deduction based on material proof demonstrates that truth can be uncovered through rational examination of circumstances. The tearing of the garment serves as a sign revealing the reality of the situation - if torn from the front, it would indicate Joseph's guilt in advancing toward her, while a tear from behind would vindicate his innocence and expose her pursuit of him. This establishes the Islamic legal principle that judgments should be based on evidence and sound reasoning, and that Allah provides means through which truth emerges and falsehood is exposed, even when false accusations are made against the innocent.

translation: And if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful.
interpretation: This verse establishes a forensic principle of justice where physical evidence determines truth in conflicting testimonies. The torn shirt serves as an objective arbiter between two opposing claims, demonstrating that Islam values empirical evidence over mere assertions. The location of the tear reveals the true nature of the encounter: a tear from behind indicates the man was fleeing, not pursuing, thereby exonerating him and exposing the false accusation. This reflects a broader Quranic principle that truth will ultimately manifest through signs and evidence, and that God's justice relies on discernible proofs rather than assumptions or social status.

translation: When he saw that his shirt was torn from the back, he said, 'This is from your women's scheming. Indeed, your scheming is mighty.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the recognition of female cunning and the power of deception in human affairs. It acknowledges that women possess a formidable capacity for plotting and manipulation when their desires are thwarted. The description of their scheming as 'mighty' or 'great' serves as both a warning to men to be vigilant and discerning, and an acknowledgment of the psychological and strategic capabilities that can be employed in interpersonal conflicts. It reflects the Qur'anic understanding that trials and temptations can come through sophisticated means, requiring wisdom and sound judgment to navigate. The verse also vindicates the innocent party by revealing the truth of the situation through physical evidence, demonstrating that God's justice ultimately prevails when falsehood is exposed.

translation: Yusuf, turn away from this. And [you], ask forgiveness for your sin. Indeed, you have been of those who sinned.
interpretation: This verse reveals the wisdom and justice in handling a situation of attempted seduction. The command to Yusuf to turn away demonstrates the importance of moving beyond dwelling on others' faults and maintaining dignity even when wronged. The instruction to the woman to seek forgiveness acknowledges human fallibility while offering a path to redemption through repentance. This teaches that while sin must be acknowledged, the door to divine forgiveness remains open for those who genuinely turn back to God, emphasizing mercy alongside accountability in Islamic ethics.

translation: And women in the city said, 'The wife of the al-Aziz is seeking to seduce her slave boy. He has impassioned her with love. Indeed, we see her [to be] in clear error.'
interpretation: This verse reveals how gossip and public scrutiny can serve as divine instruments to expose hidden sins and bring them into the open for accountability. The women's observation that Zulaykha is 'in clear error' demonstrates how violations of social and moral boundaries become subject to communal judgment, which in turn pressures individuals toward repentance or further reveals their spiritual state. The public nature of her exposed desire contrasts with the private nature of her original temptation, illustrating how sins concealed in darkness eventually come to light, and how reputation and social consequence function as earthly manifestations of divine justice and moral order.

translation: So when she heard of their scheming, she sent for them and prepared for them a banquet and gave each one of them a knife and said [to Joseph], 'Come out before them.' And when they saw him, they greatly admired him and cut their hands and said, 'Perfect is Allah! This is not a man; this is none but a noble angel.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates how divine beauty and purity can transcend human comprehension, causing people to lose awareness of their physical surroundings and actions. The women's inadvertent self-harm while mesmerized by Joseph's appearance demonstrates that true spiritual and moral excellence manifests outwardly in ways that can overwhelm worldly concerns. Their exclamation that he must be an angel rather than a human reflects the reality that exceptional righteousness elevates a person beyond ordinary human standards, serving as a defense of Zulaykha's temptation by showing that Joseph's beauty was so extraordinary that it could excuse her loss of self-control, while simultaneously vindicating Joseph by emphasizing his otherworldly, untouchable nature.

translation: She said, 'This is the one about whom you blamed me. And I certainly sought to seduce him, but he firmly refused. And if he does not do what I order him, he will surely be imprisoned and will be of those debased.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the corruption of power when wielded without moral restraint, demonstrating how desire unchecked by conscience transforms into coercion and tyranny. The speaker's public confession, rather than showing remorse, exhibits shamelessness in admitting wrongdoing and compounds it by threatening punishment for virtue itself. This illustrates the spiritual disease of the self that commands evil (nafs al-ammara), which when given authority can invert justice entirely—punishing righteousness and demanding sin. The verse teaches that true honor lies not in social position but in steadfastness against corruption, and that the weak may possess moral strength that the powerful lack. It warns against environments where vice is normalized and virtue is persecuted, showing how worldly power without accountability becomes an instrument of moral destruction.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, prison is more beloved to me than that to which they invite me. And if You do not avert from me their plan, I might incline toward them and be of the ignorant.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound spiritual struggle of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) when faced with seduction, demonstrating that true strength lies in recognizing one's vulnerability before God. His preference for prison over sin illustrates that a believer should choose apparent worldly harm over spiritual corruption. More significantly, his admission that without divine intervention he might succumb shows that human willpower alone is insufficient against temptation - one must actively seek God's protection and acknowledge complete dependence on Him. This teaches that wisdom lies not in self-reliance during trials, but in humble supplication and recognition that only through God's grace can one resist the pull of base desires.

translation: So his Lord responded to him and turned away from him their plot. Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Knowing.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the divine principle that sincere supplication to Allah is met with His mercy and protection. When a believer finds themselves surrounded by temptation and calls upon Allah with genuine intent, Allah exercises His sovereignty to shield them from harmful schemes and desires. It illustrates that human willpower alone may be insufficient against worldly trials, but through humble acknowledgment of one's weakness and reliance on divine assistance, Allah intervenes with His infinite knowledge of both the seen and unseen circumstances, and His attentive hearing of heartfelt prayers, thereby redirecting the course of events in favor of the believer's spiritual wellbeing.

translation: Then it appeared to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him for a time.
interpretation: This verse refers to the decision made by the Egyptian authorities regarding Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) after witnessing clear evidence of his innocence. Despite the manifest signs proving that Yusuf was falsely accused—such as the torn garment from behind and the testimony that exonerated him—the ruling elite chose to imprison him temporarily to protect the reputation of the elite class and suppress the scandal. This demonstrates how human judgment can be clouded by worldly considerations of honor and social standing, leading people to commit injustice even when truth is evident. It also reflects a test in Yusuf's life where he would be unjustly confined despite his righteousness, teaching believers that trials may come even to the innocent, and that patience and trust in Allah's wisdom are essential virtues when facing oppression.

translation: And there entered with him into the prison two young men. One of them said: 'Indeed, I saw myself pressing wine.' The other said: 'Indeed, I saw myself carrying bread upon my head from which birds were eating.' They said: 'Inform us of its interpretation, for indeed we see you to be among those who do good.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates how divine wisdom manifests through seemingly chance encounters, as Joseph's reputation for righteousness and insight attracted those seeking spiritual guidance even in his darkest circumstances. The prisoners' appeal to Joseph demonstrates that genuine moral excellence becomes a beacon that draws others toward truth and understanding, suggesting that one's character and connection to divine knowledge remain evident regardless of worldly station or unjust suffering. Their recognition of Joseph as 'among the doers of good' reveals how spiritual authority emerges not from social position but from inner virtue that others instinctively recognize and trust.

translation: He said: 'No food will come to you as provision but I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you. That is from what my Lord has taught me. Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah, and they, regarding the Hereafter, are disbelievers.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates that true knowledge and spiritual insight come from divine instruction rather than worldly learning. Joseph's ability to interpret dreams before their manifestation symbolizes the comprehensive understanding granted to those who sincerely turn to God. His declaration of abandoning the faith of disbelievers illustrates that prophetic wisdom requires a complete break from false belief systems, and that genuine knowledge of the unseen is intrinsically linked to monotheistic faith and belief in accountability in the afterlife. The verse establishes that spiritual perception and interpretive ability are gifts bestowed by God upon those who reject disbelief and embrace His guidance.

translation: And I have followed the religion of my fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It is not for us to associate anything with Allah. That is from the favor of Allah upon us and upon the people, but most of the people are not grateful.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that true monotheism is both a divine grace and a conscious commitment that transcends personal choice alone. The speaker acknowledges that the ability to worship Allah alone without associating partners is itself a gift from God, not merely a human achievement. This suggests that spiritual insight and the capacity to recognize and maintain pure monotheism comes through divine facilitation rather than human effort alone. The mention that most people fail to show gratitude indicates that recognizing this blessing requires spiritual awareness that many lack, implying that ingratitude stems from an inability to perceive the profound favor of being guided away from shirk (associating partners with God) toward authentic tawhid (divine unity).

translation: O my two companions of the prison, are separate lords better or Allah, the One, the Prevailing?
interpretation: This verse employs a rhetorical question to establish the logical superiority of monotheism over polytheism. Prophet Yusuf, while imprisoned, uses rational argumentation to demonstrate that unity in divinity is inherently more coherent than multiplicity. The question implies that divided authorities would lead to conflict, chaos, and competing demands, whereas Allah's singular sovereignty ensures perfect justice, absolute power, and unchallenged authority. The attributes 'the One' and 'the Prevailing' emphasize both Allah's uniqueness in essence and His overwhelming dominance over all creation, leaving no room for partnership or rival claimants to divinity. This represents da'wah through intellectual persuasion rather than mere assertion.

translation: What you worship besides Him are merely names you and your forefathers have invented, for which Allah has sent down no authority. Judgment belongs to none but Allah. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the fundamental Islamic principle of Tawhid by exposing the emptiness of false worship. The worship of anything besides Allah—whether idols, celestial bodies, or other deities—is shown to be the worship of mere names and labels without divine sanction or reality. These objects of worship have no inherent power or divinity; they are simply constructs given significance by human tradition and imagination across generations. The verse establishes that true sovereignty and legislative authority belong exclusively to Allah, and that authentic religion requires directing all worship solely to Him. The concluding statement about most people's ignorance suggests that deviation from monotheism often stems not from malice but from blind adherence to inherited traditions without critical reflection on their validity or divine authorization.

translation: O my two companions of the prison, as for one of you, he will give drink to his lord of wine; but as for the other, he will be crucified, and the birds will eat from his head. The matter has been decreed about which you both inquire.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the divine knowledge granted to Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) in interpreting dreams, revealing that true knowledge and wisdom come from Allah alone. It illustrates the principle that worldly positions and fates are predetermined by divine decree, and that those who possess spiritual insight can perceive hidden truths beyond ordinary human understanding. The finality expressed in 'the matter has been decreed' emphasizes Allah's absolute sovereignty over human affairs and the certainty of His will, reminding believers that their ultimate destiny lies in His hands, not in worldly circumstances or human planning.

translation: And he said to the one whom he thought would be saved of the two: 'Mention me to your master.' But Satan made him forget the mention [to] his master, and [Joseph] remained in prison several years.
interpretation: This verse illustrates a profound lesson about reliance upon Allah versus reliance upon created beings. Joseph's request to the fellow prisoner to mention him to the king represented a momentary turning to human intermediaries rather than placing complete trust in Allah alone. The consequence—his extended stay in prison—served as a divine lesson that true deliverance comes only through Allah's decree, and that seeking help from others while forgetting to rely primarily on the Creator can delay one's relief. This teaches believers that while taking practical means is permissible, one's heart must remain attached solely to Allah as the ultimate source of salvation and success.

translation: And the king said, 'Indeed, I have seen [in a dream] seven fat cows being eaten by seven [that were] lean, and seven green spikes [of grain] and others [that were] dry. O eminent ones, explain to me my vision, if you should interpret visions.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine wisdom in communicating crucial guidance through dreams to those in positions of authority, even if they are not believers. The king's instinctive recognition that his dream carries significance and his turning to his advisors demonstrates that God plants intuitive knowledge in human hearts about matters of consequence. The dream itself serves as a divine instrument to prepare the way for Joseph's rise to power and the salvation of Egypt and surrounding regions from famine. It shows that God's providence works through various means, including the subconscious realm, to orchestrate events that will fulfill His greater purposes, demonstrating that spiritual insight and material authority can intersect when divine will ordains it.

translation: They said, 'Confused dreams, and we are not learned in the interpretation of dreams.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates a common human tendency to dismiss profound spiritual or symbolic messages when they challenge our understanding or threaten our comfort. The dismissal of Joseph's fellow prisoners' dreams as 'confused' represents intellectual and spiritual laziness, or perhaps fear of confronting uncomfortable truths. Their claim of ignorance about dream interpretation may also reflect humility, but more likely indicates an unwillingness to engage deeply with matters that require contemplation and spiritual insight. The verse teaches that divine signs and guidance often come in forms that require effort, reflection, and openness to understand, and that rejecting or dismissing them out of hand prevents us from accessing deeper truths and wisdom that could benefit us.

translation: And the one who was saved of the two said, remembering after a period of time, 'I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates how divine will operates through human forgetfulness and remembrance according to appointed times. The cupbearer's delayed recollection of Joseph was not mere coincidence but part of God's plan to elevate Joseph at the precise moment when his wisdom would be most needed and valued. It teaches that救度 and elevation come at divinely appointed times, not when we desire them, and that periods of apparent neglect or forgotten promises serve a higher purpose in preparing both the individual and circumstances for ultimate fulfillment. The verse also illustrates how worldly people may forget the righteous in times of ease, only remembering them when faced with need, yet even this human weakness becomes an instrument of divine justice and mercy.

translation: O Joseph, O truthful one, explain to us [the dream of] seven fat cows being eaten by seven [that are] lean, and seven green spikes [of grain] and others [that are] dry - that I might return to the people; perhaps they will know [about you].
interpretation: This verse demonstrates that true knowledge and wisdom are gifts from God that transcend worldly status and circumstances. Joseph, despite being imprisoned and stripped of social standing, is recognized as 'the truthful one' and becomes the sole source of understanding for the kingdom's crisis. This teaches us that divine wisdom can manifest through the most unlikely vessels, and that those who possess genuine insight will eventually be sought out regardless of their material circumstances. The cupbearer's appeal to Joseph also illustrates how God's plan unfolds through seemingly chance encounters - their earlier meeting in prison now becomes the means for Joseph's vindication and rise to power, showing that no experience in a believer's life is without purpose in God's grand design.

translation: He said, 'You will plant for seven years consecutively; and what you harvest leave in its spikes except a little from which you will eat.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the importance of strategic planning and resource management in times of prosperity to prepare for future hardship. It teaches that immediate gratification must be balanced with long-term sustainability, instructing preservation of wealth in its most secure form. The directive to leave grain in its husks demonstrates practical wisdom in storage techniques while highlighting the principle of restraint and discipline in consumption. This reflects a broader spiritual lesson about prudent stewardship of God's provisions and the necessity of foresight in human affairs, reminding believers that material blessings come with the responsibility of wise management for the collective good.

translation: Then there will come after that seven difficult [years] which will consume what you saved for them, except a little from which you will store.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine wisdom in planning and preparation for future hardships. It teaches that prosperity should not lead to complacency, but rather to prudent management of resources. The command to preserve resources during times of plenty demonstrates that faith requires both trust in God and responsible stewardship. The cyclical nature of ease and difficulty in life is a test of human foresight and gratitude, reminding believers that worldly provisions are temporary and must be managed with wisdom and charity, keeping in mind both present needs and future uncertainties.

translation: Then after that will come a year in which the people will be given rain and in which they will press [olives and grapes].
interpretation: This verse speaks of divine mercy following hardship, indicating that after a period of difficulty and scarcity, Allah will send relief through abundant rainfall that enables agricultural prosperity. The mention of pressing olives and grapes signifies not merely survival but prosperity and blessing, as these activities represent surplus production beyond basic sustenance. It teaches believers to maintain patience during trials and retain hope in Allah's promise of relief, while also reminding them to be grateful when abundance arrives. The verse illustrates the cyclical nature of worldly conditions and emphasizes that hardship is temporary and relief is divinely ordained.

translation: And the king said, 'Bring him to me.' But when the messenger came to him, [Joseph] said, 'Return to your master and ask him what is the case of the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plan.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the importance of establishing one's innocence and reputation before accepting worldly advancement. Joseph refuses the immediate freedom offered by the king, insisting instead that the matter of the women who cut their hands - representing the false accusations against him - be properly investigated and resolved first. This teaches that true honor comes not from escaping consequences but from clearing one's name through truth and justice. Joseph's patience in seeking vindication rather than rushing to freedom shows that righteousness must be established publicly, not just accepted privately, and that a believer should prioritize their moral standing over immediate material benefit.

translation: He said, 'What was your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph?' They said, 'God forbid! We knew no evil of him.' The wife of the al-Aziz said, 'Now the truth has become evident. It was I who sought to seduce him, and indeed he is of the truthful ones.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates that truth ultimately prevails when given the proper forum for examination. The public questioning forced a confrontation with reality that private circumstances had allowed to remain hidden. The wife of al-Aziz's confession represents a moment of moral reckoning where maintaining false testimony became impossible under direct scrutiny. Her admission that Joseph was truthful validates that integrity, though temporarily obscured by false accusation and imprisonment, cannot be permanently suppressed. This teaches that patience in the face of injustice is rewarded when circumstances allow truth to manifest, and that even those who wrong others may eventually be compelled by conscience or circumstance to acknowledge reality.

translation: That is so he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the plan of the betrayers.
interpretation: This verse reflects the profound spiritual principle that true integrity is maintained even when no one is watching, and that divine justice ultimately prevails over treachery. It emphasizes that Allah's guidance is withheld from those who engage in betrayal and deceit, teaching believers that righteousness must be upheld in both public and private spheres, as God is always aware of our actions and intentions, and that those who scheme through betrayal will find themselves deprived of divine support and success.

translation: And I do not acquit myself. Indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse reveals the fundamental Islamic understanding of human nature and the necessity of divine grace. It teaches that the human soul inherently inclines toward wrongdoing and moral weakness, possessing an intrinsic tendency to command evil actions unless restrained by God's mercy and guidance. The acknowledgment of one's inability to fully absolve oneself reflects the principle that genuine righteousness cannot be achieved through human effort alone, but requires constant reliance on divine assistance, forgiveness, and transformative mercy. This represents a call to perpetual humility, self-awareness of one's moral vulnerability, and continuous dependence on God's compassionate intervention to overcome the soul's base impulses.

translation: And the king said, 'Bring him to me; I will appoint him exclusively for myself.' And when he spoke to him, he said, 'Indeed, you are today established in position and trusted with us.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the principle that true merit and integrity will ultimately be recognized and rewarded, even after trials and injustice. Joseph's wisdom and moral character, displayed through his interpretation of the dream and his patience during imprisonment, elevated him from prisoner to trusted advisor in a single conversation. It teaches that maintaining one's principles and demonstrating competence, even in adversity, can lead to divine vindication and positions of influence where one can effect positive change. The king's immediate recognition of Joseph's trustworthiness upon meeting him also illustrates how genuine virtue manifests itself clearly to those who are discerning.

translation: He said, 'Appoint me over the treasuries of the land. Indeed, I am a knowing guardian.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the permissibility of a qualified believer seeking a position of authority when they possess the necessary competence and intend to serve justice and the public good. Yusuf's request shows that humility does not require refusing positions of leadership when one has the skills needed to fulfill them properly, especially during times of crisis. His self-description as 'knowing guardian' indicates that positions of trust should be given to those with both expertise and integrity, establishing a Quranic principle that merit and capability should be the basis for appointing leaders to manage public resources.

translation: And thus We established Joseph in the land to settle therein wherever he willed. We touch with Our mercy whom We will, and We do not allow to be lost the reward of those who do good.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine principle that God's mercy and favor are bestowed according to His wisdom, not human merit alone. Joseph's elevation from prisoner to powerful administrator demonstrates that sincere devotion and moral excellence (ihsan) will ultimately be recognized and rewarded by God, even when circumstances seem hopeless. The verse reassures believers that righteous conduct is never wasted in God's sight—He preserves and honors it in His own time and manner, teaching patience and trust in divine justice beyond immediate worldly outcomes.

translation: And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and were conscious of Allah.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the superiority of eternal rewards over worldly gains for believers who maintain taqwa (God-consciousness). It teaches that those who combine faith with righteous conduct and mindfulness of Allah's boundaries should prioritize the lasting benefits of the afterlife over temporary material pleasures. The verse serves as a reminder that true success lies not in accumulating worldly wealth or status, but in earning Allah's pleasure through sincere belief and pious living, as the compensation awaiting believers in the Hereafter far exceeds anything this temporal world can offer.

translation: And the brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him; he recognized them, but they did not recognize him.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the theme of divine wisdom and timing in fulfilling prophecies. Joseph's recognition of his brothers while remaining unrecognized himself demonstrates how those in positions of power and transformation may perceive truths hidden from others. It reflects the concept that spiritual elevation and trials can so profoundly change a person that even those closest to them may fail to see their true identity. The asymmetry of recognition also suggests that the one who has endured hardship and emerged transformed possesses greater insight and awareness than those who remained in their former state, symbolizing how suffering and faith can lead to a higher level of consciousness and understanding of God's plan.

translation: And when he had furnished them with their provisions, he said, 'Bring me a brother of yours from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?'
interpretation: This verse illustrates Joseph's strategic wisdom in reuniting with his family while maintaining his concealed identity. By requesting Benjamin's presence under the pretext of generous hospitality and fair dealing, Joseph creates a legitimate reason to bring his full brother closer to him. His emphasis on fair measurement and excellent treatment serves both to build trust with his half-brothers and to ensure they will return, demonstrating how divine wisdom can work through human planning to fulfill a greater purpose of reconciliation and the preservation of familial bonds, even when those bonds were previously severed by betrayal.

translation: But if you do not bring him to me, then there will be no measure [of grain] for you from me, nor shall you approach me.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of conditional trust and accountability in human relationships. Yusuf (Joseph) establishes a firm boundary based on the fulfillment of a promise, demonstrating that trust must be earned and maintained through actions. The verse teaches that when significant commitments are made, there are real consequences for breaking them, and that protecting the vulnerable (Benjamin in this context) sometimes requires establishing non-negotiable terms. It reflects wisdom in leadership—being both generous and firm—where continued assistance depends on integrity and the honoring of agreements, reminding believers that trustworthiness is foundational to maintaining relationships and social cooperation.

translation: They said: 'We will try to persuade his father concerning him, and indeed we will do so.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the brothers' determination and confidence in their ability to manipulate their father Jacob into sending Benjamin with them to Egypt. It reveals their spiritual blindness to divine will and their reliance on human scheming rather than recognizing God's plan at work. Their statement 'we will certainly do so' demonstrates human arrogance in making absolute claims about future actions without acknowledging God's sovereignty. This also foreshadows the inevitable confrontation between human plotting and divine decree, where despite their confidence, they would ultimately fail to control the outcome, as Benjamin's fate was already ordained by Allah's wisdom to reunite Joseph with his family and complete the trial of Jacob.

translation: And he said to his servants, 'Put their merchandise into their saddlebags so they might recognize it when they return to their people; perhaps they will come back.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates Joseph's strategic wisdom and mercy in dealing with his brothers who had wronged him years before. By secretly returning their payment, Joseph created a compelling reason for his brothers to return to Egypt, ensuring he would see them again, particularly his younger brother Benjamin. This act reflects both divine providence working through human agency and the principle that mercy and kindness can be more effective than confrontation in achieving reconciliation. Joseph's approach shows that sometimes the path to justice and family reunion requires patience, indirect methods, and creating circumstances that appeal to people's sense of honor and obligation rather than forcing immediate acknowledgment of past wrongs.

translation: So when they returned to their father, they said, 'O our father, [further] measure has been denied to us, so send with us our brother [that] we will be given measure. And indeed, we will be his guardians.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates a moment of profound moral testing where the brothers must convince their father to trust them again with another beloved son, despite their past betrayal with Joseph. Their appeal reveals both their worldly need and their claim of reformed character - they promise to guard Benjamin as they failed to guard Joseph. This reflects the human condition of seeking second chances after past failures, and the tension between material necessity (obtaining grain) and moral credibility (proving trustworthiness). The verse illustrates how circumstances can force individuals to confront their past failings and make renewed commitments, while also highlighting a father's dilemma in balancing practical needs against painful memories of previous loss and betrayal.

translation: He said: 'Shall I entrust him to you except as I entrusted his brother to you before? But Allah is the best guardian, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful.'
interpretation: This verse reveals Jacob's deep internal conflict between his protective love as a father and his recognition of divine sovereignty. His rhetorical question expresses the learned wisdom from past trauma—he remembers how his trust was betrayed when Joseph was lost, yet he simultaneously demonstrates profound theological maturity by surrendering ultimately to Allah's care rather than relying solely on human promises. The verse teaches that while past wounds may inform our caution, true faith requires releasing control to divine providence, acknowledging that Allah's protection transcends all human safeguarding, and His mercy encompasses even our fears and failures as parents and guardians.

translation: And when they opened their baggage, they found their merchandise returned to them. They said, 'O our father, what more can we desire? This is our merchandise returned to us. We will supply our family and protect our brother and obtain an increase of a camel's load; that is an easy measurement.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates divine providence working through human circumstances and the principle that when one acts with sincerity and faith, Allah facilitates their affairs in unexpected ways. The brothers' discovery of their returned goods serves as a sign that their mission was blessed, and their response demonstrates how recognizing divine favor should strengthen one's resolve to fulfill familial obligations and trust in Allah's continued provision. It teaches that material blessings should inspire gratitude and motivate us toward greater responsibility, not complacency.

translation: He said, 'I will never send him with you until you give me a pledge [sworn] by Allah that you will bring him back to me, unless you are surrounded [by circumstances beyond your control].' And when they gave him their pledge, he said, 'Allah is Witness over what we say.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of taking necessary precautions and establishing trust through sacred commitments while simultaneously acknowledging human limitations and divine sovereignty. Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob) demonstrates wisdom by requiring his sons to make a solemn oath before Allah before entrusting them with his beloved son Binyamin (Benjamin), yet he recognizes that even the most sincere human promises are subject to circumstances beyond one's control. By invoking Allah as Witness over their covenant, he establishes that ultimate accountability lies with the Divine, teaching us that while we must take reasonable measures to protect what is precious to us, we must also submit to Allah's will and recognize that He alone has full knowledge and control over all outcomes. This reflects the Islamic balance between tawakkul (reliance on Allah) and taking appropriate worldly means.

translation: And he said, 'O my sons, do not enter from one gate but enter from different gates. And I cannot avail you against Allah at all. The decision is only for Allah; upon Him I have relied, and upon Him let those who would rely [indeed] rely.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the balance between taking practical precautions and maintaining complete trust in divine decree. Jacob's instruction to his sons to enter through separate gates represents the principle that believers should employ available means and exercise wisdom in their affairs, while his immediate acknowledgment that such measures ultimately cannot protect against God's will demonstrates that true reliance (tawakkul) means recognizing that all outcomes rest solely with Allah. The verse teaches that genuine faith involves both responsible action in the material world and absolute spiritual surrender to divine sovereignty, rejecting both fatalistic passivity and the illusion that human effort alone determines results.

translation: And when they entered from where their father had ordered them, it did not avail them against Allah at all except [it was] a need within the soul of Jacob, which he satisfied. And indeed, he was possessed of knowledge because of what We had taught him, but most of the people do not know.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the distinction between taking worldly precautions and placing ultimate trust in divine decree. Jacob's instruction to his sons to enter from different gates was a manifestation of prudent human planning that provided him psychological comfort, yet it could not alter what Allah had decreed. The verse teaches that while believers should employ reasonable means and strategies in their affairs, they must recognize that true protection and outcomes rest solely with Allah. Jacob's knowledge, granted by divine teaching, enabled him to understand this balance between human effort and divine will, though most people fail to grasp that worldly precautions, while permissible and sometimes wise, cannot override divine destiny.

translation: And when they entered upon Joseph, he took his brother to himself. He said, 'Indeed, I am your brother, so do not despair over what they used to do.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the divine wisdom in trials and separation, showing that apparent loss and suffering can be part of a greater plan leading to eventual reunion and relief. Joseph's private disclosure to his full brother Benjamin demonstrates that moments of isolation and intimate connection can provide solace and hope even in difficult circumstances. The instruction not to grieve over past injustices teaches that dwelling on past wrongs becomes unnecessary when divine providence brings about restoration, and that knowledge of a better reality can transform one's perspective on previous hardships. It illustrates how God prepares hearts for revelation in His own time, and how true brotherhood and faith provide comfort that transcends years of separation and pain.

translation: So when he had furnished them with their supplies, he put the drinking cup in his brother's saddlebag. Then an announcer called out: 'O people of the caravan! Indeed, you are thieves!'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates divine wisdom working through human affairs to fulfill a predetermined plan. Joseph's strategic placement of the cup represents how God orchestrates circumstances to bring about a greater purpose - in this case, retaining Benjamin in Egypt as part of the prophetic narrative. The accusation of theft, though technically initiated by Joseph's command, serves as a test of character for the brothers and sets the stage for their moral reckoning. It illustrates how apparent injustices or confusing situations in life may be instruments of divine providence, leading to ultimate truth and reconciliation. The verse teaches that God's plans unfold through seeming contradictions, where an act that appears deceptive serves a higher truth and moral lesson.

translation: They said, while turning towards them, 'What is it that you have lost?'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of transparency and innocence in the face of accusation. The immediate turning toward the accusers and direct questioning demonstrates a posture of openness that comes from a clear conscience. It teaches believers that when wrongly accused, one should not flee or avoid confrontation, but rather face the situation directly with confidence in one's integrity. This dignified response reflects the behavior of those who have nothing to hide and trust in the ultimate justice of Allah, who knows the truth of all matters. The verse also emphasizes the importance of seeking clarity and understanding the nature of accusations before responding defensively, showing wisdom in communication even under pressure.

translation: They said, 'We are missing the measure of the king, and for he who produces it is [the reward of] a camel's load, and I am responsible for it.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of incentivizing truth and justice by offering a substantial reward for the recovery of what was lost. It demonstrates that establishing clear consequences and rewards is a legitimate approach in seeking to resolve matters of theft or loss. The steward's personal guarantee ('I am responsible for it') shows the importance of accountability and standing behind one's promises in positions of authority. This also sets the stage for divine wisdom to unfold, as the promise made here will become the very instrument through which Benjamin is retained with Joseph, showing how Allah's plan works through seemingly ordinary human transactions and commitments.

translation: They said: 'By Allah! You certainly know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and we are not thieves.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the moral integrity and reputation of Prophet Yusuf's brothers, who despite their past wrongdoing against him, had established themselves as honest individuals. Their emphatic oath invokes Allah's name to affirm their innocence, showing that their character had transformed over the years. The verse teaches that a person's established reputation and demonstrated trustworthiness should be considered when accusations arise, and that divine justice operates through both hidden wisdom and manifest circumstances. It also illustrates how Allah tests believers through unexpected trials even when they are innocent, preparing them for greater wisdom and ultimate reunion.

translation: They said, 'Then what will be its recompense if you are liars?'
interpretation: This verse addresses the issue of accountability and justice in cases of false accusation. When the brothers of Yusuf accused the caravan members of theft, they were asked what punishment should apply if the accusation proved true. The verse teaches that those who make claims or accusations must be willing to specify the consequences and accept responsibility for their words. It establishes the principle that justice requires clear terms agreed upon beforehand, and that accusers cannot escape the implications of their own proposed standards. This reflects divine wisdom in ensuring fairness: people are held to the very measures they themselves set forth, demonstrating that justice in Islam is not arbitrary but based on explicit agreement and self-imposed standards.

translation: They said: 'The recompense for it is that he in whose bag it is found, he himself shall be the recompense for it. Thus do we punish the wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of personal accountability and just retribution according to the law that Jacob's sons themselves proposed. Their declaration reflects a system where the guilty party bears the full consequence of their transgression, not allowing the crime to be compensated through alternative means. This demonstrates that justice requires the perpetrator to directly face the punishment, and it establishes that those who commit wrongdoing must personally answer for their actions. The divine wisdom here shows how human beings, through their own words and commitments, can become bound by standards they set, which ultimately serves God's greater plan while maintaining the integrity of moral and legal responsibility.

translation: So he began with their bags before his brother's bag, then he extracted it from his brother's bag. Thus did We plan for Joseph. He could not have taken his brother according to the king's law, unless Allah willed. We raise in degrees whom We will, and above every possessor of knowledge is one more knowing.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates how divine wisdom operates beyond human law and convention, showing that Allah's plan can intervene in earthly affairs to achieve a higher purpose. The stratagem that allowed Joseph to retain his brother was divinely orchestrated, illustrating that when Allah wills something to occur for the benefit of His servants, He creates the means within the framework of justice. Furthermore, the concluding statement about knowledge establishes the principle of intellectual and spiritual humility—no matter how much one knows, there is always greater knowledge above, ultimately culminating in Allah's infinite wisdom, reminding believers that human understanding is always limited and should inspire continuous seeking of knowledge and recognition of divine omniscience.

translation: They said, 'If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before.' But Joseph kept it secret within himself and did not reveal it to them. He said, 'You are worse in position, and Allah is most knowing of what you describe.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the depth of spiritual restraint and the contrast between human judgment and divine knowledge. Joseph's silence in the face of his brothers' slander—their false accusation that both he and Benjamin were thieves—demonstrates the highest form of self-control and trust in God's justice. Rather than defending himself or exposing their far greater crime of attempted fratricide, Joseph internalizes his pain and responds with a measured statement that shifts judgment to Allah. The interpretation here is that true strength lies not in retaliation or self-vindication, but in entrusting one's cause to God who knows all hidden truths. The brothers judge based on superficial appearances and their own guilty projections, while Joseph models the believer's response to false accusation: dignified silence coupled with certainty that Allah's knowledge encompasses all, including the injustices we suffer and the truths we choose not to speak.

translation: They said, 'O noble one, indeed he has a father, an old man advanced in age, so take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the transformation in the character of Yusuf's brothers, demonstrating their growth from their earlier betrayal of him. Their willingness to sacrifice themselves for Benjamin reflects genuine concern for their father Ya'qub's welfare, showing that they have developed empathy and responsibility. Their appeal to Yusuf's nobility and recognition of his goodness represents both a strategic plea and an acknowledgment of moral authority, setting the stage for the eventual reconciliation and revealing how hardship can refine character and lead to redemption.

translation: He said, 'God forbid that we should take anyone except him with whom we found our goods; indeed, we would then be wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates Joseph's commitment to divine justice over human sentiment. Despite his brothers' plea and their father's condition, Joseph refuses to substitute Benjamin with another brother, as doing so would constitute injustice—taking an innocent person for a guilty one's crime. This reflects a fundamental Islamic principle that justice must be upheld even when mercy is desired, and that the ends do not justify unjust means. Joseph's response also shows that true righteousness requires adherence to moral principles even when they conflict with emotional appeals or familial bonds.

translation: So when they had despaired of [moving] him, they secluded themselves in private consultation. The eldest of them said, 'Do you not know that your father has taken upon you an oath by Allah and [that] before you failed in [your duty to] Joseph? So I will never leave [this] land until my father permits me or Allah decides for me, and He is the best of judges.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the concept of moral accountability and the weight of broken promises before God. The eldest brother's decision to remain behind reflects a deeper understanding that returning home after failing their oath would compound their transgression. His statement represents a moment of spiritual maturity where he recognizes that divine judgment supersedes human convenience, and that true repentance sometimes requires bearing the consequences of one's failures rather than fleeing from them. It teaches that when we fail in our responsibilities, especially those sworn before God, the path forward is not to add failure upon failure, but to stand firm and await either reconciliation or divine resolution.

translation: Return to your father and say, 'O our father, indeed your son has stolen, and we did not testify except to what we knew, and we were not guardians of the unseen.'
interpretation: This verse teaches us about the limits of human testimony and knowledge. The brothers of Joseph acknowledge that they can only bear witness to what they directly observed - the apparent theft - but cannot testify to hidden intentions, circumstances, or divine plans that were beyond their perception. It establishes an important principle that humans are bound by observable evidence and cannot claim knowledge of the unseen realm or hidden realities that belong only to Allah's knowledge. The verse also reflects the tension between surface appearances and deeper truths, reminding us that our judgments must be humble and restricted to what we can actually know, while recognizing that greater wisdom and purpose may lie beyond our immediate understanding.

translation: And ask the town where we were and the caravan in which we came - and indeed, we are truthful.
interpretation: This verse employs a powerful rhetorical device (majaz mursal) where the speaker directs the listener to verify their testimony by consulting inanimate entities - the town and the caravan. The true meaning is to question the people of the town and the members of the caravan. This illustrates the profound confidence of the speakers in their truthfulness, as they appeal to witnesses and verifiable evidence rather than merely asserting their honesty. The instruction demonstrates that truth can be established through investigation and corroboration, and that sincere believers should have no fear of scrutiny. It teaches us that when making claims, especially serious ones, we should be prepared to provide evidence and direct others to sources that can confirm our statements, reflecting the Islamic emphasis on truthfulness and the importance of substantiating one's words with proof.

translation: He said: 'Nay, but your souls have enticed you to something. So patience is most fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them all back to me. Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the spiritual maturity and profound trust in divine wisdom that characterizes true faith during trials. Prophet Jacob's response demonstrates that believers must resist the temptation to accept superficial explanations when deeper truths are at stake, maintaining unwavering certainty in Allah's knowledge of hidden realities. His beautiful patience (sabr jameel) represents a dignified, complaint-free endurance that neither despairs nor rebels against divine decree, but rather surrenders to it with grace. The verse teaches that even when human analysis fails and circumstances appear hopeless, the believer anchors their hope in Allah's comprehensive knowledge and perfect wisdom, trusting that He orchestrates events according to purposes beyond our immediate comprehension, and that apparent losses may contain hidden mercies destined to unfold in His perfect timing.

translation: And he turned away from them and said, 'Oh, my sorrow over Joseph!' And his eyes became white from grief, for he was suppressing [his anguish].
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound spiritual trial of Prophet Jacob, demonstrating that even the prophets experience intense human grief while maintaining their faith in God's decree. His physical blindness from weeping symbolizes the depth of legitimate paternal love, yet his suppression of complaint shows the balance between authentic emotion and trust in divine wisdom. It teaches that suppressing one's grief inwardly while turning to God, rather than expressing despair outwardly, represents the highest form of patience (sabr), and that losing Joseph - who represents both a beloved son and a future prophet - constitutes a test of faith that requires both human feeling and spiritual surrender to God's inscrutable plan.

translation: They said: 'By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill or become of those who perish.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the spiritual blindness of Joseph's brothers who mistake their father Jacob's profound faith and patience for destructive obsession. Their inability to comprehend that Jacob's grief is intertwined with trust in Allah's promise demonstrates how worldly perspectives can fail to grasp the depth of prophetic endurance. Jacob's persistent remembrance of Joseph is not weakness but rather an expression of divinely sustained hope, teaching believers that maintaining faith during prolonged trials—even when others perceive it as harmful—can be an act of worship when rooted in reliance upon Allah's wisdom and timing.

translation: He said: 'I only complain of my anguish and my sorrow to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know.'
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Prophet Jacob (Ya'qub) peace be upon him regarding his grief over Joseph, establishes the principle that true refuge in times of overwhelming distress lies exclusively with Allah. It teaches that while humans may seek comfort from others, the deepest sorrows and most profound anguish should be directed to the Creator alone, for only He possesses the power to grant relief and the wisdom to understand the full depth of one's pain. Jacob's statement about knowing what others do not know refers to his divinely-inspired hope and certainty that Allah's promise would be fulfilled, demonstrating that maintaining good opinion of Allah and trusting in His wisdom even during prolonged hardship is the hallmark of true faith and patience.

translation: O my sons, go and search for Joseph and his brother, and do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, no one despairs of Allah's mercy except the disbelieving people.
interpretation: This verse teaches that maintaining hope in Allah's mercy and relief is intrinsically connected to faith itself. The father's instruction reveals that despair is not merely an emotional state but a theological position that reflects one's understanding of Allah's attributes. To lose hope in divine mercy is to fundamentally misunderstand Allah's nature and power, which is why only those who deny Him fall into such despair. The believer, regardless of how dire circumstances appear, must maintain certainty that Allah's mercy encompasses all things and that His ability to change situations is unlimited. This verse establishes hope as a religious obligation and despair as incompatible with true faith.

translation: So when they entered upon him, they said, 'O al-'Aziz (the Minister), adversity has touched us and our family, and we have come with goods of little value, but give us full measure and be charitable to us. Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the proper conduct of those in desperate need when seeking help from those in positions of authority and abundance. The brothers' approach demonstrates humility, honesty about their circumstances, and an appeal to both justice and mercy - first requesting what is rightfully due to them, then asking for additional charity. Their reference to God rewarding charitable acts serves as a reminder that true generosity is ultimately compensated by the Divine, not merely by human gratitude. This teaches that when seeking assistance, one should acknowledge both the natural rights one possesses and the higher moral obligation of the powerful to show compassion, while recognizing that acts of kindness are witnessed and recompensed by God, thus elevating the transaction from a purely worldly exchange to one with spiritual significance.

translation: He said, 'Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother when you were ignorant?'
interpretation: This verse reveals a profound moment of moral reckoning where past wrongs are brought to light not with immediate condemnation, but through questioning that invites reflection and repentance. The reference to 'ignorance' suggests that sins committed in states of spiritual blindness or youthful folly, while still wrong, may be forgiven when the perpetrators achieve awareness and remorse. It teaches that true accountability involves helping wrongdoers recognize their actions' gravity, and that Divine justice often works through gradual awakening of conscience rather than sudden punishment. The verse also demonstrates that forgiveness is most meaningful when preceded by acknowledgment of harm, showing mercy's power to transform relationships even after severe betrayal.

translation: They said, 'Are you indeed Joseph?' He said, 'I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Allah has certainly favored us. Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient, then indeed, Allah does not allow to be lost the reward of those who do good.'
interpretation: This verse teaches that righteousness and patience in the face of adversity are the pathways to divine reward and ultimate success. Joseph's affirmation reveals that his rise from the depths of slavery and imprisonment to power was not mere fortune, but the fruit of maintaining God-consciousness (taqwa) and steadfastness (sabr) through years of trials. It establishes a universal spiritual principle: that God's justice operates with certainty, ensuring that no good deed or patient endurance goes unrewarded, even when the reward is delayed or invisible to human eyes.

translation: They said: 'By Allah, certainly Allah has preferred you over us, and indeed we have been sinful.'
interpretation: This verse represents a moment of profound humility and recognition of truth by Joseph's brothers after years of denial and wrongdoing. Their invocation of Allah's name in acknowledging Joseph's superiority demonstrates a sincere admission that divine wisdom operates beyond human manipulation - despite their past attempts to eliminate him, God's plan elevated Joseph to a position of honor and authority. Their confession of sin indicates genuine remorse and spiritual awakening, showing that true repentance requires acknowledging both God's justice in favoring the righteous and one's own moral failures, ultimately teaching that divine decree cannot be thwarted by human schemes and that recognition of one's errors is the first step toward reconciliation and redemption.

translation: He said, 'No blame upon you today. May Allah forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the profound Islamic principle of forgiveness and reconciliation, particularly when the wronged party chooses mercy over retribution despite having the power to exact justice. The speaker, having attained a position of strength, opts to pardon those who previously wronged him, emulating divine mercy by releasing others from blame and invoking Allah's forgiveness upon them. This teaches that true nobility lies not in revenge but in magnanimity, and that human forgiveness should mirror the boundless mercy of Allah, who remains the ultimate source and exemplar of compassion. The verse emphasizes that pardoning others, especially when one has the upper hand, is among the highest moral virtues and reflects the character believers should strive to embody.

translation: Go with this shirt of mine and cast it upon my father's face; he will become seeing. And bring to me your family all together.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the prophetic certainty of Yusuf (Joseph) regarding Allah's power to restore his father's sight through divine intervention. The shirt serves as a tangible medium through which Allah's healing would manifest, showing that material objects can become vessels of spiritual mercy when ordained by divine will. Yusuf's confidence in commanding his brothers reflects his complete trust in Allah's promise and his assurance that the reunion of the family is divinely decreed. The instruction to bring the entire family indicates the completion of the trials and the beginning of a new chapter where the scattered family would be reunited under Allah's grace, fulfilling the earlier vision and demonstrating that patience through adversity leads to divine reward and reconciliation.

translation: And when the caravan departed, their father said: 'Indeed, I sense the scent of Joseph, if only you would not think me senile.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the profound spiritual connection and intuition that can exist between loved ones, particularly between a parent and child. Jacob's ability to sense Joseph's presence despite the great distance symbolizes how true faith transcends physical limitations and rational explanation. His awareness of his sons' skepticism, expressed in his caveat about them thinking him senile, reflects the tension between spiritual perception and worldly reasoning. The verse teaches that divine inspiration and spiritual sensitivity can grant believers knowledge beyond ordinary means, yet such gifts are often met with doubt by those who rely solely on material evidence. It also illustrates the enduring nature of hope and love, as Jacob never abandoned his trust in God's promise despite years of separation and grief.

translation: They said, 'By Allah, indeed you are in your same old error.'
