In the Hereafter, when the reality becomes undeniable and escape impossible, those who refused to submit willingly in the world will find themselves in complete surrender - not out of faith, but out of helplessness before the overwhelming truth they can no longer deny. This submission comes too late to benefit them, serving as a tragic irony that their resistance in the world, where submission would have been voluntary and praiseworthy, gives way to forced submission when it no longer carries any merit or possibility of redemption.

translation: And they will turn to one another, questioning each other.
interpretation: This verse depicts the scene of the righteous believers in Paradise engaging in conversation with one another. They will inquire about their past lives, the trials they faced, and how they were saved from the torment of Hell. This mutual questioning serves to highlight Allah's mercy and blessings upon them, as they reflect on their journey from the worldly life to eternal bliss. It demonstrates that Paradise is not only a place of physical pleasure but also of intellectual and spiritual fulfillment, where the believers will have companionship and the opportunity to reflect on the divine wisdom that guided them to salvation.

translation: They will say: 'Indeed, you used to come to us from the right side.'
interpretation: This verse addresses the complaint of those who were misled in the worldly life against those who misled them. The phrase 'from the right side' signifies that the deceivers approached them through the guise of righteousness, truth, and good counsel, exploiting their trust and making evil appear as good. It illustrates how Satan and his allies seduce people by making falsehood attractive through seemingly legitimate or authoritative means, thus leading them astray while they believed they were following the correct path. This highlights the deceptive nature of temptation and the importance of verifying sources of guidance against divine revelation.

translation: They will say, 'Rather, you were not believers.'
interpretation: This verse addresses a scene of reckoning where the misled followers confront those who led them astray. The response 'you were not believers' reveals that the corruption was not merely external influence but stemmed from an internal absence of true faith. It indicates that genuine belief (iman) serves as an inherent protection against misguidance, and those who were led astray lacked the foundation of sincere faith that would have enabled them to recognize and resist falsehood. The verse thus establishes personal accountability - one cannot blame others for one's misguidance when the root cause was one's own deficiency in faith and lack of sincere commitment to truth.

translation: And we had no authority over you, but you were a transgressing people.
interpretation: This verse represents the disavowal of the misleaders from those they led astray on the Day of Judgment. The devils and corrupt leaders will declare that they never possessed any coercive power to force their followers into sin; rather, the followers themselves were already inclined toward transgression and willingly accepted the misguidance. This establishes the principle of individual moral responsibility - that people cannot excuse their sins by blaming those who tempted them, since ultimately each person chooses whether to follow truth or falsehood. The verse underscores that human beings possess free will and cannot transfer blame for their choices, even when influenced by others, because they had the capacity to resist and were predisposed to excess.

translation: Thus the word of our Lord has come true against us; indeed, we are to taste [the punishment].
interpretation: This verse reflects the acknowledgment by those who denied or disobeyed God's message that the divine decree and warning of punishment has been realized upon them. It signifies the inevitable fulfillment of God's promise regarding the consequences of disbelief and sin. The statement captures a moment of regret and recognition that they must now experience the punishment they were warned about, emphasizing the certainty of divine justice and the inescapability of God's judgment once it has been decreed.

translation: We led you astray because we ourselves were astray.
interpretation: This verse reflects the confession of the devils or misleaders on the Day of Judgment, acknowledging their role in leading others astray while admitting they themselves were in error. It illustrates the principle that those who mislead others share in the sin and punishment, yet also reveals that misguided leaders cannot excuse their followers, as each soul bears responsibility for its own choices. The verse emphasizes that spiritual corruption spreads from those who are themselves corrupted, and that on the Day of Reckoning, all deceptions will be laid bare with honest admissions of guilt.

translation: Indeed, they on that Day will be sharing in the punishment.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the principle of collective accountability for those who reject faith and engage in wrongdoing. The shared punishment reflects that both the leaders who misled others and the followers who willingly embraced falsehood bear responsibility for their choices. It teaches that on the Day of Judgment, partnerships in sin during worldly life result in shared consequences in the Hereafter, demonstrating divine justice where no one can escape accountability by blaming others, as each person's voluntary participation in rejection of truth makes them equally deserving of the consequences.

translation: Indeed, thus do We deal with the criminals.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's consistent pattern of divine justice in dealing with those who reject faith and persist in wrongdoing. It reflects the principle that Allah's punishment is not arbitrary but follows a systematic application of justice based on human choices and actions. The verse serves as both a warning to disbelievers and reassurance to believers that evil will not go unpunished, reinforcing the accountability that all humans face for their moral decisions in this life and the consequences that follow in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, when it was said to them, 'There is no deity except Allah,' they were arrogant.
interpretation: This verse criticizes those who rejected the fundamental Islamic declaration of monotheism (tawhid) out of pride and arrogance. Their refusal was not due to intellectual doubt or lack of evidence, but rather stemmed from their haughtiness and unwillingness to submit to a higher authority. The verse highlights that the primary obstacle to faith can be the ego and self-importance, which prevents people from acknowledging the truth and humbling themselves before God. It serves as a warning against allowing pride to become a barrier between oneself and divine guidance, showing that true faith requires the abandonment of arrogance and the acceptance of one's position as a servant of Allah.

translation: And they say, 'Are we to abandon our gods for a mad poet?'
interpretation: This verse reveals the psychological defense mechanism of the disbelievers who refused to accept Prophet Muhammad's message. By labeling him as both a 'poet' and 'mad,' they attempted to rationalize their rejection of monotheism without engaging with the truth of his message. Their attachment to their ancestral gods was so deep that they perceived the call to abandon them as absurd, demonstrating how deeply ingrained polytheistic beliefs can blind people to divine truth. The verse exposes their unwillingness to examine their inherited beliefs critically, preferring to dismiss the messenger rather than confront the possibility that their entire worldview might be false. This reflects a universal human tendency to cling to familiar falsehoods rather than embrace uncomfortable truths that demand fundamental change.

translation: Rather, he came with the truth and confirmed the messengers.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Prophet Muhammad came with divine truth that validates and confirms the message brought by all previous prophets, establishing the continuity and consistency of God's guidance throughout history. It emphasizes that his mission is not a deviation or innovation, but rather a confirmation of the same fundamental message of monotheism and moral guidance that was conveyed by earlier messengers, thereby linking the final revelation to the unbroken chain of prophetic tradition.

translation: Indeed, you will surely taste the painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stern warning to those who reject faith or persist in wrongdoing, emphasizing the certainty and inevitability of divine accountability. The use of the emphatic particles 'inna' and 'la' underscores that experiencing this punishment is not a mere possibility but an absolute certainty for those addressed. The 'painful punishment' (al-'adhab al-alim) refers to both the physical and spiritual torment that awaits wrongdoers in the Hereafter, reflecting the principle that God's justice demands consequences for those who deny truth and commit evil. The direct address 'you will taste' makes the warning personal and immediate, removing any sense of distance or abstraction, and the verb 'taste' (dha'iqun) suggests an intimate, unavoidable experience of suffering that will be deeply felt by the recipient.

translation: And you are not recompensed except for what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse establishes the divine principle of proportional justice and accountability, emphasizing that human beings will receive consequences in the Hereafter that precisely correspond to their earthly actions. It affirms God's perfect fairness in judgment, where no soul will be rewarded or punished beyond what it has earned through its own choices and deeds. This serves as both a warning against evil actions and an encouragement toward righteousness, as it guarantees that divine recompense is neither arbitrary nor unjust, but rather a direct reflection of one's moral agency and responsibility. The verse underscores the Islamic concept that salvation and damnation are earned through one's own conduct, not through mere wishful thinking or claims of special status.

translation: Except the chosen servants of Allah (or: the sincere/devoted servants of Allah).
interpretation: This verse establishes a critical exception to divine punishment or Satan's influence, indicating that those who have achieved sincere devotion and purity in their worship of Allah are protected from spiritual harm and misguidance. The term 'mukhlaṣīn' refers to those whom Allah has purified and chosen, or alternatively those who have purified their intentions solely for Him, suggesting that genuine sincerity in faith and action serves as a divine shield, exempting the believer from the fate that befalls others who lack this quality of devotion.

translation: Those will have a provision well-known.
interpretation: This verse refers to the righteous believers who will receive a predetermined and guaranteed sustenance in Paradise. The phrase 'well-known provision' indicates that their reward is established, consistent, and never-changing - unlike worldly sustenance which may fluctuate or cease. It emphasizes Allah's promise of certain reward for the faithful, suggesting that just as their provision is known and secured by divine decree, the believers can have complete trust in the fulfillment of God's promise. This known provision represents both the material blessings of Paradise and the spiritual satisfaction that comes from being in divine favor, all of which are fixed and eternal.

translation: Fruits, and they will be honored.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the rewards awaiting the righteous in Paradise, emphasizing that the believers will not only receive material blessings like abundant fruits, but more significantly, they will be treated with honor and dignity. The juxtaposition of physical provision with spiritual elevation suggests that true felicity in the Hereafter encompasses both bodily pleasure and the soul's recognition of its worth before God, indicating that the greatest blessing is not merely the comforts of Paradise but the status of being honored guests in the divine presence.

translation: In Gardens of Delight.
interpretation: This phrase describes the ultimate reward for the righteous believers in the afterlife - Paradise, characterized by perpetual bliss, comfort, and divine favor. The use of 'Na'im' (delight/bliss) emphasizes that this is not merely a physical garden but a state of complete spiritual and physical pleasure, where every form of happiness and satisfaction is present without any suffering, pain, or deficiency, representing the fulfillment of the soul's deepest longings in the presence of Allah.

translation: On thrones facing one another.
interpretation: This verse describes the arrangement of the righteous believers in Paradise, seated on elevated couches in a state of mutual honor and fellowship. The face-to-face positioning symbolizes the removal of all rancor, envy, and division that may have existed in worldly life, replaced by perfect harmony, love, and spiritual brotherhood. It emphasizes the social and communal dimension of Paradise, where the blessed enjoy not only individual pleasures but also the company of like-minded souls in an atmosphere of complete peace and affection, reflecting the perfection of human relationships when purified from earthly imperfections.

translation: They will be circulated with a cup from a flowing spring.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the pleasures of Paradise, where the blessed will be served pure, flowing beverages by attendants. The mention of 'flowing spring' (ma'īn) emphasizes the purity, freshness, and inexhaustible nature of the drink, contrasting with earthly wines that can be impure or harmful. The passive construction 'yuṭāfu' indicates effortless service, symbolizing the dignified and luxurious nature of Paradise where believers' needs are met without toil or effort on their part. This reflects Allah's generosity and the complete fulfillment that awaits the righteous in the Hereafter.

translation: White, delicious to those who drink.
interpretation: This verse describes the wine of Paradise as being pure white in color and providing complete pleasure and delight to those who consume it, unlike worldly wine which can cause harm and intoxication. The whiteness symbolizes its purity and perfection, while the phrase 'delicious to those who drink' emphasizes that it brings only enjoyment without any of the negative effects associated with earthly wine, such as loss of reason, headaches, or illness. This is part of the Qur'anic descriptions of the pleasures awaiting the believers in Paradise, where all experiences are perfected and free from any defect or harmful consequence.

translation: There is no intoxication in it, nor will they be depleted from it.
interpretation: This verse describes the wine of Paradise as fundamentally different from earthly wine, highlighting that the pleasures of the Hereafter are pure and perfect, free from the harmful consequences that accompany worldly indulgences. The absence of 'ghawl' (headache, intoxication, or loss of reason) and the fact that it does not deplete or exhaust the drinker demonstrates that Paradise offers complete enjoyment without any negative aftermath, teaching us that true divine rewards transcend the limitations and imperfections inherent in material pleasures, and that God's bounty in the next life is designed to provide endless joy without any trace of harm or diminishment.

translation: And with them will be [companions] of modest gaze and beautiful eyes.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the blessings of Paradise, referring to the companions (houris) who are characterized by their chastity and modesty, as indicated by 'qasiraat al-tarf' - those who restrain their glances exclusively for their spouses. The phrase emphasizes spiritual and moral beauty alongside physical beauty, symbolizing the perfect companionship that reflects purity, loyalty, and devotion. These companions represent the fulfillment of lawful desires in the Hereafter, contrasting with worldly temptations, and serve as a reward for righteous believers who restrained their own gazes and desires in the worldly life for the sake of Allah.

translation: As if they were hidden eggs.
interpretation: This verse describes the fair complexion and protected purity of the maidens of Paradise, comparing them to eggs that have been carefully preserved and shielded from external elements. The metaphor emphasizes their delicate beauty, pristine nature, and the care with which they have been maintained in an untouched state. Just as a hidden egg retains its natural perfection away from contamination and damage, these companions possess an unblemished beauty that has been divinely preserved, symbolizing both physical attractiveness and spiritual purity as rewards for the believers in the Hereafter.

translation: Then they turned to one another, questioning each other.
interpretation: This verse describes a moment of mutual inquiry and reflection among a group of people, likely the companions of the garden in Surah Al-Qalam. It illustrates the human tendency to seek understanding and accountability through dialogue when faced with unexpected calamity or loss. The turning toward one another represents a communal search for explanation and wisdom, suggesting that truth often emerges through honest questioning and examination of one's actions and intentions. This mutual questioning serves as a prelude to self-realization and recognition of wrongdoing, demonstrating that collective reflection can lead to acknowledgment of mistakes and, ultimately, to repentance and seeking forgiveness from Allah.

translation: One of them will say, 'Indeed, I had a companion'
interpretation: This verse refers to a believer in Paradise recounting his experience in the worldly life, where he had a companion who was a disbeliever or skeptic. The believer is reflecting on how this companion used to mock him for his faith in resurrection and accountability. This serves as a reminder that the company one keeps can either strengthen or weaken one's faith, and illustrates the ultimate vindication of the believers who remained steadfast despite ridicule. It emphasizes the importance of choosing one's companions wisely and standing firm in faith even when challenged by those who deny the truth of the Hereafter.

translation: Do you say, 'Are you indeed among those who believe [in the resurrection]?'
interpretation: This verse reflects the skepticism and mockery of the disbelievers toward the concept of resurrection and the Day of Judgment. It captures their incredulous attitude when confronted with the prophetic message about life after death. The rhetorical question demonstrates their astonishment and rejection, as they found it difficult to accept that after death and decomposition, humans would be raised again and held accountable. This verse highlights the fundamental disagreement between believers and disbelievers regarding the afterlife, and it serves as a reminder that such doubt has been a recurring theme throughout human history when people are called to reflect on their ultimate destiny and accountability before God.

translation: What! When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be brought to judgment?
interpretation: This verse captures the skeptical reaction of disbelievers to the concept of resurrection and divine accountability. The rhetorical questions express their incredulity at the idea that after complete physical decomposition into dust and scattered bones, they could somehow be reconstituted and held accountable for their deeds. This doubt stems from their materialistic worldview that cannot conceive of life beyond physical existence, and it reflects their denial of God's absolute power to recreate and restore life. The verse highlights a fundamental theological tension between those who limit reality to the observable physical world and the Islamic teaching that divine omnipotence transcends natural limitations, making resurrection not only possible but certain as part of God's justice system.

translation: He said, 'Would you [care to] look?'
interpretation: This verse captures a moment where a believer in Paradise invites his companions to witness the fate of his former companion who had mocked belief in the Hereafter. It illustrates the vindication of faith and serves as a reminder that divine justice ultimately prevails. The believer's invitation to observe is not born of malice but rather demonstrates the stark reality of choices made in worldly life and their eternal consequences, emphasizing the wisdom of choosing faith over skepticism.

translation: Then he looked and saw him in the midst of the Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the ultimate vindication of the believers and the justice of divine judgment. It depicts a moment where a righteous person in Paradise is granted the ability to perceive the fate of someone who had mocked or rejected faith in the worldly life. The vision serves as a confirmation that Allah's promise is true and that the choices made in this life have real, eternal consequences. It emphasizes the stark contrast between the final destinations of those who believed and those who denied, reinforcing the principle that divine justice will manifest fully in the Hereafter, where pretenses fall away and every soul receives exactly what it earned through its deeds and intentions.

translation: He said: 'By Allah, you had almost ruined me.'
interpretation: This verse reflects a moment of profound realization and gratitude, where the speaker acknowledges how close they came to destruction or deviation through temptation or misguidance. The invocation 'By Allah' emphasizes the seriousness of the statement and the speaker's recognition of divine protection. The interpretation centers on the human tendency to be drawn toward harmful desires or false beliefs, and the necessity of divine intervention to save one from such peril. It serves as a reminder that without God's guidance and mercy, humans are vulnerable to influences that could lead them away from truth and righteousness, whether these be material temptations, false ideologies, or harmful relationships. The verse teaches believers to remain vigilant about what or whom they allow to influence them, and to constantly seek Allah's protection from anything that might lead them astray from the straight path.

translation: And had it not been for the favor of my Lord, I would have been among those brought [to Hellfire].
interpretation: This verse reflects profound gratitude and humility before God's mercy, acknowledging that salvation and guidance are purely gifts from the Divine rather than achievements of human effort. The speaker recognizes their complete dependence on God's grace, understanding that without His intervention and favor, they would have been among those destined for punishment. This represents a core Islamic teaching about the relationship between divine mercy and human inadequacy—that no matter how righteous one's deeds may seem, ultimate deliverance comes only through God's compassionate will. It serves as a reminder to believers to maintain humility, never attributing their success or salvation to their own merit alone, and to remain perpetually grateful for God's unmerited favors that shield them from the consequences they might otherwise deserve.

translation: Are we not to die?
interpretation: This verse expresses the astonishment and gratitude of the inhabitants of Paradise, rhetorically questioning their former state of mortality in contrast to their current state of eternal life. It reflects the believers' amazement at having been saved from death and granted everlasting bliss, emphasizing the transition from the temporary nature of worldly existence to the permanence of the Hereafter. The question serves to highlight the immense favor Allah has bestowed upon them by granting them immortality in Paradise, making them reflect on how they have escaped the cycle of death that characterized their earthly lives.

translation: Except our first death, and we will not be punished.
interpretation: This verse reflects the response of the blessed inhabitants of Paradise, affirming that after experiencing the initial death that transitions them from worldly life, they will face no further death or punishment. It emphasizes the eternal nature of Paradise and the absolute security its dwellers enjoy - they are forever protected from both the termination of their blissful existence and any form of divine chastisement. This statement encapsulates the ultimate reward: immortality combined with complete immunity from suffering, representing the fulfillment of the believer's hope for everlasting peace and joy in the hereafter.

translation: Indeed, this is truly the great triumph.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the ultimate success and victory that awaits the believers in the Hereafter. The 'great triumph' refers to entering Paradise and attaining Allah's pleasure, which surpasses any worldly achievement. The emphatic particles 'inna' and 'la-huwa' intensify the affirmation, indicating that true success is not measured by material gains or temporal victories, but by spiritual achievement and eternal reward. This serves as a reminder to believers that they should orient their lives toward this ultimate goal, recognizing that worldly accomplishments are fleeting compared to the everlasting success of the afterlife. The verse redirects human ambition from temporary pursuits to the permanent success that comes from righteousness and submission to Allah.

translation: For the like of this let the workers work.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine call to action, urging believers to strive and exert their utmost efforts toward achieving the ultimate reward of Paradise and God's pleasure. It emphasizes that the magnificent blessings and eternal bliss described in the context of the hereafter should be the primary motivation and goal that drives human endeavor. The verse suggests that worldly pursuits, while necessary, should be subordinated to the higher purpose of earning divine favor. It establishes a hierarchy of values, wherein believers are encouraged to invest their time, energy, and resources in righteous deeds, worship, and moral excellence rather than being consumed by transient material gains. The phrase implies that true success lies in recognizing what is truly worthy of human effort and dedicating oneself to that noble cause with full commitment and sincerity.

translation: Is that a better accommodation or the tree of zaqqum?
interpretation: This verse poses a rhetorical question contrasting the rewards of Paradise with the punishment of Hell, specifically referencing the zaqqum tree which is described elsewhere in the Qur'an as a bitter, thorny tree that grows in the depths of Hellfire and serves as torturous food for its inhabitants. The question is designed to make the listener reflect on the stark difference between the eternal bliss awaiting the righteous and the severe punishment awaiting the wicked, emphasizing divine justice and the consequences of one's choices in worldly life. It serves as both a warning and an invitation to choose the path leading to Paradise rather than Hell.

translation: Indeed, We have made it a trial for the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Zaqqum tree mentioned in the preceding verses, which Allah has made a test of faith for those who reject divine truth. The disbelievers mock the concept of a tree growing in Hellfire, considering it rationally impossible, thus revealing their obstinate rejection of God's power. Their denial and ridicule of what seems paradoxical to their limited understanding becomes a means by which Allah distinguishes between those who have faith in His absolute power and those who arrogantly reject what they cannot comprehend. The trial lies in whether one accepts Allah's revelation with submission or rejects it based on their own limited reasoning, making their disbelief itself a proof against them.

translation: Indeed, it is a tree emerging from the bottom of Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse describes the Zaqqum tree, a symbol of divine punishment and consequence for the deniers of truth. The placement of this tree at the very foundation of Hell emphasizes the totality and inescapability of the torment awaiting those who reject faith. The imagery serves as a warning that the consequences of disbelief are deeply rooted and fundamental, not superficial or temporary, reminding believers of the reality of accountability and the importance of righteous action in this life.

translation: Its emerging fruit as if it was heads of devils.
interpretation: This verse uses vivid imagery to describe the fruit of the Zaqqum tree in Hell, comparing it to devils' heads to evoke extreme repulsiveness and terror. The interpretation is that Allah employs the most horrifying imagery conceivable to the human mind to emphasize the punishment and torment of the disbelievers. Since no one has seen actual devils' heads, the comparison works on psychological revulsion - something so inherently ugly and frightening that it represents the ultimate in repugnance. This serves both as a deterrent from disbelief and disobedience, and as a demonstration that even the food provided in Hell will be a source of suffering rather than nourishment or comfort. The description appeals to the imagination to convey that everything in Hell, even what would normally sustain life, becomes an instrument of punishment.

translation: Indeed, they will eat from it and fill their bellies with it.
interpretation: This verse describes the punishment of the disbelievers in Hell, where they will consume from the tree of Zaqqum despite its bitterness and harm. The interpretation emphasizes that this eating is not for nourishment or satisfaction but represents a perpetual torment - they are compelled to fill themselves with this vile sustenance as part of their punishment. It illustrates the complete reversal of earthly provisions; while food in this world sustains and pleases, in Hell even the act of eating becomes a source of additional suffering. This reflects the comprehensive nature of divine justice, where those who rejected faith and filled themselves with worldly excess and false beliefs will literally fill themselves with the fruits of their spiritual corruption.

translation: Then indeed, mixed with it for them is a drink of scalding water.
interpretation: This verse describes a component of the punishment in Hell, where the denizens will be forced to mix their already torturous sustenance with boiling water that intensifies their suffering. The interpretation emphasizes the compounded nature of divine retribution - that wrongdoers will not experience a single form of punishment, but rather multiple, simultaneous torments that reinforce one another. The scalding water represents how sin corrupts and adulterates even the most basic necessities of existence, transforming what should sustain life into an instrument of agony. This reflects the theological principle that those who corrupted truth and goodness in worldly life will find everything in the afterlife similarly corrupted and turned against them, as their spiritual state manifests in physical torment.

translation: Then indeed, their return will be to the Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the inevitable consequence and final destination of those who reject faith and persist in disbelief. It serves as a warning that despite any temporary respite or worldly enjoyment, the ultimate return of the disbelievers will be to the punishment of Hell. The use of 'then' (thumma) indicates a sequence - after their life on earth and their accountability on the Day of Judgment, their final abode is predetermined as the Hellfire. This reflects the divine justice that those who choose to turn away from God's guidance and deny the truth will face the consequences of their choices in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, they found their forefathers astray.
interpretation: This verse highlights the danger of blind adherence to ancestral traditions and inherited beliefs without exercising critical thought or seeking truth. It emphasizes that people often continue in error simply because they follow the misguided paths of their predecessors, accepting falsehood as truth merely due to familial or cultural loyalty. The verse serves as a warning against intellectual complacency and the uncritical acceptance of inherited ways, calling believers to distinguish between truth and falsehood based on divine guidance rather than mere tradition, and to break free from the chains of ancestral error when it conflicts with revealed truth.

translation: So they hastened in their footsteps.
interpretation: This verse describes the urgent pursuit of the believers following in the tracks of those who had gone astray, likely referencing a situation where people rush headlong after others without reflection. It illustrates the dangerous tendency of humans to blindly follow the path of their predecessors or community, even when that path leads away from truth. The imagery of hastening on footprints suggests a mindless conformity and lack of independent judgment, warning against the abandonment of reason and critical thinking in favor of mere imitation of tradition or social pressure.

translation: And certainly, most of the former peoples went astray before them.
interpretation: This verse reminds believers that deviation from divine guidance is not a new phenomenon but a recurring pattern throughout human history. It serves to contextualize contemporary disbelief by showing that the majority of previous generations also rejected their messengers and strayed from the straight path. The verse provides consolation to Prophet Muhammad and the believers that they should not be disheartened by opposition, as this resistance to truth is part of an ancient cycle. It also serves as a warning that following the majority is not necessarily the path to truth, since historically, most people have chosen misguidance over guidance. The emphasis on 'most' rather than 'all' indicates that there have always been minorities who remained faithful, giving hope that righteousness persists even in times of widespread deviation.

translation: And We had certainly sent among them warners.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's mercy and justice by highlighting that He never punishes a people without first sending them messengers to warn them of the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing. It establishes the principle of divine accountability - that punishment only comes after clear guidance has been delivered and rejected. The verse serves as a reminder that human beings are given ample opportunity to reform and that their destruction or punishment is ultimately a result of their own choices after receiving unmistakable divine warning through the prophets.

translation: So look how was the end of those who were warned.
interpretation: This verse serves as a reminder and lesson for believers to reflect upon the fate of previous nations who rejected divine warnings and messengers. It emphasizes that those who were given clear admonitions but persisted in disbelief and disobedience ultimately faced divine punishment and destruction. The command to 'look' or 'observe' is an invitation to study history and draw lessons from the consequences that befell those who ignored prophetic warnings, thereby encouraging the current audience to heed the message and avoid the same tragic outcome. It underscores the principle of divine justice and the inevitable consequences of rejecting guidance.

translation: Except the chosen servants of Allah.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes divine election and sincere devotion as protective shields against spiritual harm or Satan's influence. It indicates that those whom Allah has purified and selected for His service, or those who have achieved sincere devotion (ikhlas) in their worship, are granted immunity from the deceptions and temptations that affect others. The term 'mukhlasin' can be understood both as those who are made sincere by Allah and those who actively purify their intentions, suggesting a reciprocal relationship between divine grace and human effort in achieving spiritual protection and elevation.

translation: And Noah certainly called upon Us, and how excellent are We in responding!
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's attribute of being the best responder to sincere supplication. When Prophet Noah called out to Allah after centuries of rejection by his people, Allah answered his prayer by destroying the disbelievers through the flood and saving the believers. The verse teaches that Allah never abandons those who call upon Him sincerely, and His response is always perfect in timing and wisdom, even if it may not come immediately. It encourages believers to maintain trust in Allah's responsiveness and to persist in prayer during times of hardship, knowing that He hears and will respond in the best possible manner.

translation: And We saved him and his family from the great distress.
interpretation: This verse refers to Allah's mercy and divine intervention in rescuing a prophet and his household from a severe trial or calamity. The 'great distress' signifies a profound test that threatened their faith, lives, or mission, and Allah's deliverance demonstrates His power to protect His chosen messengers and their followers when they remain steadfast. This salvation serves as a sign of Allah's care for those who submit to Him and as a lesson that no hardship is insurmountable when one places trust in the Almighty, reinforcing the theme that divine support accompanies sincere belief and righteous conduct.

translation: And We made his descendants those who remained.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes divine selection and the continuation of a righteous lineage through a chosen prophet. It indicates that God's blessing extends beyond an individual to encompass their progeny, establishing a lasting covenant through subsequent generations. The verse suggests that the preservation of faith and prophethood was entrusted to this lineage, making them the carriers of divine guidance for humanity. It also reflects the principle that righteousness and divine favor can have generational impact, where the legacy of a faithful servant of God becomes the foundation for future communities of believers.

translation: And We left for him [favorable mention] among later generations.
interpretation: This verse establishes the principle that Allah honors His righteous servants by preserving their good reputation and legacy throughout subsequent generations, allowing their names to be remembered with praise and respect long after their passing as a reward for their faithfulness and devotion to Allah's message.

translation: Peace be upon Noah among the worlds.
interpretation: This verse represents Allah's eternal honor and blessing bestowed upon Prophet Noah (Nuh) for his unwavering faith and perseverance in calling his people to monotheism for 950 years despite facing rejection and mockery. The phrase 'among the worlds' indicates that Noah's legacy of faith, patience, and obedience to Allah transcends time and place, making him a model for all generations and communities across human history. Allah's declaration of peace upon Noah serves as divine recognition of his status as a chosen messenger and his pivotal role in preserving humanity and faith after the great flood, establishing him as an exemplar of steadfastness in the face of adversity for all believers throughout the ages.

translation: Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse establishes a divine principle that Allah's reward system is based on excellence in conduct and righteousness. It indicates that those who excel in their faith, worship, and moral behavior toward others will receive compensation from Allah that befits their good deeds. The verse emphasizes divine justice and encourages believers to strive for ihsan - excellence and perfection in their actions - knowing that Allah recognizes and recompenses such effort. It serves as both motivation for righteous conduct and reassurance that no good deed goes unnoticed or unrewarded in Allah's sight, reinforcing the Islamic concept that the quality of one's character and actions has direct consequences in terms of divine recompense.

translation: Indeed, he was one of Our believing servants.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine attestation and seal of approval upon the faithfulness of a particular servant of God. It indicates that true belief is not merely a claim or outward declaration, but a state that is ultimately validated by God Himself. The use of 'Our servants' emphasizes the honored relationship between God and those who sincerely believe, suggesting that genuine faith manifests through devoted servitude and submission to the Divine will. This verse reminds believers that ultimate success lies not in worldly achievements or human recognition, but in being acknowledged by God as among the faithful, which is the highest honor a servant can attain.

translation: Then We drowned the others.
interpretation: This verse refers to Allah's decisive judgment upon those who rejected His message and opposed His prophets, demonstrating the ultimate consequence of persistent disbelief and transgression. The drowning mentioned is historically understood to reference Pharaoh's army who pursued Moses and the Children of Israel into the sea, symbolizing how divine justice ultimately prevails over oppression and tyranny. It serves as a powerful reminder that worldly power and arrogance cannot stand against divine will, and that those who persist in rejection of truth despite clear signs will face inevitable destruction. The verse emphasizes Allah's absolute sovereignty and His protection of the believers while establishing that no oppressor, regardless of their earthly strength, can escape divine retribution when they cross the boundaries set by Allah.

translation: And indeed, among his followers was Abraham.
interpretation: This verse establishes a spiritual and ideological connection between Abraham and Noah, indicating that Abraham followed the same monotheistic path and divine methodology that Noah championed. It emphasizes the continuity of the prophetic mission across generations, showing that all prophets belong to one unified tradition of submitting to God's will and calling people to pure monotheism. The verse demonstrates that prophethood is not merely chronological succession but a shared commitment to the same fundamental truth, with later prophets affirming and following the way of earlier ones in their devotion to God alone.

translation: When he came to his Lord with a sound heart.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the paramount importance of spiritual purity and sincerity in one's relationship with God. A 'sound heart' (qalb saleem) refers to a heart free from shirk (associating partners with God), hypocrisy, malice, and spiritual diseases, while being wholly devoted to God alone. It suggests that true success lies not in outward actions or material achievements, but in the internal state of one's heart when standing before God. This sound heart is characterized by complete submission, sincerity of faith, freedom from doubt, and purification from base desires and attachments that distract from divine remembrance. The verse teaches that salvation ultimately depends on approaching God with this purified, sincere, and undivided heart.

translation: When he said to his father and his people, 'What do you worship?'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the prophetic methodology of questioning and dialogue as a means of intellectual and spiritual awakening. By posing this fundamental question about the object of worship, the speaker (Ibrahim/Abraham in context) employs a pedagogical approach that forces his audience to reflect critically on their religious practices rather than simply accepting inherited traditions. The question challenges them to examine the rational basis of their devotion and represents the beginning of a logical argument that exposes the inadequacy of idol worship, demonstrating that true da'wah (calling to faith) begins with stirring consciousness and prompting self-examination rather than mere denunciation.

translation: Do you desire gods other than Allah out of falsehood?
interpretation: This verse challenges those who worship false deities alongside or instead of Allah, questioning their motivation and reasoning. The interrogative form emphasizes the absurdity of choosing fabricated, powerless objects of worship when the true Creator exists. It highlights that such worship stems from deception (ifk - falsehood/lies) rather than truth, pointing to the illogical nature of associating partners with Allah. The verse serves as a rhetorical rebuke, urging people to reflect on why they would turn to invented gods that possess no divine attributes, when Allah alone is worthy of worship and possesses all power and majesty. It underscores that polytheism is based on lies and human invention rather than reality.

translation: Then what do you think of the Lord of the worlds?
interpretation: This rhetorical question challenges the listener to reflect on their conception and expectations of Allah. It comes in a context where proper understanding of God's nature, justice, and mercy is being examined. The verse invites believers to consider whether their assumptions about Allah align with His true attributes - His perfect wisdom, ultimate justice, and comprehensive knowledge. It serves as a call to examine one's relationship with the Creator and to ensure that one's beliefs and actions are consistent with the majesty and justice of the Lord of all existence, prompting self-reflection about whether one truly comprehends the magnitude of standing before the Supreme Judge.

translation: And he glanced a glance at the stars
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Ibrahim's strategic use of celestial observation as a means to excuse himself from participating in idol worship with his people. By looking at the stars and claiming illness or preoccupation based on astronomical signs, he created an opportunity to separate himself from the community's false rituals and later confront their idolatry by destroying their idols. This demonstrates how prophets sometimes employed wisdom and indirect methods to challenge falsehood while protecting themselves from immediate harm, showing that strategic thinking in da'wah and resistance to oppression is permissible when done for the sake of establishing truth.

translation: He said, 'Indeed, I am ill.'
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Ibrahim's statement when he sought to excuse himself from accompanying his people to their festival. The interpretation is that Ibrahim used a strategically ambiguous statement to avoid participating in idolatry while not directly confronting his people at that moment. Some scholars interpret 'ill' as a spiritual sickness from witnessing their polytheism, while others see it as a permissible use of equivocation (tawriyah) for a higher purpose - namely, to remain behind and demonstrate the impotence of their idols by destroying them, thereby calling people to monotheism. This teaches that a believer may use wisdom and indirect speech when facing overwhelming opposition, provided the ultimate aim is to uphold truth and combat falsehood.

translation: So they turned away from him, departing.
interpretation: This verse describes a moment of rejection and abandonment, where people physically and spiritually turn their backs on a messenger or sign from God. The act of turning away 'departing' or 'with their backs' emphasizes not just passive disbelief but active rejection - they deliberately chose to distance themselves rather than contemplate or engage with the truth presented to them. This reflects a hardening of hearts and a willful choice to remain in ignorance or denial, which is a recurring theme in the Qur'an regarding those who reject divine guidance despite clear evidence. The departure symbolizes both physical movement and spiritual estrangement from the path of truth.

translation: Then he turned to their gods and said, 'Will you not eat?'
interpretation: This verse illustrates Abraham's strategic approach to demonstrating the futility of idol worship. By addressing the idols directly and questioning why they do not eat the food presented to them, Abraham employs irony and reasoning to expose their absolute powerlessness and lifelessness. The rhetorical question serves to highlight that these objects of worship lack the most basic attributes of living beings—they cannot eat, respond, or interact. This moment represents a powerful pedagogical method where Abraham uses direct confrontation with falsehood to awaken his people's consciousness about the irrationality of worshipping man-made objects that possess no divine qualities whatsoever. His approach combines courage with wisdom, as he challenges the prevailing beliefs of his society through practical demonstration rather than mere argumentation.

translation: What is the matter with you that you do not speak?
interpretation: This verse, addressed to the idols or false gods, exposes their absolute powerlessness and inability to respond or defend themselves. It serves as a rhetorical challenge demonstrating that objects of worship besides Allah possess no divine attributes whatsoever - they cannot speak, hear, or act. This rhetorical question emphasizes the foolishness of worshipping that which has no consciousness or ability to benefit or harm, thereby reinforcing the core Islamic principle of tawhid (monotheism) and the futility of associating partners with Allah who alone possesses all power and ability to respond to His creation.

translation: Then he turned upon them, striking with [his] right hand.
interpretation: This verse describes Prophet Ibrahim's (Abraham's) deliberate act of destroying the idols worshipped by his people, using his right hand to emphasize the strength and purposefulness of his action. The phrase illustrates Ibrahim's strategic confrontation with idol worship after the people had left for a festival, demonstrating his courage in challenging false beliefs and his commitment to establishing monotheism. The use of 'right hand' may signify both physical strength and the righteousness of his cause, as he sought to awaken his community to the futility of worshipping powerless objects instead of Allah.

translation: Then they came rushing towards him.
interpretation: This verse describes a hasty and agitated approach, typically referring to the idolaters who rushed toward Abraham when they discovered their idols had been destroyed. The term 'yaziffūn' conveys rapid movement with anger or concern, indicating their emotional state of distress upon finding their objects of worship broken. This moment precedes Abraham's famous dialogue where he challenges their idol worship by pointing to the largest idol, demonstrating the foolishness of worshipping powerless objects. The verse captures the tension between those clinging to falsehood and the prophet exposing the absurdity of their beliefs through his prophetic wisdom.

translation: He said, 'Do you worship that which you carve?'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absurdity of idolatry by highlighting the contradiction inherent in worshipping something that is created by human hands. The rhetorical question exposes how irrational it is for humans to submit themselves in worship to objects they themselves have fashioned from stone or wood, when logically the creator should be superior to the created. It demonstrates that true worship belongs only to Allah, the actual Creator, not to lifeless idols that have no power, awareness, or ability to benefit or harm, and which exist only through human craftsmanship.

translation: And Allah created you and that which you do.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty and creative power of Allah over all existence, including human actions. It addresses the theological tension between divine predestination and human agency by affirming that while humans perform actions through their own will and effort, the very capacity to act, the materials used, and the ability itself are all created by Allah. This reflects the Islamic understanding that human free will operates within the framework of divine creation and sustenance, meaning that nothing exists or occurs outside Allah's creative power, yet humans remain morally responsible for their choices because they exercise genuine volition within the parameters Allah has established.

translation: They said, 'Build for him a structure and throw him into the blazing fire.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the ultimate consequence of rejecting faith and standing firmly for monotheism in the face of tyrannical opposition. The command to build a structure and cast the believer into fire represents the futile attempt of disbelievers to extinguish the truth through persecution and violence. It demonstrates that when rational arguments fail, oppressors resort to brute force and spectacle to maintain their authority. However, this verse also foreshadows divine intervention, as no worldly power can overcome those under God's protection. The fire they kindle becomes a test not of the believer's resolve, but of God's absolute sovereignty over His creation, showing that the laws of nature themselves submit to the Divine will when He chooses to manifest His support for the righteous.

translation: They intended to harm him with a plot, but We made them the lowest.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates Allah's absolute power in reversing the schemes of evildoers. When adversaries plot against the righteous, their cunning ultimately becomes their own downfall. God's justice operates by transforming the intended harm back upon its perpetrators, elevating the victim while debasing the oppressor. This establishes the principle that no human conspiracy can overcome divine protection, and that those who scheme against Allah's chosen servants will find themselves humiliated and defeated, regardless of their worldly power or elaborate planning.

translation: And he said, 'Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the profound trust and submission of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) as he departed from his people who rejected monotheism. His statement 'I am going to my Lord' signifies both a physical migration away from idolatry and a spiritual journey toward divine proximity. The phrase 'He will guide me' demonstrates complete reliance on Allah's providence and direction, embodying the concept of tawakkul (trust in God). This serves as a model for believers facing opposition or uncertainty: to prioritize their relationship with Allah and trust that sincere devotion and migration for His sake will be met with divine guidance and support in their worldly and spiritual affairs.

translation: My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.
interpretation: This supplication reflects the proper etiquette of asking Allah for offspring, where the emphasis is placed not merely on having children, but on having righteous children who will be a source of goodness. It teaches that a believer should prioritize the quality of faith and character in their progeny over quantity or worldly status. The prayer demonstrates humility before Allah as the ultimate Granter of all blessings, and shows that righteous children are among the greatest of blessings because they benefit both this world and the Hereafter through their good deeds and prayers for their parents.

translation: So We gave him glad tidings of a forbearing boy.
interpretation: This verse refers to God's promise to Abraham of a son who would be characterized by gentleness and patience. The emphasis on 'forbearing' (halim) rather than physical attributes or intelligence suggests that the true blessing lies in righteous character. It teaches that patience and forbearance are among the highest virtues that a parent could hope for in their offspring, and that God's gifts are not merely material but deeply spiritual in nature. The verse also demonstrates God's mercy in answering the prayers of the faithful, fulfilling His promise to Abraham despite his advanced age and apparent impossibility of the situation.

translation: So when he reached with him [the age of] working, he said, 'O my son, indeed I have seen in a dream that I [must] sacrifice you, so see what you think.' He said, 'O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, of the steadfast.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound nature of divine testing and the essence of true submission to God's will. The test presented to Abraham was not merely about physical sacrifice, but about surrendering one's deepest attachment - a beloved son - demonstrating that love for God must transcend all other loves. The son's immediate acceptance without questioning or hesitation exemplifies perfect trust in both divine wisdom and paternal guidance. His response, 'do as you are commanded,' shows recognition that God's commands, even when they appear incomprehensible, contain wisdom beyond human understanding. The phrase 'if Allah wills' reflects humility and awareness that even our steadfastness depends on God's enabling grace. This trial teaches that faith is authenticated through action and sacrifice, and that complete submission means being willing to offer what we cherish most when God calls for it.

translation: Then when they had both submitted and he laid him down upon his forehead
interpretation: This verse describes the ultimate moment of submission to God's will by both Prophet Ibrahim and his son Ismail. The act of laying down represents the zenith of trust and obedience, where both father and son surrender completely to divine command despite the apparent tragedy. It exemplifies that true faith requires absolute submission even when God's wisdom seems incomprehensible, and that such unconditional obedience to Allah transcends natural human attachments and instincts. This trial demonstrates that nothing, not even the most beloved relationships, should come between a believer and their devotion to God's command.

translation: And We called to him, 'O Abraham!'
interpretation: This verse marks a pivotal moment of divine intervention where God directly addresses Abraham at the critical instant before he would have sacrificed his son. The divine call demonstrates God's intimate awareness and immediate response to Abraham's obedience. It signifies that God's command was a test of faith and submission rather than a literal requirement of sacrifice. The divine intervention teaches that God does not desire the sacrifice of human life, but rather the willingness to surrender completely to His will. Abraham's readiness to obey, even in the most difficult circumstance, fulfilled the purpose of the trial, and God's merciful call prevented the actual sacrifice, establishing a fundamental principle that true devotion lies in the heart's submission rather than the completion of the physical act itself.

translation: You have fulfilled the vision. Indeed, this is how We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse reveals a fundamental principle of divine justice: that sincere intention coupled with complete submission to God's will is itself the essence of righteousness, regardless of the worldly outcome of the action. The verse teaches that true excellence (ihsan) lies not merely in performing good deeds, but in the willingness to surrender one's deepest attachments when commanded by God. The reward mentioned is multi-layered: it includes both the prevention of actual harm while preserving the spiritual merit of the intended sacrifice, and the eternal commemoration of this act of devotion. This establishes that God's tests are not meant to cause suffering but to elevate the human soul, and that He honors the sincerity of intention as much as the completion of the act itself. The verse thus offers comfort to all believers that their struggles and sacrifices in obedience to God, even when difficult beyond measure, are seen, valued, and rewarded by the Most Merciful.

translation: Indeed, this is the clear trial.
interpretation: This verse refers to the profound test of faith that Prophet Abraham faced when commanded to sacrifice his son. It describes the moment as a 'clear trial' (balā' mubīn), indicating that this was an unmistakable test of Abraham's submission to God's will. The trial was 'clear' because it demanded the ultimate sacrifice - choosing obedience to God over the deepest human attachment to one's own child. This represents the essence of faith: the willingness to surrender everything to God, even when the command seems to contradict natural human instincts and emotions. The verse teaches that true faith is proven through trials that test the limits of one's devotion and trust in divine wisdom, even when understanding is incomplete.

translation: And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.
interpretation: This verse refers to the divine intervention in the story of Prophet Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to Allah's command. The 'great sacrifice' represents Allah's mercy and His acceptance of Ibrahim's complete submission, substituting a ram for the boy. The magnitude of the sacrifice lies not merely in its physical size, but in its profound spiritual significance: it commemorates absolute faith, establishes the principle that Allah does not desire human sacrifice, and sets a perpetual example of devotion for believers. This event became the foundation for the annual sacrifice during Eid al-Adha, where Muslims commemorate Ibrahim's obedience and Allah's mercy by offering animal sacrifices, symbolizing their own willingness to submit entirely to Allah's will.

translation: And We left for him [favorable mention] among later generations.
interpretation: This verse establishes the concept of lasting legacy and divine honor bestowed upon the righteous. It indicates that Allah preserves the good reputation and praiseworthy remembrance of His faithful servants across generations, ensuring their names are mentioned with respect and their examples are followed by those who come after them. This represents a form of divine reward that transcends temporal existence, where the righteous continue to benefit from the prayers and positive remembrance of future believers, and their good deeds inspire others long after their earthly life has ended.

translation: Peace be upon Abraham
interpretation: This verse represents Allah's divine salutation and blessing upon the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), honoring him for his unwavering faith, complete submission to God's will, and his pivotal role as a patriarch of monotheism. The greeting of 'peace' (salam) signifies not merely absence of conflict but a comprehensive state of divine favor, protection, and spiritual wholeness bestowed upon Ibrahim as recognition of his trials, sacrifices, and steadfast devotion. This salutation also serves as a model for believers to invoke blessings upon the prophets and reflects the continuity of divine guidance through messengers, with Ibrahim being particularly revered across Abrahamic faiths as the exemplar of pure monotheistic worship and total reliance on God.

translation: Thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse establishes a divine principle that Allah's methodology of rewarding excellence and righteous conduct is consistent and universal across time and circumstances. It indicates that anyone who perfects their faith through sincere worship, moral conduct, and compassionate treatment of others will receive Allah's recompense, which may manifest as protection from harm, relief from difficulty, spiritual elevation, or ultimate salvation. The verse reinforces that divine justice operates on merit and that doing good (ihsan) - whether in worship by serving Allah as if seeing Him, or in dealings by benefiting His creation - inevitably attracts divine favor and positive outcomes in this life or the hereafter.

translation: Indeed, he was of Our believing servants.
interpretation: This verse serves as divine testimony and certification of a servant's faith and righteousness. It indicates that true faith is not merely a claim or outward appearance, but a status confirmed by Allah Himself based on genuine belief and sincere devotion. The statement emphasizes that being counted among 'Our believing servants' is an honor bestowed by Allah, reflecting that the individual fulfilled the covenant of faith, maintained loyalty to Allah, and embodied the qualities of true servitude. This divine acknowledgment also serves as a model for believers, showing that ultimate success lies not in worldly achievements but in attaining Allah's recognition as one of His faithful servants. The verse underscores that faith must be internalized and lived, transforming a person's character and actions, such that Allah Himself bears witness to their status as a believer.

translation: And We gave him good tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.
interpretation: This verse highlights the divine fulfillment of promise and the concept of prophetic lineage. The good news of Isaac represents God's mercy and His pattern of selecting messengers from righteous households. The announcement that Isaac would be both a prophet and among the righteous indicates that prophethood is not merely hereditary but requires personal righteousness and moral excellence. This demonstrates that divine favor manifests through generations when maintained by virtue, and that God's promises to His faithful servants extend beyond their own lives to their descendants, establishing a continuity of guidance and blessing.

translation: And We blessed him and Isaac. But among their descendants are some who do good and some who clearly wrong themselves.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine principle that righteousness is not inherited through lineage but earned through individual choice and action. Despite being descendants of blessed prophets Abraham and Isaac, each person bears personal responsibility for their deeds. The mention of both the righteous (muhsin) and the self-wronging (zalim) among their progeny demonstrates that prophetic ancestry does not guarantee salvation, nor does it predetermine one's moral character. This serves as a warning against relying solely on noble heritage while neglecting personal accountability, and emphasizes that faith and good deeds must be actively cultivated by each individual regardless of their ancestral blessings.

translation: And We certainly bestowed favor upon Moses and Aaron.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's divine grace and favor upon two of His greatest prophets, Moses and Aaron. The use of 'manna' (bestowed favor) indicates that their prophethood, their brotherhood in mission, their deliverance from Pharaoh, and their guidance of the Israelites were all acts of divine mercy and blessing, not earned through their own power but granted by Allah's will. It reminds believers that all positions of leadership and spiritual authority in Allah's service are ultimately gifts from Him, requiring gratitude and proper stewardship rather than pride or self-aggrandizement.

translation: And We saved them both and their people from the great distress.
interpretation: This verse highlights Allah's divine intervention and mercy in delivering prophets and their followers from severe trials and persecution. The 'great distress' refers to the overwhelming affliction they faced from their opposing communities, demonstrating that those who remain steadfast in faith and follow divine guidance will ultimately be granted relief and victory by Allah. It serves as a reminder that no matter how insurmountable worldly difficulties may appear, Allah's power to rescue and protect His faithful servants is absolute, and that patient perseverance in the face of adversity is rewarded with divine deliverance.

translation: And We supported them, so they became the victors.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine principle that true victory comes from Allah's support rather than human strength alone. It emphasizes that when Allah grants His assistance to those who follow His guidance and remain steadfast in their mission, success becomes inevitable regardless of the apparent odds. The verse teaches believers that worldly power and numbers are secondary to divine favor, and that those who align themselves with Allah's will and trust in His aid will ultimately prevail over their adversaries. It serves as both a historical reminder of past nations who received Allah's help and a promise to future believers that divine support ensures triumph for the righteous.

translation: And We gave them both the clear Scripture.
interpretation: This verse refers to Allah granting Moses and Aaron the Torah, which served as a clear and manifest divine guidance for the Children of Israel. The description of the Scripture as 'al-mustabeen' (the clear/manifest) emphasizes that it was not ambiguous or obscure, but rather a book whose truth, divine origin, and commandments were evident and unmistakable to those who received it. This clarity made the recipients accountable for following its teachings, as they could not claim ignorance or confusion about what was required of them. The verse highlights Allah's mercy in providing unambiguous guidance through His prophets, removing any excuse for deviation from the straight path.

translation: And We guided them to the straight path.
interpretation: This verse indicates that divine guidance is a gift bestowed by Allah upon His chosen servants. The 'straight path' (al-sirat al-mustaqim) refers to the path of monotheism, righteousness, and obedience to Allah's commands. The use of 'guided them' emphasizes that true guidance comes from Allah alone, and that the prophets mentioned in context were granted this divine guidance as a means to fulfill their missions and serve as examples for humanity. This guidance encompasses both knowledge of the truth and the ability to act upon it, demonstrating that intellectual understanding and practical application are inseparable in the Islamic conception of guidance.

translation: And We left for them [favorable mention] among later generations.
interpretation: This verse indicates that Allah preserved the honorable memory and legacy of these righteous individuals throughout subsequent generations, establishing them as exemplary figures whose stories would be recounted with praise and reverence. The divine preservation of their good reputation serves as a reward for their steadfastness in faith and obedience, demonstrating that those who fulfill their covenant with Allah will be remembered favorably by humanity across time, their noble deeds becoming part of the collective moral consciousness that guides future believers toward righteousness.

translation: Peace be upon Moses and Aaron.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates Allah's recognition and honoring of His prophets Moses and Aaron by bestowing peace upon them, acknowledging their faithfulness in delivering the divine message and their perseverance in facing Pharaoh's tyranny. The invocation of peace signifies divine approval of their prophetic mission and serves as a model for believers to honor and respect God's messengers, while also illustrating that those who fulfill their covenant with Allah will receive His eternal blessing and commendation.

translation: Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse establishes a divine principle of reciprocity between righteous action and divine reward. It emphasizes that God's system of justice ensures that those who perform acts of excellence and goodness (ihsan) in their faith, worship, and dealings with others will receive proportionate recompense from Allah. The use of 'thus' indicates that the reward mentioned in the preceding context serves as an example of God's consistent pattern of honoring those who strive for moral and spiritual excellence, reinforcing the motivation for believers to pursue ihsan in all aspects of life.

translation: Indeed, they both were among Our believing servants.
interpretation: This verse affirms the righteous status of two individuals in the sight of Allah, emphasizing that true faith is demonstrated through sincere servitude and devotion to God. It highlights the divine recognition and approval of those who maintain steadfast belief and worship, regardless of worldly trials or circumstances they may face. The phrase serves as both a commendation of their faith and a testament to the eternal principle that Allah acknowledges and honors those who remain committed to Him as His believing servants, distinguishing them from others who may have wavered or rejected faith.

translation: And indeed, Elias was from among the messengers.
interpretation: This verse affirms the prophethood of Elias (Elijah) and his inclusion among the chosen messengers sent by Allah to guide humanity. It establishes his legitimate status as a divinely appointed prophet, emphasizing the continuity of Allah's guidance through various prophets across different times and peoples. By mentioning Elias specifically, the Qur'an validates the prophetic tradition that spans beyond the Arabian context, connecting the message of Islam to earlier revelations and demonstrating that Allah's messengers were sent to all nations throughout history.

translation: When he said to his people, 'Will you not fear Allah?'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the prophetic duty to call one's community to conscious awareness of God and accountability. The rhetorical question 'Will you not fear Allah?' serves as both an invitation and a warning, appealing to the innate human capacity for moral discernment. The prophet's approach demonstrates that genuine faith begins with taqwa—a reverential consciousness that guards against wrongdoing—and that religious guidance must be directed toward one's immediate community before extending outward. The use of a question rather than a command reflects the respect for human free will while simultaneously highlighting the urgency and obviousness of the moral choice being presented.

translation: Do you call upon Ba'l and leave the best of creators?
interpretation: This verse criticizes the illogical nature of idolatry by highlighting the absurdity of invoking a powerless deity (Ba'l, a Canaanite storm god) while abandoning Allah, who is supreme in His creative power and perfection. It emphasizes that turning to false gods when the True Creator exists is both intellectually inconsistent and spiritually destructive, as these idols possess no divine attributes and cannot fulfill the needs that only the Supreme Creator can address. The verse appeals to human reason, suggesting that worshipping anything other than the ultimate source of creation is fundamentally irrational.

translation: Allah is your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers.
interpretation: This verse establishes the continuity of divine lordship across generations, emphasizing that Allah's sovereignty is not a new concept but has been the fundamental truth since the beginning of human existence. It serves to remind believers that their submission to Allah connects them to a timeless tradition of monotheism that predates them, while simultaneously challenging those who follow ancestral traditions blindly. The verse underscores that true heritage and lineage in faith trace back to the same singular divine authority, making devotion to Allah both a personal commitment and participation in an ancient covenant that transcends temporal and familial boundaries.

translation: Then they denied him, so indeed, they will surely be brought [for punishment].
interpretation: This verse establishes the principle of divine accountability, warning that those who reject the messengers of God will inevitably face the consequences of their disbelief. The certainty expressed through the emphatic structure indicates that denial of divine guidance does not grant immunity from judgment, but rather guarantees one's presence before God's tribunal, where the truth they rejected will be made manifest and they will be held to account for their rejection of the messenger sent to guide them.

translation: Except the sincere servants of Allah
interpretation: This verse emphasizes divine protection and salvation for those who have achieved true sincerity (ikhlas) in their devotion to God. The term 'mukhlasin' refers to those whom God has purified and chosen, indicating that genuine servanthood and exclusive dedication to Allah serves as a shield against spiritual corruption, satanic influence, and divine punishment. It establishes that sincerity in worship and intention is the distinguishing characteristic that separates the saved from the lost, suggesting that outward actions alone are insufficient without the inner purity of devotion that makes one truly belong to God.

translation: And We left for him [favorable mention] among later generations.
interpretation: This verse establishes the divine practice of preserving honorable remembrance and legacy for righteous figures throughout history. It indicates that Allah ensures that those who fulfill His mission and remain steadfast in faith will be commemorated positively by subsequent generations, their good reputation enduring as a form of divine reward and as a source of guidance for future believers. This eternal praise serves both as recognition of their sacrifice and as an inspiration for others to follow their example of righteousness and submission to God's will.

translation: Peace be upon the family of Yasin.
interpretation: This verse extends divine peace and blessings upon the household or followers of Yasin, which is understood by many classical commentators to refer to Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), as Yasin is one of his names mentioned in the Qur'an. The phrase emphasizes God's favor and protection upon the prophetic lineage and those connected to the prophetic message. It reflects the honor bestowed upon prophets and their righteous families, and serves as a reminder of the continuity of divine guidance through prophetic households. Some scholars also interpret 'Al Yasin' as referring to the Prophet Elias (Elijah) and his family, indicating God's recognition and blessing of those who uphold His message across different prophetic traditions.

translation: Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse establishes a divine principle of reciprocity and justice in Allah's governance, affirming that excellence in faith and conduct invariably receives divine recompense.
