The true and eternal reward—the Hereafter—is reserved exclusively for those who are conscious of God and live righteously. It serves as a spiritual admonition against placing ultimate value on material accumulation, redirecting focus toward cultivating taqwa (God-consciousness) and righteous deeds that secure everlasting success in the Hereafter, which holds infinitely greater worth than any worldly treasure.

translation: And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful - We appoint for him a devil, and he is to him a companion.
interpretation: This verse establishes a spiritual law: when a person willfully blinds themselves to God's remembrance and guidance, they create a vacuum in their soul that becomes filled by demonic influence. The 'turning away' (ya'shu) implies a deliberate closing of one's inner eye to divine truth. God's response is not arbitrary punishment but rather the natural consequence of this choice - He assigns (nuqayyid) a devil as a constant companion (qarin). This companionship represents the complete spiritual darkness that befalls those who reject divine guidance; the devil becomes their intimate associate, leading them further astray and making them perceive falsehood as truth. The verse warns that abandoning remembrance of God doesn't result in neutral indifference, but actively opens one to satanic influence that reinforces and perpetuates their state of heedlessness, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of spiritual blindness.

translation: And indeed, they avert them from the way [of Allah] while they think that they are [rightly] guided.
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound spiritual deception that occurs when devils or misguided influences lead people astray from the true path. The tragedy lies not merely in the deviation itself, but in the fact that those being led astray remain utterly convinced of their righteousness. This speaks to how deeply corruption can penetrate the human heart and mind—when one's moral compass becomes so inverted that evil appears as good and misguidance as guidance. It warns of the danger of spiritual complacency and the importance of constantly seeking authentic guidance, as the most dangerous error is the one we don't recognize as error at all.

translation: Until, when he comes to Us [on the Day of Judgment], he will say [to his companion from Satan], 'Oh, I wish there was between me and you the distance between the two easts [i.e., the greatest possible distance]! What a wretched companion!'
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound regret of those who followed their evil companions and satanic influences in the worldly life, showing that the relationships built upon misguidance and sin will transform into bitter enmity and remorse on the Day of Resurrection. The companion who once seemed appealing and persuasive in leading one astray becomes the source of greatest anguish, as the misguided person realizes the irreversible consequences of having heeded such companionship. It warns believers to carefully choose their companions and influences in this life, as the bonds formed through righteousness lead to eternal joy, while those formed through corruption lead to mutual blame and the desire for maximum separation when the truth becomes manifest.

translation: And it will not benefit you that Day, since you were unjust, that you are [all] sharing in the punishment.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who wronged themselves through disbelief and sin, informing them that on the Day of Judgment, finding others suffering the same punishment will provide no comfort or relief. The shared nature of their torment offers no consolation because each soul bears the full weight of its own accountability before God. The verse emphasizes that collective suffering does not diminish individual responsibility or make the punishment easier to bear, refuting any false hope that misery loves company or that shared consequences somehow lessen one's personal anguish or guilt.

translation: Can you then make the deaf hear, or guide the blind and those who are in manifest error?
interpretation: This verse employs a powerful rhetorical question to emphasize the limitations of the Prophet's role and the fundamental principle of divine guidance. The metaphors of deafness and blindness represent spiritual incapacity rather than physical disabilities - those who willfully close their hearts and minds to the truth cannot be forced to accept it, no matter how eloquent or persistent the messenger. The verse establishes that guidance ultimately comes from Allah alone, and the Prophet's responsibility is only to convey the message clearly, not to compel belief. It serves as both a consolation to the Prophet regarding those who reject his message and a reminder to believers that true faith requires an open heart and sincere seeking, which cannot be imposed externally but must come from within through divine enablement.

translation: And whether We take you away [in death], indeed We will take retribution upon them.
interpretation: This verse reassures the Prophet Muhammad that divine justice will inevitably prevail regardless of whether he lives to witness it. It establishes that God's retribution against those who reject the message is not contingent upon the Prophet's physical presence, emphasizing that divine will operates independently of human lifespans. The verse serves to comfort the Prophet during times of opposition and persecution, affirming that his mission's success and the accountability of disbelievers rest entirely in God's hands, liberating him from anxiety about outcomes beyond his control.

translation: Or We show you that which We have promised them, for indeed, We are fully capable over them.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute power and sovereignty over all creation, particularly those who deny His message. It presents two possibilities: either the Prophet will witness in his lifetime the fulfillment of divine promises of punishment and accountability upon the disbelievers, or he may pass away before seeing it. Regardless of timing, the certainty of Allah's ability to execute His will remains unquestionable. The verse serves as both a warning to those who reject faith and a reassurance to believers that divine justice will prevail, whether immediately observable or not. It highlights that Allah's power transcends human limitations of time and perception, and that His promises are inevitable regardless of whether any particular generation witnesses their fulfillment.

translation: So hold fast to that which has been revealed to you. Indeed, you are upon a straight path.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet Muhammad to remain steadfast and unwavering in adhering to the divine revelation he has received, despite any opposition or doubt from others. The command to 'hold fast' implies both internal conviction and external practice, suggesting that commitment to revealed truth requires active, determined effort rather than passive acceptance. The affirmation that he is 'upon a straight path' serves as divine reassurance that this adherence to revelation leads to ultimate truth and success, providing psychological and spiritual fortification against challenges. This establishes a model for all believers that steadfastness in faith, particularly during trials, is both a duty and a source of guidance, and that God's revelation serves as the objective criterion for distinguishing right guidance from error.

translation: And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people, and you will be questioned.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the Qur'an's role as a source of honor and remembrance for the Prophet Muhammad and his community, the Arabs who received it in their language. The phrase 'you will be questioned' serves as a profound warning that both the Prophet and his people bear a special responsibility for this divine message—they will be held accountable for how they received it, preserved it, acted upon it, and conveyed it to others. The questioning implies that receiving divine guidance is not merely a privilege but carries weighty obligations, and those who are given such honor must answer for their stewardship of this trust on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And ask those We sent before you of Our messengers: Have We made besides the Most Merciful gods to be worshipped?
interpretation: This verse establishes the continuity and consistency of divine revelation across all prophetic missions. God challenges anyone to examine the messages of previous prophets and messengers to verify that monotheism has been the unwavering core of every divine message throughout history. The rhetorical question implies that no authentic prophet ever called people to worship deities other than the One God, the Most Merciful. This serves as proof of the universal truth of Islamic monotheism and validates Muhammad's message by showing its harmony with all prior revelations. It also refutes any claims that different prophets brought contradictory messages regarding the nature of God and worship, demonstrating that polytheism has never had divine sanction in any authentic prophetic tradition.

translation: And certainly We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, and he said: 'Indeed, I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse establishes the universal authority that Moses claimed when confronting temporal power. By identifying himself as messenger of 'the Lord of the worlds' rather than merely 'the Lord of the Israelites,' Moses was asserting that divine sovereignty transcends all human hierarchies and ethnic boundaries. This universal claim directly challenged Pharaoh's pretension to absolute authority within his realm, revealing that true prophethood does not accommodate itself to the limited worldview of rulers but rather calls them to recognize a higher accountability. The mention of 'signs' accompanying Moses indicates that divine authority comes with evidential proof, not mere assertion, teaching that faith rooted in revelation is supported by reason and demonstration.

translation: So when he came to them with Our signs, at once they laughed at them.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the hardness of heart and spiritual blindness that can afflict those who reject divine guidance. The laughter represents not mere amusement but a dismissive arrogance and mockery toward Allah's clear proofs, demonstrating how pride and obstinacy can prevent people from recognizing truth even when it is manifestly presented to them. Their immediate ridicule reveals that their rejection was not based on lack of evidence but rather on their unwillingness to submit to the truth, choosing instead to treat sacred signs with contempt. This serves as a warning against allowing worldly attachments and hubris to corrupt one's ability to discern and accept divine revelation.

translation: And We showed them not a sign except that it was greater than its sister, and We seized them with suffering so that perhaps they might return.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the progressive nature of divine revelation and warning, where each sign or miracle sent to the disbelievers surpassed the previous one in magnitude and clarity, leaving them with no excuse for denial. The affliction mentioned served a redemptive purpose - not as mere punishment, but as a corrective measure intended to awaken consciousness and prompt repentance. It reflects the divine mercy that even in chastisement, the ultimate aim is to guide humanity back to the truth, demonstrating that God's justice is always coupled with an opportunity for return and reformation.

translation: And they said, 'O magician, invoke your Lord for us by what He has promised you. Indeed, we will be guided.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the irony of the disbelievers' situation when afflicted with punishment - they acknowledge Moses' connection to God and seek his intercession, yet still call him 'magician' out of stubbornness and pride. Their promise to be guided is shown to be insincere, as they repeatedly broke such promises when relief came. This demonstrates how hardship can temporarily soften hearts, but without true faith, such repentance is fleeting and conditional, highlighting the difference between genuine submission to God and mere desperation in times of crisis.

translation: Then when We removed the punishment from them, at once they broke their promise.
interpretation: This verse illustrates a recurring human weakness: the tendency to quickly forget divine warnings and return to previous patterns of disobedience once relief is granted. It demonstrates that trials and afflictions are meant to produce lasting repentance and reformation, yet some people respond only superficially to hardship. The immediate breach of their covenant upon the removal of suffering reveals that their supplications during distress were born of desperation rather than genuine faith or sincere commitment to change. This serves as a warning about the importance of maintaining gratitude and obedience to God in times of ease, not merely seeking Him during calamity, and highlights the spiritual disease of taking God's mercy for granted.

translation: And Pharaoh called out among his people; he said, 'O my people, does not the kingdom of Egypt belong to me, and these rivers flowing beneath me; then do you not see?'
interpretation: This verse reveals the essence of tyrannical pride and the delusion of earthly power. Pharaoh's rhetorical questions demonstrate how material dominance can blind a person to the reality of their servitude to the Creator. His appeal to visible, tangible power—the kingdom and rivers—represents the mistake of equating worldly control with ultimate authority. The verse teaches that when humans claim absolute sovereignty and demand recognition based solely on material possessions, they have fallen into the gravest spiritual error. Pharaoh's 'do you not see?' is deeply ironic, for he himself is blind to the true nature of existence, mistaking temporary stewardship for eternal ownership, and using physical evidence to deny metaphysical truth. This illustrates how wealth and power, rather than bringing enlightenment, can actually veil the heart from recognizing the only true Sovereign.

translation: Or am I not better than this one who is insignificant and can hardly express himself clearly?
interpretation: This verse reflects Pharaoh's arrogant dismissal of Prophet Moses, highlighting the corrupting nature of worldly power and status. Pharaoh's contempt stems from Moses's speech impediment and lack of material wealth or political authority compared to his own position. This demonstrates how tyrants measure worth by external attributes rather than moral character or divine appointment. The verse serves as a warning against judging messengers of truth by worldly standards and illustrates how pride blinds individuals to recognizing genuine guidance. It also shows that Allah often chooses humble servants to deliver His message, testing whether people will respond to truth itself or be distracted by superficial considerations of wealth and eloquence.

translation: Why then have bracelets of gold not been bestowed upon him, or why have angels not come with him in conjunction?
interpretation: This verse reflects the materialistic and superficial criteria by which the disbelievers judged prophethood and divine messengership. They demanded outward signs of worldly power and status—golden bracelets being symbols of kingship and authority in ancient cultures, and angels as visible supernatural proof—failing to recognize that true prophethood is validated by the message itself, moral character, and divine signs of a different nature. It exposes how people often reject spiritual truth when it doesn't conform to their preconceived notions of how divine authority should manifest, preferring worldly pomp over spiritual substance.

translation: So he bluffed his people, and they obeyed him. Indeed, they were a people defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse illustrates how a leader's manipulation succeeds not merely through his deceptive tactics, but because of the moral corruption already present within the people themselves. Their obedience to falsehood stems from their pre-existing state of transgression and departure from truth, suggesting that a community's susceptibility to tyranny is directly proportional to its spiritual and moral decline. It warns that when people abandon righteousness, they become vulnerable to being led astray by those who exploit their weaknesses.

translation: So when they angered Us, We took retribution from them and drowned them all.
interpretation: This verse reveals a profound principle about divine justice: that God's punishment is not arbitrary but rather a response to human transgression that crosses certain boundaries. The verse emphasizes collective accountability when a society persists in defiance and rejection of divine guidance. The drowning mentioned refers to Pharaoh and his people, demonstrating that worldly power offers no protection against divine decree. It teaches that God's forbearance has limits, and when a people's arrogance and oppression reach a point where they 'anger' the Divine—meaning they exhaust all opportunities for repentance—divine justice manifests decisively. The comprehensive nature of their destruction ('all of them') underscores that those who align themselves with tyranny and oppose truth share in the consequences, serving as an eternal warning against collective injustice and the rejection of prophetic messages.

translation: And We made them a precedent and an example for later generations.
interpretation: This verse indicates that those who were punished in the past serve a dual purpose in divine wisdom: they become both a historical precedent establishing God's pattern of dealing with wrongdoers, and a cautionary example meant to deter future generations from following similar paths of disobedience. The simultaneous use of 'precedent' and 'example' emphasizes that their fate is not merely historical record but carries ongoing moral instruction, warning believers that divine justice operates consistently across time and that the consequences of transgression are real and repeatable for those who ignore these lessons.

translation: And when the son of Mary was presented as an example, immediately your people laughed aloud.
interpretation: This verse addresses the reaction of the Quraysh when the Qur'an mentions Jesus (Isa), son of Mary, as a righteous prophet and servant of Allah. Their loud laughter and rejection stems from their cognitive dissonance - they revere Jesus yet reject Muhammad, despite both being prophets calling to the same monotheistic truth. The verse exposes how people can be selective in accepting divine guidance based on tribal loyalty and prejudice rather than rational consistency, showing that their objection to Muhammad's message is not rooted in genuine theological reasoning but in stubbornness and social conformity to their ancestral practices.

translation: And they said, 'Are our gods better or is he?' They did not present it to you except for argument. Rather, they are a people disposed to disputation.
interpretation: This verse reveals the spiritual blindness that arises from obstinate attachment to falsehood. The disbelievers' question comparing their lifeless idols to a prophet of God demonstrates that their rejection stems not from genuine intellectual inquiry but from argumentativeness and pride. When people are deeply invested in inherited traditions or social status tied to false beliefs, they engage in rhetorical games rather than sincere truth-seeking. The verse teaches that some debates are not motivated by a desire for guidance but by a competitive spirit to defend one's position at all costs, and such disputatiousness becomes a veil preventing recognition of divine truth.

translation: He is not but a servant upon whom We bestowed favor, and We made him an example for the Children of Israel.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the human nature of Jesus (peace be upon him), clarifying that despite the miracles and elevated status granted to him, he remains fundamentally a created servant of God. The verse corrects excessive veneration by reminding that Jesus was a recipient of divine grace rather than divine himself, and his life was intended as a sign and model of servanthood and prophethood specifically for the Israelites. It establishes the proper Islamic perspective that honors Jesus as a distinguished prophet while firmly rejecting any notion of divinity or sonship attributed to him, reinforcing the absolute oneness of God and the creatureliness of all messengers.

translation: And if We willed, We could have made [angels] from among you, succeeding [one another] on the earth.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute power and sovereignty over His creation, reminding humanity that their existence in its current form is by divine choice rather than necessity. The reference to angels replacing humans on earth serves as a humbling reminder that human stewardship of the earth is a privilege granted by God, not an inherent right. It underscores that Allah does not need humanity for the continuation of worship or the fulfillment of His cosmic plan, as He could easily have appointed angels as successors or inhabitants of the earth instead. This realization should instill gratitude, responsibility, and awareness of the unique position humans hold as moral agents with free will, unlike angels who have no choice but to obey, making human devotion more meaningful precisely because it is chosen rather than compelled.

translation: And indeed, he is a sign for the Hour, so do not doubt it and follow Me. This is a straight path.
interpretation: This verse refers to Jesus (peace be upon him) as a sign of the approaching Day of Judgment. His second coming before the end of times will serve as one of the major indicators that the Hour is near. The command to 'follow Me' is Allah's instruction to humanity to follow His guidance through the prophets and divine revelation. The 'straight path' represents the religion of truth that leads to salvation, characterized by submission to Allah's will and adherence to His commandments. The verse emphasizes certainty in the eschatological role of Jesus and the importance of following divine guidance without doubt or hesitation.

translation: And let not Satan avert you. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine warning against allowing Satan to distract believers from the path of righteousness and obedience to God. It emphasizes that Satan's enmity is not hidden or ambiguous but rather manifest and evident through his constant efforts to lead people astray from worship, good deeds, and spiritual growth. The verse calls believers to maintain vigilance and recognize that any temptation, doubt, or obstacle that diverts them from their religious duties and moral obligations ultimately originates from this clear adversary. By acknowledging Satan as an open enemy, believers are reminded to fortify themselves through faith, mindfulness, and seeking refuge in God against his whispers and deceptions that aim to corrupt their hearts and actions.

translation: And when Jesus came with clear proofs, he said, 'I have come to you with wisdom and to make clear to you some of that concerning which you differ. So fear Allah and obey me.'
interpretation: This verse highlights the role of divine messengers as clarifiers of religious disputes and guides toward truth. Jesus's mission was not merely to present new teachings, but to resolve existing disagreements among the people through divinely granted wisdom. The call to 'fear Allah and obey me' establishes that true resolution of religious differences comes through submission to God and acceptance of His messenger's authority. It suggests that human disputes often arise from deviation from divine guidance, and that prophets serve as arbiters who redirect communities back to the straight path through their God-given insight and clarification.

translation: Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.
interpretation: This verse establishes the fundamental principle of pure monotheism (Tawhid) by calling all people to recognize Allah's universal lordship and directing worship exclusively to Him. The statement 'my Lord and your Lord' emphasizes the shared obligation between the Prophet and his community, removing any intermediary and affirming direct relationship with the Divine. The command to worship Allah alone is presented as 'the straight path' (sirat mustaqim), indicating that true guidance and salvation lie in recognizing Allah's sovereignty and submitting to Him without associating partners, which constitutes the essence of Islamic belief and the core message delivered by all prophets throughout human history.

translation: But the sects differed among themselves, so woe to those who wronged themselves from the punishment of a painful day.
interpretation: This verse warns against religious discord and sectarian division among believers who should be united in their faith. The 'parties' or 'sects' mentioned refer to those who split into factions over religious matters, particularly regarding the truth of divine revelation and prophethood. The severe warning of 'woe' and 'painful punishment' is directed at those who wrong themselves through this divisiveness, as they abandon the unified truth for partisan interests, personal desires, or misguided interpretations. The verse emphasizes that sectarian division is itself a form of injustice (zulm) because it fragments the community, distorts the original message, and leads people away from the straight path, making those who instigate or persist in such divisions liable to divine punishment on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Are they waiting except for the Hour to come upon them suddenly while they perceive not?
interpretation: This verse serves as a stark warning against complacency and heedlessness in spiritual matters. It criticizes those who delay repentance and righteous action, living as though the Day of Judgment is a distant or uncertain event. The rhetorical question implies that disbelievers and the heedless are passively waiting without preparation, unaware that death and resurrection will arrive unexpectedly. The verse emphasizes the urgency of faith and good deeds, reminding believers that the Final Hour will strike without warning, catching the unprepared in a state of spiritual negligence. It calls for constant vigilance, mindfulness of one's mortality, and readiness to meet one's Lord at any moment, as the timing of death remains hidden from human knowledge.

translation: Friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except for the righteous.
interpretation: This verse reveals the fragility of worldly relationships built on foundations other than God-consciousness and righteousness. On the Day of Judgment, bonds formed through shared sins, material interests, or mutual corruption will transform into enmity, as former companions will blame each other for leading one another astray or for wasting opportunities for repentance. Each soul will be solely concerned with its own salvation, making previous alliances meaningless or even detrimental. The exception of the righteous (al-muttaqin) demonstrates that only relationships founded on taqwa—God-consciousness and mutual encouragement toward goodness—will endure beyond this life. True friendship is that which draws people closer to their Creator and encourages virtue, for such bonds are purified of selfish motives and will be rewarded with eternal companionship in Paradise. This serves as a criterion for evaluating one's relationships in this life: Do they bring one closer to God or further away?

translation: O My servants, no fear shall be upon you this Day, nor shall you grieve.
interpretation: This verse represents Allah's direct address to His righteous servants on the Day of Judgment, offering them divine reassurance and comfort. The interpretation emphasizes that those who have lived in true servitude to Allah, submitting to His will and following His guidance, will be granted complete security and tranquility in the Hereafter. The negation of both fear and grief indicates a comprehensive state of peace - they will neither fear what lies ahead nor grieve over what they left behind in the worldly life. This divine promise serves as encouragement for believers to remain steadfast in their worship and righteous deeds, knowing that their ultimate destination will be one of absolute serenity and divine pleasure, free from all forms of anxiety or sorrow that characterize human existence in the temporal world.

translation: Those who believed in Our signs and were Muslims (submitting to Allah).
interpretation: This verse establishes the criteria for those who will be rewarded by Allah: sincere belief in His revelations combined with complete submission to His will. The conjunction of faith (iman) and Islam (submission) indicates that true belief must manifest in practical surrender to divine commandment. It emphasizes that mere intellectual acknowledgment is insufficient without the accompanying state of willing obedience and wholehearted devotion to Allah's guidance, suggesting that authentic faith produces submission as its natural consequence.

translation: Enter Paradise, you and your spouses, rejoicing.
interpretation: This verse represents the ultimate fulfillment of divine promise, where believers are granted entry into Paradise not in isolation but accompanied by their spouses, emphasizing the preservation and elevation of righteous relationships in the afterlife. The word 'tuhbarun' (rejoicing/delighted) indicates a state of complete felicity and honor, suggesting that Paradise is not merely an absence of suffering but an active state of joy and celebration. This companionship in Paradise reflects the Islamic understanding that human bonds formed in righteousness on earth are valued by God and transcend worldly existence, and that the pleasure of Paradise is enhanced through sharing it with loved ones. The collective address 'you and your spouses' also implies that salvation and divine reward encompass both partners who supported each other in faith, indicating that spiritual partnership in worldly life merits eternal companionship in the hereafter.

translation: They will be served with trays of gold and cups, and therein is whatever the souls desire and the eyes delight in, and you will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: This verse describes the eternal blessings of Paradise, emphasizing that the rewards transcend mere physical luxuries. While gold vessels symbolize the nobility and honor bestowed upon the believers, the true essence lies in the complete fulfillment of every spiritual and emotional longing. The phrase 'whatever the souls desire and the eyes delight in' indicates that Paradise offers satisfaction at the deepest level of human nature—not just temporary pleasure, but absolute contentment where every noble wish is perpetually realized. The permanence ('you will abide therein eternally') underscores that unlike worldly pleasures which fade, these divine gifts are everlasting, reflecting God's infinite mercy and the ultimate purpose of human existence: eternal communion with the Divine through complete felicity.

translation: And that is Paradise which you have been made to inherit because of what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the principle of divine justice and reward, illustrating that entrance into Paradise is granted as an inheritance earned through righteous deeds performed in worldly life. The use of 'inheritance' suggests that believers receive Paradise as their rightful due, much like an heir receives their patrimony, indicating that their good actions have established their claim to it. This frames salvation not as arbitrary grace alone but as the fruition of faithful obedience and moral conduct, reinforcing the Qur'anic teaching that faith must be accompanied by works, and that human beings bear responsibility for their choices and actions which ultimately determine their eternal destiny.

translation: For you therein is much fruit from which you will eat.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the blessings of Paradise, emphasizing the abundance and variety of sustenance Allah has prepared for the believers. The phrase 'much fruit' signifies not only plenty but also diversity, indicating that the inhabitants of Paradise will have unlimited access to various types of fruits according to their desires. The use of 'from which you eat' suggests both the permissibility and the pleasure derived from these provisions, highlighting that in Paradise, believers will enjoy pure, wholesome sustenance without any harm, deficiency, or eventual depletion. This verse reassures believers that their ultimate reward includes complete satisfaction of both physical and spiritual needs, reflecting Allah's generosity and mercy toward those who attain His pleasure.

translation: Indeed, the criminals will be in the punishment of Hell, abiding eternally therein.
interpretation: This verse establishes the permanent consequence of willful rejection of divine guidance and persistent sinfulness. The term 'criminals' (mujrimun) refers to those who deliberately transgressed moral and spiritual boundaries, denying truth despite receiving clear signs. The perpetual nature of their punishment reflects the gravity of conscious rebellion against God and the metaphysical reality that spiritual corruption, when entrenched and unrepented, creates a state incompatible with divine mercy's full manifestation. The eternal abiding indicates that such souls have fundamentally shaped themselves into beings whose very essence has become aligned with separation from God, making their state self-perpetuating rather than merely externally imposed.

translation: It will not be lightened for them, and they therein are in despair.
interpretation: This verse describes the eternal and unrelenting nature of the punishment in Hell for its inhabitants. The phrase 'it will not be lightened' emphasizes that there will be no respite, reduction, or temporary relief from the torment they endure. The state of 'mublis' (despair) indicates a complete hopelessness and utter desperation, where the disbelievers realize the finality of their situation with no possibility of escape or redemption. This serves as a warning about the consequences of rejection of faith and divine guidance, illustrating that divine justice, once executed, is permanent for those who persistently denied the truth in their worldly life. The verse underscores the theological principle that while God's mercy is vast in this world, there comes a point of no return in the Hereafter for those who died in a state of disbelief.

translation: And We did not wrong them, but it was they who were the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse establishes divine justice by affirming that any punishment or calamity that befell certain people was not due to injustice from Allah, but rather a direct consequence of their own transgression and wrongdoing. It emphasizes the principle of divine accountability, where Allah never oppresses His creation, and any negative outcome they face is self-inflicted through their own choices, rebellion, or disbelief. The verse shifts responsibility entirely onto those who suffered consequences, making clear that they brought destruction upon themselves through their persistence in wrongdoing despite warnings and guidance.

translation: And they will call, 'O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us!' He will say, 'Indeed, you will remain.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the eternal nature of divine justice and the irreversible consequences of disbelief. The residents of Hell appeal to Malik, the guardian of Hellfire, seeking annihilation as an escape from their torment, but are informed they must remain indefinitely. This demonstrates that the punishment is not arbitrary cruelty but rather the natural and permanent state resulting from their rejection of truth in the worldly life. The delay in Malik's response—traditionally understood as lasting a thousand years—emphasizes both their desperation and the reality that no intercession or escape exists for those who persistently denied God's signs. It serves as a stark warning that the choices made in this life have permanent metaphysical consequences, and that divine justice, once enacted, cannot be negotiated or abbreviated.

translation: We have brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth.
interpretation: This verse addresses the natural human tendency to resist divine guidance when it conflicts with personal desires, established customs, or worldly interests. The aversion to truth mentioned here is not due to lack of clarity in the message, but rather stems from the difficulty people face in accepting what challenges their lifestyle, beliefs, or status quo. It highlights that rejection of truth often has psychological and moral roots rather than intellectual ones - people turn away not because the truth is unclear, but because accepting it would require uncomfortable change, sacrifice, or admission of error. This speaks to the broader Quranic theme that guidance alone is insufficient without the willingness of the heart to receive it.

translation: Or have they resolved upon a matter? Then indeed, We are resolving.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who plot and scheme against the truth or the Prophet's message. It serves as a divine warning that whatever plans the disbelievers devise in opposition to God's will, Allah has already decreed His own plan which will prevail. The rhetorical question emphasizes the futility of human plotting against divine decree, as God's resolution is absolute and cannot be thwarted. It reassures believers that attempts to undermine faith or harm the righteous will ultimately fail because God's counter-plan is already in motion and supremely effective.

translation: Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private conversations? Yes [We do], and Our messengers are with them recording.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's complete and perfect knowledge of all things, including the hidden thoughts, secret plans, and private conversations of people. It serves as a warning to those who may believe they can conceal their schemes or inner intentions from Allah. The reference to 'Our messengers' (angels) recording everything reinforces the concept of divine accountability and the comprehensive documentation of human deeds. This acts as both a deterrent against wrongdoing in private and a reminder that no action or word escapes Allah's knowledge, regardless of how secretly it is conducted. The verse challenges the false sense of security that disbelievers or hypocrites might have in thinking their hidden plots against truth or their concealed disbelief goes unnoticed by the Divine.

translation: Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers.
interpretation: This verse employs a hypothetical conditional statement to emphatically reject the notion that God has offspring. The Prophet is instructed to declare that even if such an impossibility were true, he would be foremost in worshipping that son. However, the underlying message is that this condition is inherently false and impossible, as God's transcendent nature is incompatible with having children or progeny. The verse uses this rhetorical device to affirm the absolute oneness and uniqueness of God, countering beliefs held by some contemporary groups that attributed familial relationships to the divine. It establishes that ascribing such human characteristics to God contradicts His sublime nature as the Self-Sufficient, Eternal Being who neither begets nor is begotten.

translation: Glorified is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute transcendence of Allah beyond any human attempt to fully comprehend or characterize His essence. The command to glorify God as Lord of both the heavens and earth and specifically as Lord of the Throne emphasizes His supreme sovereignty over all creation, while the phrase 'above what they describe' refutes any anthropomorphic or limiting descriptions that people might attribute to Him. It serves as a corrective to those who would diminish God's majesty through inadequate or false characterizations, reminding believers that God's reality infinitely exceeds human capacity for description and that He remains utterly free from any imperfection or limitation that human language might inadvertently impose.

translation: So leave them to plunge in vain discourse and amuse themselves until they meet their Day which they are promised.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet Muhammad to disengage from those who persist in denial and frivolous debates about faith. The command to 'leave them' signifies a divine wisdom in allowing people the freedom to continue in their heedlessness temporarily, as this world is a test. Their indulgence in empty talk and worldly pleasures is ultimately self-deceptive, for they are moving inevitably toward the Day of Judgment where they will face the consequences of their choices. The verse emphasizes divine patience and the certainty of accountability, warning that those who waste their opportunity for reflection and repentance in this life will eventually confront an inescapable reckoning. It also provides comfort to the Prophet, reminding him that guidance is in Allah's hands, and his duty is only to convey the message, not to force acceptance.

translation: And He is the One Who is God in the heaven and God on the earth, and He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty and unity of God across all realms of existence, affirming that His divinity is not confined to a particular domain but extends universally throughout the heavens and the earth. The concluding attributes of wisdom and knowledge reinforce that His governance of both celestial and terrestrial realms is executed with perfect wisdom and complete awareness, meaning that nothing in creation falls outside His divine authority, and His rule is characterized by purposeful design and comprehensive knowledge of all things.

translation: Blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and with Him is knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: This verse establishes God's absolute sovereignty over all creation while connecting His temporal authority to His exclusive knowledge of the Final Hour. The juxtaposition of cosmic dominion with eschatological knowledge emphasizes that the same Power who controls the present order will determine its ultimate conclusion. The inevitable return to God underscores human accountability and the purposefulness of existence, reminding believers that their lives unfold within a divine framework where present actions have ultimate consequences. This knowledge should inspire both reverence for God's majesty and mindfulness of one's responsibility in the temporal realm.

translation: And those they invoke besides Him possess no power of intercession, except for those who testify to the truth while they know it.
interpretation: This verse establishes that intercession on the Day of Judgment is granted only by Allah's permission and to those who bore witness to the truth with knowledge and certainty during their lives. The false deities worshipped by polytheists have no ability to intercede, as intercession requires both divine authorization and a foundation of truthful testimony. Only those who consciously affirmed tawhid (divine unity) and lived by this truth earn the possibility of intercession, demonstrating that salvation is rooted in sincere belief rather than misplaced devotion to powerless intermediaries.

translation: And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, 'Allah.' So how are they deluded?
interpretation: This verse highlights a profound contradiction in human nature: even those who associate partners with Allah or deny His exclusive right to worship acknowledge Him as their Creator when questioned. The rhetorical question 'how are they deluded?' emphasizes the irrationality of recognizing Allah as the source of existence yet turning away from His worship or attributing divine qualities to others. It demonstrates that the truth of Tawhid (divine oneness) is embedded in human consciousness, yet people allow themselves to be diverted from its logical implications through various forms of spiritual and intellectual deviation.

translation: And his saying: 'O my Lord, indeed these are a people who do not believe.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the Prophet's deep concern and sorrow over his people's persistent rejection of faith despite his sincere efforts to guide them. It demonstrates the proper conduct of a messenger when faced with obstinate disbelief - turning to Allah in supplication rather than responding with revenge or despair. The verse teaches that a believer's ultimate recourse when human efforts fail is to place the matter before Allah, acknowledging both the reality of the situation and one's own limitations in guiding others, since guidance itself is in Allah's hands alone. It also serves as a witness that the Prophet fulfilled his duty of conveying the message, and that the responsibility for disbelief lies with those who chose to reject the truth.

translation: So turn away from them and say, 'Peace.' For they will soon come to know.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet Muhammad to adopt a posture of dignified withdrawal and gracious farewell toward those who persist in rejection and mockery. The command to say 'peace' (salām) is not merely a farewell but represents a prophetic distancing from their conduct while maintaining moral superiority through composure. The ominous phrase 'they will soon come to know' serves as a divine warning that their rejection will have consequences they cannot yet comprehend—whether through witnessing the truth of the message, facing divine judgment in this life, or confronting the reality in the Hereafter. This reflects a broader Qur'anic pattern where the Prophet is counseled to exercise patience and leave ultimate judgment to God, while those who deny will inevitably encounter the consequences of their choices.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ha Mim.
interpretation: The isolated letters 'Ha Mim' (Ḥā Mīm) are among the mysterious opening letters of certain Quranic chapters whose precise meaning is known only to Allah, though they serve multiple purposes: they challenge the eloquence of the Arabs by using the very letters they know yet produce an inimitable composition, they draw attention to the miraculous nature of the Qur'an as divine speech constructed from ordinary letters yet unmatched in beauty and guidance, and they invite contemplation on the limits of human knowledge while establishing that some divine wisdom remains beyond complete human comprehension, thereby reinforcing humility before Allah's infinite knowledge and the sacred nature of the revelation that follows.

translation: And the clear Book.
interpretation: This refers to the Qur'an itself, described as 'clear' (mubin) to emphasize its clarity in guidance, its explicit nature in conveying truth, and its role as a manifest evidence that distinguishes between right and wrong, leaving no ambiguity for those who seek understanding with sincerity.

translation: Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night. Indeed, We were to warn [mankind].
interpretation: This verse emphasizes divine sovereignty in revelation and establishes the Qur'an's purpose as a warning to humanity. The 'blessed night' refers to Laylat al-Qadr, signifying that the timing of revelation was ordained by divine wisdom, not human choice. By using 'We' (the royal plural), Allah asserts His majesty and authority. The verse connects the act of revelation with its ultimate purpose: to serve as a warning system for mankind, alerting people to the consequences of their choices and guiding them toward righteousness. The blessing of the night underscores that divine communication with humanity is itself a mercy, even when it comes in the form of warning, as it provides opportunity for repentance and correction before facing ultimate accountability.

translation: In it every matter of wisdom is made distinct.
interpretation: This verse refers to Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Decree), indicating that during this blessed night, Allah ordains and distinguishes all the decrees and matters for the coming year - including provisions, lifespans, and all events that will occur. The divine wisdom behind each decree is made clear and separated in the heavenly realm, as the angels receive their instructions for executing Allah's commands throughout the year. This demonstrates Allah's perfect knowledge, planning, and sovereignty over all affairs, where nothing occurs randomly but rather everything proceeds according to divine wisdom and predetermined measures established on this momentous night.

translation: A command from Us. Indeed, We were sending messengers.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes divine authority and initiative in the process of revelation and prophethood. The phrase 'a command from Us' establishes that the sending of messengers is not arbitrary but flows from God's sovereign will and decree. It underscores that prophecy and divine communication originate solely from Allah's decision, not from human desire or worldly circumstances. The use of the plural 'We' reflects the royal plural denoting majesty, while 'We were sending' in the past continuous tense indicates that dispatching messengers has been God's consistent practice throughout human history, demonstrating His ongoing mercy and guidance to humanity across different times and peoples.

translation: A mercy from your Lord. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that whatever blessing or divine guidance has been mentioned is purely an act of mercy from Allah, not earned through human merit alone. The dual attributes of As-Samee' (the All-Hearing) and Al-'Aleem (the All-Knowing) together signify that Allah's mercy is neither arbitrary nor blind—He hears the prayers, pleas, and needs of His servants, and His perfect knowledge encompasses their circumstances, intentions, and what is best for them. This combination assures believers that divine mercy is responsive and wisely dispensed, addressing both the expressed and unexpressed needs of creation with perfect awareness.

translation: Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you would be certain.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that true certainty (yaqeen) in faith comes through recognizing Allah's absolute lordship over all existence. The conditional 'if you would be certain' serves as both a challenge and an invitation - suggesting that those who genuinely seek certainty will find it by contemplating the comprehensive dominion of Allah over the heavens, earth, and everything between them. It implies that rational reflection on the cosmos and its Creator leads naturally to firm conviction, and that intellectual doubt dissolves when one properly considers the magnitude and unity of divine sovereignty over all realms of existence.

translation: There is no deity except Him; He gives life and causes death. [He is] your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute oneness of God and His exclusive sovereignty over life and death, establishing that the same divine authority that governs our existence also governed our ancestors. The reference to forefathers serves to connect present believers with the unbroken chain of divine lordship throughout human history, reminding us that God's dominion transcends time and generations. By linking the power over life and death with lordship, the verse illustrates that true worship belongs only to the One who controls our ultimate beginning and end, making devotion to anything or anyone else fundamentally misplaced.

translation: Rather, they are in doubt, amusing themselves.
interpretation: This verse criticizes those who treat matters of faith and the afterlife frivolously, occupying themselves with worldly distractions and pleasures while harboring uncertainty about divine truth. Their doubt is not sincere inquiry seeking knowledge, but rather a state of heedlessness where they engage in idle play and entertainment, avoiding serious contemplation of their ultimate purpose and accountability. The verse suggests that their skepticism serves as a convenient excuse to remain in their comfort zone of worldly pursuits, revealing a spiritual immaturity where they treat sacred matters as if they were games, thereby failing to recognize the gravity of their existential situation and the consequences of their choices.

translation: So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke.
interpretation: This verse warns of a future day of trial and tribulation, where the appearance of visible smoke from the sky serves as a sign of divine judgment and the severity of the consequences awaiting those who reject faith. The imagery of smoke represents obscurity, confusion, and suffering that will envelope disbelievers, serving as both a literal and metaphorical manifestation of God's power and the gravity of denying His signs. This is interpreted by scholars as either referring to a specific historical event of hardship that befell the early community, or as an eschatological sign preceding the Day of Judgment, emphasizing the certainty of divine accountability and the need for vigilance and repentance.

translation: It will cover the people; this is a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse describes a comprehensive and inescapable torment that will engulf humanity, emphasizing both its universal scope and its intensely painful nature. The imagery of 'covering' or 'enveloping' suggests that this punishment will be all-encompassing, leaving no refuge or escape for those subjected to it. The declaration 'this is a painful punishment' serves as a divine warning about the severity of consequences for those who reject faith or persist in wrongdoing, reminding believers of the reality of divine justice and the importance of accountability in the Hereafter.

translation: Our Lord, remove from us the punishment; indeed, we are believers.
interpretation: This verse reflects a moment of desperation where people call upon God to lift their suffering while claiming faith, yet the context suggests their belief is conditional and temporary—arising only in times of hardship rather than being rooted in sincere, lasting conviction. It reveals a human tendency to turn to God when faced with calamity while possibly neglecting Him in times of ease, demonstrating that true faith must be proven through consistency in both adversity and prosperity, not merely professed when seeking relief from trials.

translation: How can there be a reminder for them when there has already come to them a clear Messenger?
interpretation: This verse questions the benefit of admonition for those who persist in disbelief despite having received clear guidance through a messenger. It suggests that those who rejected the Prophet's clear message have already made their choice, and further reminders may be futile for hearts that have become sealed through obstinate rejection. The verse highlights the tragedy of wasted opportunity - when divine guidance comes in its clearest form yet is spurned, what additional reminder could possibly penetrate such willful blindness? It serves as a warning about the hardening of hearts that occurs when people consistently turn away from truth despite its manifest clarity.

translation: Then they turned away from him and said, 'A teacher possessed by madness' or 'One taught by others, a madman.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the psychological defense mechanism of willful rejection employed by those who refuse divine guidance. When confronted with truth that challenges their worldview or threatens their status, they resort to character assassination rather than intellectual engagement. By dismissing the messenger as either mentally unstable or merely repeating what others taught him, they avoid confronting the actual message. This represents a common human tendency to protect cognitive dissonance through ad hominem attacks, revealing that their rejection stems not from rational assessment but from spiritual stubbornness and fear of the implications of accepting the truth.

translation: Indeed, We will remove the torment for a little while; indeed, you will return [to disbelief].
interpretation: This verse addresses the persistent pattern of human forgetfulness and ingratitude, particularly in times of adversity and ease. When affliction is lifted temporarily, people tend to revert to their old ways of denial and transgression rather than maintaining steadfast faith. It serves as a divine warning about the cyclical nature of human weakness—how relief from hardship often leads not to increased gratitude and righteousness, but to a return to heedlessness. This reflects the broader Quranic theme that temporary respites are tests of character, revealing whether individuals will use moments of ease to reform themselves or will squander these opportunities by falling back into patterns of disbelief and moral decline.

translation: The Day We will strike with the greatest strike, indeed, We will take retribution.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment when Allah will execute His ultimate justice and retribution against those who denied His signs and persisted in disbelief. The 'greatest strike' symbolizes the comprehensive and decisive punishment that will befall the disbelievers, particularly the Quraysh who opposed the Prophet Muhammad. It serves as both a warning and a reminder that divine justice, though delayed in this worldly life, will be fully realized on the Day of Resurrection when all wrongs will be righted and the arrogant will face the consequences of their rejection of truth. The verse emphasizes Allah's sovereignty and His inevitable fulfillment of justice.

translation: And We had certainly tried before them the people of Pharaoh, and there came to them a noble messenger.
interpretation: This verse establishes a pattern of divine testing throughout history, reminding the audience that trials and the sending of messengers are part of God's consistent way with nations. The emphasis on the nobility of the messenger (Moses) underscores that rejection of divine guidance is not due to any deficiency in the messenger but rather stems from the arrogance and stubbornness of those who refuse to submit. The mention of Pharaoh's people serves as a warning that power and worldly strength do not exempt communities from accountability, and that previous nations who rejected their messengers faced consequences, implying a similar fate awaits any who follow their path.

translation: That you should deliver to Me the servants of Allah. Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.
interpretation: This verse represents the words of a prophet addressing his people, emphasizing his divine mission to guide God's servants back to their Creator. The phrase 'deliver to Me the servants of Allah' signifies the prophet's role in liberating people from servitude to false authorities, tyrants, or worldly attachments, and redirecting their worship and allegiance solely to God. The declaration of being a 'trustworthy messenger' establishes the prophet's credibility and moral authority, assuring the people that he seeks no personal gain and carries God's message with complete integrity and fidelity. This reflects the Islamic principle that prophets are chosen for their exceptional trustworthiness and that true guidance comes through sincere, uncorrupted transmission of divine revelation.

translation: And do not exalt yourselves against Allah. Indeed, I have come to you with clear authority.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the fundamental principle of humility before God and warns against arrogance in dealing with divine commandments. The command not to 'exalt yourselves' signifies that humans must recognize their position as servants and not challenge God's sovereignty through rejection, rebellion, or claims of superiority. The messenger's assertion of bringing 'clear authority' indicates that the divine message comes with undeniable proofs and signs, leaving no legitimate excuse for denial. This teaches that true faith requires acknowledging God's supreme authority over all creation and submitting to His will without pride or defiance, as arrogance in spiritual matters leads to destruction while humility opens the path to salvation.

translation: And indeed, I seek refuge with my Lord and your Lord lest you stone me.
interpretation: This verse reflects the prophet's acknowledgment that ultimate protection comes from God alone when facing threats of violence or persecution. It demonstrates the proper response to physical danger - turning to God for sanctuary while recognizing His sovereignty over both the believer and the persecutors. The use of 'my Lord and your Lord' emphasizes the shared divine authority over all parties, subtly reminding the aggressors that they too are accountable to the same God, which serves as both a spiritual defense and a moral appeal to their conscience.

translation: And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone.
interpretation: This verse represents a moment of prophetic resignation and boundary-setting, where the messenger, having exhausted attempts at persuasion, requests separation from those who reject his message. It illustrates the principle that after conveying the truth clearly, a prophet may withdraw from fruitless engagement, allowing people the freedom to disbelieve while protecting the integrity of the prophetic mission. This reflects divine wisdom that faith cannot be coerced, and that sometimes the most dignified response to persistent rejection is peaceful disengagement rather than continued confrontation, leaving final judgment to God while maintaining the messenger's honor and the message's purity.

translation: So he called upon his Lord, 'Indeed, these are a criminal people.'
interpretation: This verse reflects a moment of prophetic despair and turning to divine assistance when faced with persistent rejection and hostility. The prophet's appeal to God demonstrates the proper course of action for a believer when human efforts at guidance have been exhausted - to entrust the matter to divine judgment. The designation of the people as 'criminals' or 'guilty' indicates their culpability is not merely in disbelief but in active transgression and harm, having crossed moral boundaries in their opposition to truth. This supplication marks a transition point where the prophet acknowledges the futility of further appeal to his people and seeks divine intervention, recognizing that ultimate accountability lies with God alone.

translation: Then set out with My servants by night. Indeed, you are to be pursued.
interpretation: This verse commands the prophet to lead the believers away under the cover of darkness, indicating divine protection during a time of imminent danger. The instruction to travel at night suggests a strategic withdrawal from threat, while the warning of pursuit emphasizes that trials and opposition are inevitable for those on the path of faith. It teaches that Allah provides means of escape and safety for His servants, but they must take action and trust in His plan even when enemies follow. The verse establishes that deliverance often requires both divine intervention and human effort, and that the faithful must remain vigilant and obedient to divine guidance even in times of peril.

translation: And leave the sea in stillness. Indeed, they are an army to be drowned.
interpretation: This verse commands Moses to leave the parted sea as it is after the Israelites have crossed, allowing it to return to its natural state and thereby drown Pharaoh's pursuing army. It demonstrates that divine deliverance of the believers is simultaneously divine retribution upon the oppressors, teaching that God's justice encompasses both mercy for the faithful and punishment for the tyrants who persecute them. The stillness of the sea represents the calm confidence believers should have in God's plan, knowing that threats against them will ultimately destroy themselves when they pursue believers beyond their bounds.

translation: How many gardens and springs they left behind!
interpretation: This verse reflects on the transient nature of worldly possessions and power, reminding us that even those who accumulated great wealth and enjoyed abundant resources in this life ultimately had to leave everything behind. It serves as a warning against attachment to material abundance and a reminder that death separates people from all their earthly belongings, regardless of how vast their estates or how plentiful their resources were. The verse encourages reflection on the ultimate fate of previous nations who were blessed with prosperity but failed to use it righteously, emphasizing that worldly comfort and luxury are temporary and should not distract believers from preparing for the eternal life to come.

translation: And crops and noble station.
interpretation: This verse highlights the worldly blessings and elevated status that the people being described once enjoyed in their earthly life. The 'noble station' refers to their high social standing, positions of honor, and comfortable life they possessed. The mention of these material comforts serves as a reminder that worldly prosperity and status are temporary and can be taken away by divine decree, especially when people become ungrateful or disobedient. It emphasizes that neither wealth nor social position can protect one from divine punishment when it is decreed, teaching that true security lies in righteousness rather than material abundance or social prestige.

translation: And comfort wherein they were amused.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the spiritual danger of becoming completely absorbed in worldly luxuries and pleasures to the point of heedlessness. The term 'fākihīn' (amused/delighting) suggests a state of distraction and self-indulgence where people become so consumed by material comfort that they forget their ultimate purpose and accountability before God. It serves as a warning that excessive attachment to worldly ease can lead to moral complacency and neglect of one's duties toward the Creator, ultimately resulting in spiritual loss. The verse implies that those who allow themselves to become intoxicated by comfort and amusement, without gratitude or remembrance of God, risk facing consequences when that comfort is taken away or when they are called to account in the Hereafter.

translation: Thus it was, and We caused another people to inherit it.
interpretation: This verse illustrates Allah's absolute sovereignty over nations and His ability to transfer power and inheritance from one people to another according to His divine wisdom. It demonstrates that worldly dominion is not permanent for any group, and that Allah grants stewardship of lands, resources, and blessings to those He wills, while removing them from those who prove unworthy through disbelief, tyranny, or corruption. The verse serves as a warning that no civilization is immune to divine retribution if they persist in wrongdoing, and as a reminder that all earthly possessions ultimately belong to Allah, who distributes them among His creation as part of His grand plan and as a test of gratitude and righteousness.

translation: Neither the heaven nor the earth wept for them, nor were they given respite.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the insignificance and lack of cosmic mourning for those who were destroyed due to their rejection of divine guidance. When the righteous or beloved servants of God pass away, tradition holds that creation itself mourns their loss. However, these wrongdoers left no positive impact worthy of lamentation from the heavens or earth, indicating their spiritual bankruptcy and the justice of their sudden punishment without delay or opportunity for reprieve. It serves as a stark reminder that those who persist in defiance against God's message will face consequences swiftly, with no mercy or postponement, and their departure will be unmourned by the universe itself.

translation: And We certainly saved the Children of Israel from the humiliating torment.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's mercy and deliverance of the Israelites from their oppression in Egypt under Pharaoh. The 'humiliating torment' refers to the degradation and enslavement they endured, which stripped them not only of physical freedom but of human dignity. The deliverance represents God's intervention in history to rescue the oppressed and restore honor to those who were humiliated, establishing a pattern of divine justice where God sides with the downtrodden against tyrannical oppressors. This serves as a reminder that temporal power and oppression are ultimately subject to divine authority and that God responds to the suffering of the afflicted.

translation: From Pharaoh. Indeed, he was arrogant, one of the transgressors.
interpretation: This verse warns against the spiritual danger of arrogance and excessive behavior by using Pharaoh as the archetypal example. It teaches that elevation in worldly status or power, when combined with haughtiness and transgression of divine boundaries, leads to destruction. The verse connects pride with wasteful extravagance and sin, suggesting that these traits are interconnected manifestations of rejecting divine authority. It serves as a reminder that no matter how high one's position, rejection of truth and moral limits will ultimately lead to downfall, just as it did for Pharaoh.

translation: And We certainly chose them, by knowledge, over the worlds.
interpretation: This verse indicates that Allah's selection of the Children of Israel was not arbitrary but was based on divine knowledge and wisdom. Their chosenness was conditional and purposeful - they were given prophethood, scripture, and guidance to fulfill a specific role in human history as carriers of monotheistic truth during their time. However, this selection was temporal and context-specific, meant for a particular epoch, and was contingent upon their adherence to the covenant. The phrase 'over the worlds' refers to the people of their time period, not an absolute superiority for all eternity, as chosenness in Islamic theology is ultimately determined by righteousness and faith rather than lineage or ethnic identity.

translation: And We gave them signs in which there was a clear trial.
interpretation: This verse indicates that Allah provided these people with manifest signs and miracles that served as both evidence of divine truth and a test of their faith and obedience. The signs were so clear and undeniable that they constituted a decisive trial, meaning people would be held accountable based on how they responded to these evident proofs - whether they accepted them with gratitude and submission, or rejected them with arrogance and disbelief. The 'clear trial' implies that the signs removed all ambiguity, making the choice between faith and rejection a matter of moral will rather than intellectual uncertainty.

translation: Indeed, these [people] are saying
interpretation: This verse opens with a tone of emphasis and mild reproach, drawing attention to the claims or statements of the Quraysh disbelievers who denied the resurrection and afterlife. The demonstrative pronoun 'these' suggests a distancing from their position, indicating that what follows will be a statement of their false beliefs that contradict divine truth. The particle 'inna' provides emphasis, highlighting the gravity or absurdity of what they assert. This introductory phrase sets the stage for refuting their arguments about death being final and denying any return after mortality, preparing the listener to recognize the contrast between human presumption and divine reality.

translation: There is nothing but our first death, and we will not be resurrected.
interpretation: This verse captures the argument of the disbelievers who deny the resurrection and the afterlife. They assert that death is a singular, final event with no continuation beyond it. This reflects a materialistic worldview that rejects divine accountability and the Day of Judgment. The verse exposes their fundamental error in reasoning: they limit reality to what they perceive in this worldly life, denying the power of Allah to recreate them after death. Their statement reveals spiritual blindness and an inability to recognize that the One who created them initially has complete power to bring them back to life for reckoning. This denial of resurrection undermines the entire moral framework of divine justice, as it suggests no consequences for one's actions beyond this temporal existence.

translation: So bring back our forefathers, if you are truthful.
interpretation: This verse reflects the skepticism of disbelievers who challenge the concept of resurrection and afterlife. They sarcastically demand that if the believers are truthful about life after death and resurrection, they should prove it by bringing their deceased ancestors back to life in the present world. This challenge reveals their fundamental misunderstanding of resurrection as something that occurs in this worldly life rather than in the Hereafter. It demonstrates how disbelief often manifests as demanding impossible proofs in the wrong context, while ignoring the signs and rational arguments already presented to them. The verse exposes the obstinacy of those who reject faith not due to lack of evidence, but due to arrogance and unwillingness to accept accountability in the Hereafter.

translation: Are they better or the people of Tubba' and those before them? We destroyed them; indeed, they were criminals.
interpretation: This verse employs a rhetorical question to humble the disbelievers of Makkah by reminding them that previous powerful civilizations who rejected their messengers, such as the people of Tubba' in Yemen, were annihilated despite their strength and prosperity. The verse serves as a warning that worldly power and success do not guarantee divine protection, and that persistence in criminality and rejection of truth leads inevitably to divine punishment, regardless of one's apparent superiority or accomplishments.

translation: And We did not create the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them in play (or amusement).
interpretation: This verse establishes the fundamental principle that divine creation is purposeful and meaningful, not arbitrary or frivolous. It affirms that the universe exists with intentionality and divine wisdom, refuting any notion that existence is random, meaningless, or created for mere entertainment. The verse underscores that God's creative act has serious purposes including testing humanity, manifesting divine attributes, and leading creation toward ultimate accountability and justice. It calls believers to reflect on the purposefulness of existence and to live with awareness that life has consequential meaning beyond superficial pursuits.

translation: We did not create them except in truth, but most of them do not know.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the creation of the heavens and earth, or all existence, was purposeful and meaningful rather than random or frivolous. The phrase 'in truth' indicates that creation has an inherent purpose, wisdom, and ultimate reality that points to accountability and the Day of Judgment. The lament that 'most of them do not know' highlights human ignorance or heedlessness regarding the purposeful nature of existence, suggesting that people often live as though life has no ultimate meaning or consequence, when in fact everything was created with divine wisdom and will culminate in a Day of Reckoning where all will be held accountable.

translation: Indeed, the Day of Judgment is the appointed time for them all.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the universal and inescapable nature of divine accountability. The 'Day of Judgment' (Yawm al-Fasl) represents the moment when all distinctions between truth and falsehood, belief and disbelief, righteousness and wickedness will be definitively established. The use of 'all of them' (ajma'īn) underscores that no individual, group, or nation will be exempt from this appointed time. It serves as both a warning to the wrongdoers that their actions will not go unaccounted for, and a comfort to the oppressed that justice will ultimately prevail. The verse reminds believers that despite the apparent chaos and injustice in worldly life, there exists a divinely ordained moment when all accounts will be settled and every soul will receive its due recompense according to its deeds.

translation: A Day when no relation will avail another relation at all, nor will they be helped.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of Allah on the Day of Judgment and the complete severance of worldly ties and dependencies. It teaches that all human relationships, bonds of kinship, friendship, and patronage that people rely upon in this world will be rendered utterly powerless on that Day. No intercessor can benefit another unless Allah permits it, and no one can provide assistance or protection to another soul. This serves as a reminder to believers that they must cultivate their individual relationship with Allah and perform righteous deeds independently, as salvation cannot be achieved through reliance on others' status or intervention, but only through Allah's mercy and one's own faith and actions.

translation: Except those upon whom Allah has mercy. Indeed, He is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the boundless nature of divine mercy and Allah's sovereign authority in bestowing it. The combination of Al-'Aziz (the Mighty) and Ar-Rahim (the Merciful) reveals that Allah's mercy is not a sign of weakness but flows from His absolute power - He is mighty enough to forgive whom He wills without fear of consequence. The exception clause teaches that salvation and guidance are ultimately gifts of divine grace rather than solely human achievement, reminding believers to maintain humility and hope simultaneously, knowing that while they must strive righteously, their ultimate success depends on Allah's mercy which He grants according to His perfect wisdom and justice.

translation: Indeed, the tree of Zaqqum
