This understanding should orient the believer toward prioritizing spiritual development and preparation for the eternal afterlife over excessive concern with fleeting worldly matters.

translation: And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.
interpretation: This verse affirms the eternal, everlasting nature of Allah's essence while all of creation perishes. The 'Face' (wajh) represents Allah's essence and being, not a physical countenance, as Allah transcends corporeal attributes. The verse emphasizes that while everything in existence is temporal and will cease to exist, only Allah's divine essence endures eternally. The attributes 'Owner of Majesty and Honor' (dhu al-jalal wa al-ikram) highlight both Allah's overwhelming majesty that inspires awe and reverence, and His honor and generosity toward His creation. This serves as a profound reminder of the absolute permanence of the Divine contrasted with the transitory nature of all created things, calling believers to attach their hearts to the Eternal rather than the ephemeral world.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful rhetorical refrain that calls humanity and jinn to acknowledge God's countless blessings and manifestations of divine grace. It challenges both species to reflect honestly on whether they can truly reject or deny any of the favors bestowed upon them by their Creator. The interrogative form is not seeking information but rather prompting deep contemplation and gratitude, emphasizing that denial of God's blessings is both intellectually dishonest and spiritually ungrateful. The repeated nature of this verse throughout Surah Ar-Rahman creates a rhythmic meditation that compels the listener to continuously examine their relationship with divine bounty, making ingratitude increasingly untenable with each repetition.

translation: Everyone in the heavens and the earth asks Him (for their needs). Every day He is in a (new) matter.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's constant, active involvement in His creation, managing countless affairs simultaneously across the universe. The phrase 'every day He is in a new matter' signifies that Allah continuously brings things into existence, provides sustenance, answers prayers, grants life, causes death, elevates some and humbles others, and responds to the changing needs of all creatures. It demonstrates that Allah's sovereignty is dynamic and immediate—He is not a passive deity but actively engaged in governing every aspect of existence at every moment. The verse also highlights the absolute dependence of all creation upon Allah, as every being in the heavens and earth constantly needs Him for their sustenance, guidance, and very existence, while He remains completely independent and self-sufficient, needing nothing from His creation.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a recurring refrain that calls humanity and jinn to reflect on and acknowledge God's countless blessings and signs of His power in creation. It functions as a rhetorical question emphasizing that denying divine favors is both irrational and ungrateful, prompting believers to cultivate gratitude and recognize their dependence on their Creator. The repetition of this verse throughout Surah Ar-Rahman creates a rhythmic reminder that permeates consciousness, making the acknowledgment of God's blessings an unavoidable reality that confronts those who witness the signs of creation, redemption, and ultimate justice.

translation: We will attend to you, O you two classes (of jinn and mankind)!
interpretation: This verse conveys a divine promise that Allah will turn His full attention to judging and reckoning both jinn and mankind on the Day of Judgment. The use of 'We will attend to you' carries an implicit warning - that despite being occupied with managing the entire universe, Allah will not neglect to call these two weighty communities to account for their deeds. The term 'thaqalaan' (two weighty ones) refers to humans and jinn as the two species bearing moral responsibility and the weight of religious obligations. The verse serves as both a reminder of inevitable accountability and a deterrent against heedlessness, emphasizing that no one from either realm will escape divine justice and that the apparent delay in judgment should not be mistaken for divine neglect.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful rhetorical refrain that invites both humans and jinn to reflect on their ingratitude and challenges them to recognize the countless blessings bestowed upon them by their Creator. It functions as a divine reminder that denial of God's favors is intellectually untenable when one honestly examines the overwhelming evidence of His generosity in creation, sustenance, guidance, and mercy. The repetition of this verse throughout Surah Ar-Rahman emphasizes that each blessing mentioned deserves acknowledgment and that the appropriate response to divine benevolence is gratitude rather than rejection or neglect.

translation: O company of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass. You will not pass except by authority/power.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute sovereignty of Allah over His creation and the fundamental limitations inherent in human and jinn existence. The challenge issued here is not merely physical but existential - it addresses the impossibility of escaping divine jurisdiction or transcending the boundaries Allah has established for creation. The word 'sultan' (authority/power) indicates that any transcendence of these cosmic boundaries would require a power that can only emanate from Allah Himself. Thus, the verse emphasizes human and jinn dependence on divine permission for any significant cosmic movement or achievement, reminding both species of their creaturely status and their inability to operate independently of their Creator's will and knowledge. It establishes that the heavens and earth are not open domains for unrestricted travel, but rather governed realms where movement requires divine authorization.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This recurring verse serves as a divine rhetorical question that invites humanity and jinn to reflect upon and acknowledge God's countless blessings and manifestations of power throughout creation. It functions as a refrain that punctuates descriptions of divine mercy, creative power, and eschatological realities, compelling the listener to recognize their dependence on God and the impossibility of rationally denying His benevolence. The question is not seeking information but rather cultivating gratitude, humility, and awareness of one's obligations toward the Creator, while also serving as a gentle yet firm admonishment against ingratitude and the denial of obvious truths about God's lordship and generosity.

translation: There will be sent upon you both a flame of fire and smoke, and you will not defend yourselves.
interpretation: This verse warns of the inescapable punishment awaiting those who reject faith on the Day of Judgment. The imagery of flames and molten brass or smoke represents divine retribution that cannot be evaded through human strength or strategy. It emphasizes human powerlessness before God's justice and serves as a reminder that worldly defenses and alliances will be utterly useless when facing accountability for one's deeds. The dual address (you both) traditionally refers to jinn and mankind, indicating that all rational beings will be held accountable regardless of their nature or capabilities.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a rhetorical refrain throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, challenging both humans and jinn to recognize and acknowledge the countless blessings bestowed upon them by Allah. It functions as a divine reminder that denying God's favors is not only ingratitude but also a rejection of observable reality, as His mercies permeate every aspect of existence from the natural world to spiritual guidance. The repetition emphasizes that no matter how much one might rationalize or resist, the evidence of divine benevolence is overwhelming and undeniable, making any rejection of these favors an act of willful blindness rather than reasonable doubt.

translation: Then when the sky splits open and becomes rose-colored like red oil or molten brass.
interpretation: This verse describes a profound cosmic transformation on the Day of Judgment, when the very fabric of the heavens will undergo a fundamental change in its nature and appearance. The comparison to a rose or reddish hue suggests the sky will take on the appearance of something molten and liquid-like, indicating the dissolution of the established cosmic order. This imagery serves to emphasize the total breakdown of natural laws and the temporary nature of the physical universe, reminding believers that the seemingly permanent celestial realm is ultimately transient and subject to Allah's command. The visceral description aims to awaken in the reader an awareness of the temporary nature of worldly existence and the inevitability of divine judgment.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a rhetorical refrain emphasizing divine accountability and gratitude. It challenges both humans and jinn to reflect upon the countless blessings bestowed by Allah, implying that denial of these favors is both irrational and ungrateful. The repetition of this verse throughout Surah Ar-Rahman creates a rhythmic reminder that compels the listener to acknowledge God's beneficence in creation, provision, guidance, and the promise of paradise. It functions as a divine interrogation that leaves no room for legitimate denial, as the evidence of God's favors permeates every aspect of existence, from the cosmic order to the minutest details of human life. The verse ultimately calls believers to a state of perpetual recognition and thankfulness.

translation: On that Day, neither man nor jinn will be asked about his sin.
interpretation: This verse indicates that on the Day of Judgment, there will be a stage where no questioning occurs because Allah's omniscience makes inquiry unnecessary - the sins will be so manifest and evident through the records, witnesses, and bodily testimonies that formal interrogation becomes superfluous. It emphasizes the completeness of divine knowledge and the transparency of all deeds on that Day, where guilt will be recognized by the visible signs on faces and bodies, making verbal confession or denial meaningless. This reflects the absolute justice of Allah, who needs no testimony to establish truth, as He is the ultimate Witness to all actions.

translation: Then which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a recurring refrain emphasizing divine accountability and gratitude. It challenges both humans and jinn to acknowledge God's countless blessings and mercies, implying that denial of these favors is both illogical and ungrateful. The rhetorical question creates a pause for reflection, compelling the audience to recognize that despite their shortcomings and the warnings of judgment, God's benevolence remains manifest in creation, sustenance, guidance, and the promise of paradise. The dual address ('you two' referring to mankind and jinn) universalizes the message across conscious creation, making ingratitude indefensible when confronted with the overwhelming evidence of divine grace in both the physical and spiritual realms.

translation: The criminals will be known by their marks, and they will be seized by their forelocks and their feet.
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Judgment when the guilty will be immediately recognizable through distinctive signs or marks on their faces and bodies, making their spiritual state manifest in physical form. The seizing by forelocks and feet symbolizes complete subjugation and humiliation, as these are vulnerable points of the body. This imagery emphasizes that on that Day, there will be no hiding one's true nature or deeds—righteousness and sin will be made apparent—and the wicked will face inescapable accountability, being forcibly dragged to their reckoning in a state of utter helplessness and disgrace.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a rhetorical refrain emphasizing divine accountability and the undeniability of God's blessings. It challenges both humans and jinn to recognize and acknowledge the countless manifestations of divine mercy and power surrounding them. The question is posed not to elicit information but to awaken consciousness and cultivate gratitude, making denial of these favors an absurdity when the evidence of creation, sustenance, guidance, and promised resurrection are manifest. The repeated nature of this verse throughout Surah Ar-Rahman creates a rhythmic reminder that penetrates the heart, compelling reflection on one's relationship with the Creator and one's response to His generosity.

translation: This is Hell, which the criminals used to deny.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stark moment of realization where the ultimate reality that was rejected in worldly life becomes undeniably manifest. The interpretation highlights the concept of consequential truth - that denial of accountability and divine justice during one's lifetime does not negate their existence, but rather makes the eventual confrontation with them more severe. The term 'criminals' (mujrimoon) indicates those who transgressed divine bounds and moral limits, and their 'denial' (yukadhdhibu) represents not just intellectual rejection but willful defiance motivated by arrogance, worldly desires, or following base impulses. The demonstrative 'this' emphasizes the immediacy and concrete reality of what was once considered abstract or dismissible. The verse underscores a fundamental Qur'anic theme: that human beings will ultimately face the consequences of their choices, and that reality operates according to divine justice regardless of whether it was acknowledged in the temporal world.

translation: They will go around between it and scalding water, boiling hot.
interpretation: This verse describes a form of punishment in Hell where the disbelievers will alternate between different torments - moving between the Fire itself and drinking boiling water. The interpretation emphasizes the relentless and cyclical nature of the punishment, where there is no respite or escape. The condemned are driven back and forth between these two agonies, symbolizing the completeness of their suffering and the absence of any comfort or relief. This serves as a powerful warning about the consequences of rejection of faith and a reminder of divine justice, intended to encourage believers to remain steadfast in their obedience to Allah and to deter them from actions that would lead to such a fate.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful rhetorical refrain that calls humanity and jinn to reflect upon and acknowledge the countless blessings and signs of God's mercy and power that surround them. It challenges both communities to contemplate the manifestations of divine favor in creation, sustenance, guidance, and the promise of ultimate justice, while emphasizing that denial of these evident blessings is both irrational and ungrateful. The question format creates a moment of introspection, compelling the listener to recognize that denying God's blessings when confronted with their overwhelming evidence reflects spiritual blindness rather than intellectual reasoning, and it invites a transformation from ingratitude to grateful acknowledgment of the Divine source of all goodness.

translation: And for him who fears the standing before his Lord, there are two gardens.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the spiritual reward for those who maintain consciousness of divine accountability throughout their lives. The 'fear of standing before one's Lord' refers not to terror, but to reverential awareness that cultivates moral restraint and righteous action. When faced with temptation or wrongdoing, the believer remembers they will stand in judgment and thus restrains themselves. The 'two gardens' symbolize abundant, multifaceted rewards in Paradise - perhaps representing both spiritual and sensory bliss, or rewards for both internal piety and external good deeds. The duality suggests completeness and overflowing generosity from God, indicating that divine recompense far exceeds human effort, and that those who exercise self-discipline out of divine consciousness will receive blessings beyond measure in multiple dimensions of paradisiacal existence.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This rhetorical question serves as a powerful reminder of divine accountability and human gratitude. It challenges believers and disbelievers alike to acknowledge God's countless blessings and mercies, making denial of them intellectually and morally untenable. The verse employs a pedagogical technique that encourages self-reflection by forcing the audience to confront the evidence of God's benevolence in creation, sustenance, guidance, and promised rewards. By framing it as a question rather than a command, it appeals to human reason and conscience, suggesting that recognizing divine favors is a natural response to observing the world honestly. The repetition of this verse throughout Surah Ar-Rahman creates a rhythmic pattern that reinforces the message and invites continuous contemplation of blessings both manifest and hidden.

translation: Possessing branches
interpretation: This phrase from Surah Ar-Rahman describes the two gardens promised to believers in Paradise as having abundant, spreading branches full of vegetation and fruit. The interpretation indicates Allah's generous provision in Paradise, where the gardens are so lush and well-maintained that their trees extend outward with plentiful branches, symbolizing the completeness and abundance of divine blessings. The multiplicity of branches suggests endless varieties of fruits and shade, reflecting that the rewards of Paradise are comprehensive, varied, and eternally satisfying for the righteous souls who inhabit them.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine rhetorical question that challenges both humans and jinn to acknowledge God's countless blessings and bounties. It emphasizes the absurdity of denying divine favors when evidence of God's mercy, provision, and creative power surrounds creation. The repetitive use of this verse throughout Surah Ar-Rahman creates a rhythmic reminder that compels reflection on ingratitude and encourages gratitude, suggesting that recognition of blessings is both a rational conclusion and a moral obligation. The dual address to both categories of conscious beings underscores the universality of divine beneficence and the shared responsibility to acknowledge it.

translation: In both of them are two springs flowing.
interpretation: This verse describes the abundant blessings of Paradise, where the two springs represent continuous divine provision and refreshment for the believers. The flowing water symbolizes the perpetual nature of Allah's mercy and generosity in the Hereafter, never ceasing or diminishing, indicating that the inhabitants of these gardens will never experience thirst or deprivation, enjoying eternal comfort and sustenance without effort or toil.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a rhetorical refrain emphasizing divine accountability and human gratitude. It challenges both humans and jinn to recognize and acknowledge God's countless blessings and manifestations of power in creation. The interrogative form is not seeking information but rather compelling reflection—it assumes the impossibility of legitimate denial while simultaneously warning against ingratitude. The dual address underscores that accountability for recognizing divine favor transcends the human realm alone, establishing a universal principle that all conscious beings must acknowledge their dependence on and indebtedness to their Creator. The repetition of this verse throughout Surah Ar-Rahman creates a rhythmic meditation that prevents heedlessness and cultivates awareness of the pervasive nature of divine benevolence in every aspect of existence.

translation: In both of them are two kinds of every fruit.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the abundance and variety of blessings in Paradise, where every type of fruit exists in pairs or multiple varieties. The pairing may signify completeness and perfection of divine provision, indicating that the believers will experience the fullness of pleasure and satisfaction. The duality also suggests balance and harmony in Paradise's provisions, where nothing is lacking and everything exists in its most perfect form, reflecting Allah's generosity and the comprehensive nature of rewards for the righteous in the Hereafter.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine rhetorical question that appears repeatedly throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, functioning as a refrain that punctuates the enumeration of Allah's blessings upon humanity and jinn. The interrogative form is not seeking information but rather employing a powerful rhetorical device to awaken consciousness and provoke reflection. By asking which blessing one would dare to deny, it implicitly affirms that all of creation testifies to the overwhelming generosity and mercy of the Creator. The dual form 'you two' addresses both humans and jinn, reminding both species of their shared dependence on divine grace. The verse creates a rhythm of accountability, making denial of God's favors appear increasingly unreasonable as the surah progresses through manifestations of divine power in nature, provision, guidance, and the promise of eternal reward. It transforms the listener from a passive recipient of information into an active participant who must confront their own ingratitude or affirm their recognition of the divine benevolence permeating existence.

translation: Reclining on couches whose linings are of brocade, and the fruit of the two gardens is near at hand.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle that if the inner linings of Paradise's furnishings are made of the finest silk brocade, then what is visible on the outside must be even more magnificent, teaching us that Allah's generosity in the Hereafter surpasses human imagination. The proximity of the fruits signifies not only physical accessibility but also the immediate fulfillment of desires without effort or delay, reflecting the perfect harmony between wish and attainment that characterizes eternal bliss, where the righteous are freed from all forms of toil and hardship they endured in worldly life.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This recurring verse serves as a rhetorical challenge that emphasizes human accountability and gratitude. It functions as a divine reminder that denying God's blessings is both intellectually dishonest and spiritually destructive. The question is posed to both humans and jinn, creating a universal call to recognize the countless manifestations of divine grace in existence—from the cosmic order to the smallest provisions of life. By framing it as a question rather than a statement, it engages the conscience directly, forcing reflection on the undeniable evidence of God's benevolence surrounding creation, making denial an act of willful ingratitude rather than reasonable doubt.

translation: Therein are maidens of modest gaze, untouched before them by man or jinn.
interpretation: This verse describes the spiritual rewards of Paradise, emphasizing the purity and exclusivity of the blessings granted to the righteous. The 'maidens of modest gaze' symbolize companions of perfected virtue and chastity, representing blessings that are pristine and unprecedented. The emphasis on their being untouched by either human or jinn before underscores the concept that Paradise offers pleasures and experiences that are entirely new and unique, transcending any earthly experience. This serves to illustrate the incomparable nature of divine reward and the complete fulfillment that awaits believers in the afterlife, where all blessings exist in their most perfect and pure form, untainted by any previous claim or experience.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful rhetorical refrain that invites reflection and gratitude rather than expecting a literal answer. It challenges both humans and jinn to acknowledge God's countless blessings and mercies that permeate existence - from the created order of the universe to divine guidance and the promise of paradise. The repetition of this verse throughout Surah Ar-Rahman creates a rhythmic reminder that denial of God's favors is ultimately untenable when one honestly contemplates the evidence of His generosity in creation, provision, and spiritual guidance. It functions as a call to intellectual honesty and spiritual awakening, prompting believers to cultivate gratitude and non-believers to reconsider their rejection of divine grace.

translation: As if they were rubies and coral.
interpretation: This verse describes the maidens of Paradise, emphasizing their exceptional beauty and purity through the metaphor of precious stones. The comparison to rubies (or corundum) suggests a brilliant, translucent quality with a reddish hue, while coral represents delicate beauty and rarity. The imagery conveys that these beings possess a supernatural radiance and perfection that surpasses anything known in earthly experience, reflecting the Qur'anic theme that the rewards of Paradise transcend human imagination and earthly comparison. The specific mention of these two precious materials also suggests a combination of strength and delicacy, transparency and color, indicating completeness in beauty.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a recurring refrain throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, functioning as a divine rhetorical question that invites reflection rather than expecting an answer. It emphasizes Allah's countless blessings upon humanity and jinn, challenging them to recognize and acknowledge these favors rather than reject or be ungrateful for them. The repetition throughout the surah creates a rhythm that reinforces the message of gratitude and awareness, reminding both species of their dependence on the Creator and the absurdity of denying His generosity. It also carries an implicit warning that denial of God's blessings is a form of ingratitude that distances one from the truth and from spiritual well-being.

translation: Is the reward for goodness anything but goodness?
interpretation: This verse establishes a divine principle of reciprocity and justice in Allah's dealings with His servants. It affirms that those who do good deeds, show kindness, and excel in their worship and conduct towards others will be rewarded proportionately with goodness from Allah. The rhetorical question emphasizes the certainty and fairness of this divine law - that excellence and benevolence naturally merit excellent recompense. This principle extends beyond mere material transactions to encompass spiritual rewards, where sincere devotion and righteous actions are met with Allah's mercy, blessings, and ultimately Paradise. It serves as both a promise to motivate believers toward excellence in faith and character, and as reassurance that no good deed, however small, goes unnoticed or unrewarded by the All-Just Creator.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a rhetorical refrain that invites humanity and jinn to reflect upon and acknowledge the countless blessings bestowed by Allah. It challenges both groups to honestly assess whether they can truly deny any of God's manifest favors—from the gift of existence itself to the natural world's provisions, guidance through revelation, and the promise of divine mercy. The repetition of this verse throughout Surah Ar-Rahman creates a rhythmic emphasis that compels self-examination and cultivates gratitude, while simultaneously serving as a gentle admonishment against ingratitude and denial of the divine benevolence that permeates all aspects of creation and human experience.

translation: And below these two are two [other] gardens.
interpretation: This verse indicates a hierarchy in Paradise, where beyond the two primary gardens mentioned earlier for those brought nearest to Allah, there exist two additional gardens of lesser rank but still magnificent in nature. These are prepared for the righteous believers of a lower spiritual station - specifically the Companions of the Right Hand. The verse demonstrates Allah's abundant generosity, showing that even the lower ranks of Paradise contain dual gardens of delight. It also illustrates the principle of divine justice, where rewards are proportionate to one's faith and deeds, yet all inhabitants of Paradise receive bounties beyond imagination. The mention of 'below' or 'besides' these gardens emphasizes that Paradise has multiple levels and degrees of nearness to Allah, motivating believers to strive for higher stations while assuring them that any place in Paradise is an ultimate success.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a rhetorical refrain that punctuates Surah Ar-Rahman, challenging both humans and jinn to reflect upon and acknowledge the countless blessings bestowed by Allah. It functions as a divine reminder that denial of God's bounties is both irrational and ungrateful, compelling the audience to recognize that every aspect of creation—from the cosmic order to the minutest provisions of life—testifies to divine mercy and generosity. The interrogative form is not seeking information but rather inducing contemplation and humility, making it psychologically impossible for the sincere believer to deny any of the Lord's manifold gifts. The dual address ("your Lord" in dual form) emphasizes that both species of rational creation share equally in these blessings and thus bear equal responsibility for gratitude and worship.

translation: Dark green [in color].
interpretation: This verse from Surah Ar-Rahman (55:64) describes the two gardens of Paradise as being intensely green, so lush and well-watered that they appear almost black from the density and richness of their vegetation. This darkness of green symbolizes the ultimate abundance, fertility, and blessing that awaits the righteous believers in the Hereafter, reflecting Allah's infinite generosity and the perfection of Paradise's provision.

translation: Then which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine rhetorical question that invites reflection and acknowledgment rather than expecting an actual answer. The verse challenges listeners to honestly assess whether they can justifiably deny any of God's favors after being presented with evidence of His creative power, mercy, and provision. It creates a rhythm of contemplation, punctuating descriptions of divine bounties with this penetrating question that appeals to human conscience and reason, making denial increasingly difficult as the enumeration of blessings continues. The question implies that rational reflection should naturally lead to recognition and gratitude rather than ingratitude or rejection.

translation: In both of them are two springs, gushing forth.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the abundant blessings and perpetual freshness of Paradise, where the gushing springs symbolize the continuous flow of divine mercy and provision that never ceases or diminishes, reflecting the inexhaustible nature of God's generosity to the righteous believers in the hereafter.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a recurring refrain throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, functioning as a divine rhetorical question that compels humanity and jinn to reflect upon and acknowledge God's countless blessings. It establishes a pattern of contemplation where each mention of divine favors is followed by this challenge, making denial increasingly difficult as the evidence accumulates. The verse employs a pedagogical technique that transforms the recitation into an interactive spiritual experience, where the listener is constantly prompted to recognize gratitude as the only rational response to divine benevolence. The dual address to both humans and jinn emphasizes the universality of God's generosity across all conscious creation, while the interrogative form suggests that denial of these favors would be both intellectually dishonest and spiritually destructive, ultimately calling believers to cultivate a state of perpetual thankfulness.

translation: In both of them are fruit, palm trees, and pomegranates.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the abundance and variety of provisions in the two gardens of Paradise by specifically mentioning pomegranates and date palms in addition to other fruits. The specific mention of these two types after the general term 'fruit' serves a rhetorical purpose: it highlights their special status and excellence among all fruits, either due to their superior qualities, their beloved nature to people, or their particular benefits. This stylistic device of mentioning the specific after the general (dhikr al-khaas ba'd al-'aam) underscores that these are not merely included in the general category but deserve special recognition. It reflects Divine generosity in providing not just sustenance but delightful variety, and reminds believers that the blessings of the Hereafter will include the finest of what they knew and loved in worldly life, in perfected form.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This rhetorical question emphasizes human accountability and gratitude by challenging believers and disbelievers alike to reflect upon the countless blessings bestowed by Allah. It serves as a recurring refrain in Surah Ar-Rahman to punctuate each mentioned blessing, creating a rhythmic reminder that denial of divine favors is both irrational and ungrateful. The verse compels introspection about one's recognition of God's generosity in creation, sustenance, guidance, and mercy, while simultaneously warning against the arrogance of rejecting these manifest truths. The dual address suggests accountability extends to both humans and jinn, making it universal in scope.

translation: In them are good and beautiful women.
interpretation: This verse describes the companions of Paradise as being virtuous in character and beautiful in appearance, emphasizing that the rewards of the Hereafter combine both inner excellence and outer beauty, reflecting the perfection of divine grace bestowed upon the believers who attain Paradise.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a rhetorical refrain emphasizing divine generosity and human accountability, challenging both humans and jinn to acknowledge God's countless blessings rather than reject or show ingratitude toward them. It functions as a moment of reflection, prompting believers to contemplate the manifold gifts—physical, spiritual, and existential—that sustain their lives, while simultaneously warning against the arrogance of denying these provisions. The repeated nature of this verse throughout Surah Ar-Rahman creates a rhythmic reminder that recognition of God's favors is both a moral obligation and a path to spiritual awareness, transforming gratitude from mere acknowledgment into a fundamental aspect of faith and submission.

translation: Fair maidens secluded in pavilions
interpretation: This verse describes one of the blessings of Paradise, referring to righteous companions of pure nature reserved for the believers in the Hereafter. The imagery of seclusion in pavilions emphasizes their modesty, protection, and exclusivity as a divine reward. The verse symbolizes spiritual and physical fulfillment that awaits those who attain Paradise, representing beauty, purity, and companionship as part of the comprehensive bounties God has prepared for the righteous. It serves to motivate believers toward good deeds by illustrating the contrast between worldly life and the eternal rewards of the Hereafter.

translation: Then which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine rhetorical question that calls humanity and jinn to reflect upon and acknowledge God's countless blessings. It appears repeatedly throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, functioning as a refrain that punctuates each mention of divine grace and creative power. The verse employs a challenge format that makes denial of God's favors intellectually and spiritually untenable - by listing manifest evidences of divine mercy and then asking which one could possibly be rejected, it compels the listener toward gratitude and recognition of God's sovereignty. The dual address to both humans and jinn emphasizes the universal nature of divine bounties and the shared obligation of all conscious beings to acknowledge their Creator's benevolence rather than respond with ingratitude or defiance.

translation: Untouched by man or jinn before them
interpretation: This verse describes the purity and pristine nature of the heavenly maidens (hūr al-'īn) in Paradise, emphasizing that they have never been approached or known intimately by any created being, whether human or jinn. This underscores the concept of absolute purity and exclusivity as part of the divine reward for believers in the afterlife, highlighting that the blessings of Paradise are completely new, unspoiled, and reserved solely for the righteous inhabitants of Jannah, untainted by any previous contact or relationship.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a rhetorical refrain emphasizing divine accountability and gratitude. It challenges both humans and jinn to reflect on the countless blessings bestowed upon them by their Creator, implying that denial of these favors is unreasonable given their abundance and self-evidence. The interrogative form creates a pause for contemplation, urging recipients to acknowledge God's benevolence in creation, sustenance, guidance, and the promise of eternal reward. The dual address underscores that divine generosity extends to all conscious beings, making ingratitude or disbelief not merely incorrect but manifestly unjustifiable when one honestly surveys the totality of divine gifts surrounding existence itself.

translation: Reclining on green cushions and beautiful fine carpets.
interpretation: This verse describes the physical comforts of Paradise, where the righteous will recline in leisure on luxurious green furnishings and exquisite carpets. The imagery emphasizes the state of complete rest and honor that awaits the believers, contrasting the toil of worldly life with eternal ease. The specific mention of green and beauty reflects both aesthetic perfection and spiritual tranquility, as green is associated with life, freshness, and peace in Islamic tradition. This depicts not merely material luxury but a holistic state of contentment where the believers experience the fulfillment of every need and desire in the presence of divine mercy.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a recurring refrain that calls humanity and jinn to reflect upon and acknowledge the countless blessings bestowed by Allah. It challenges both groups to recognize their ingratitude and denial of divine favors, creating a rhetorical structure that emphasizes accountability and the futility of rejecting God's manifest gifts. The repetition throughout Surah Ar-Rahman functions as a spiritual mirror, compelling the listener to pause and contemplate the specific blessing just mentioned, thereby cultivating gratitude and humility before the Creator. It underscores that denying God's favors is both irrational and ungrateful, given the overwhelming evidence of His generosity in creation, sustenance, and guidance.

translation: Blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the eternal sanctity and exaltation of God's divine name, calling believers to recognize that every attribute and manifestation of the Divine Being is inherently blessed and worthy of reverence. The dual attributes of Majesty (Jalal) and Honor (Ikram) reflect the balance between God's transcendent greatness and His benevolent grace toward creation, reminding us that true worship encompasses both awe at His supreme power and gratitude for His generous bounty. It invites contemplation on how God's essence contains both the qualities that inspire reverential fear and those that evoke love and thankfulness.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the Event befalls.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound opener to Surah Al-Waqi'ah, establishing the absolute certainty and inevitability of the Day of Resurrection. The use of 'when' rather than 'if' emphasizes that this cosmic event is not merely possible but definitively ordained, removing any doubt about its occurrence. The term 'Al-Waqi'ah' (the Event) deliberately uses a definite article to indicate a singular, unprecedented occurrence known to all—the Day of Judgment—whose arrival will shatter the current order of existence. This phrasing creates a sense of immediacy and urgency, calling upon humanity to prepare for this inevitable moment when all will be held accountable, as its occurrence transcends human control or prediction, being solely within Allah's decree.

translation: There is no preventer of its occurrence.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute certainty and inevitability of the Day of Judgment. When Allah decrees that the Hour will come to pass, nothing in creation possesses the power to stop, delay, or invalidate it. This serves as a powerful reminder of divine sovereignty and the futility of denying the resurrection, calling believers to prepare for that inevitable day through righteous deeds and sincere faith, while warning those who reject it that their denial will not prevent its occurrence.

translation: Abasing, exalting.
interpretation: This phrase describes two of Allah's attributes in His divine governance - He lowers those who deserve humiliation through their arrogance and disobedience, and He raises those who deserve honor through their humility and obedience. It emphasizes Allah's absolute control over the stations of people, whether in worldly status or spiritual rank, and that no one can elevate themselves or debase others except by His will. This serves as a reminder that true honor comes only from Allah, not from worldly achievements, and that those who are haughty will be brought low while the humble will be elevated, both in this life and the Hereafter.

translation: When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking
interpretation: This verse refers to one of the cataclysmic events of the Day of Resurrection, when the stable earth will be convulsed and violently shaken from its foundations. The repetition and intensity of the term 'rajja' emphasizes the severity and unprecedented nature of this cosmic upheaval, signaling the complete transformation of the known world order and the transition from the temporal life to the eternal realm where all souls will be held accountable for their deeds.

translation: And the mountains are crushed into powder, crumbling utterly.
interpretation: This verse describes the catastrophic transformation of the earth during the Day of Judgment, when the mighty mountains—symbols of permanence and stability in worldly life—will be reduced to scattered dust particles. This emphasizes that nothing in creation, regardless of how solid or enduring it appears, can withstand the divine decree when Allah wills its destruction, reminding humanity that all physical existence is temporary and only Allah is eternal and unchanging.

translation: And they became scattered dust dispersed.
interpretation: This verse describes the complete annihilation and worthlessness of deeds or material things on the Day of Judgment. The imagery of scattered dust particles floating aimlessly in the air represents the utter futility and insignificance of worldly accomplishments when measured against divine standards. Whatever seemed solid and substantial in this life becomes as insubstantial as dust motes caught in sunlight, dispersed with no weight, no value, and no ability to benefit their possessor. It emphasizes the transient nature of earthly achievements and the importance of focusing on deeds that will have eternal value in the Hereafter.

translation: And you will be three kinds.
interpretation: This verse refers to the categorization of humanity on the Day of Judgment into three distinct groups based on their deeds and spiritual states: the foremost in faith (al-sabiqun) who are closest to Allah, the companions of the right hand (ashab al-yamin) who are the righteous believers, and the companions of the left hand (ashab al-shimal) who are the disbelievers and wrongdoers. This division emphasizes that human beings will be distinguished by their choices and actions in this life, resulting in different stations in the Hereafter, with each group receiving a recompense appropriate to their spiritual rank and moral conduct.

translation: And the companions of the right - what are the companions of the right?
interpretation: This rhetorical question emphasizes the elevated and blessed status of the righteous believers who will receive their records in their right hands on the Day of Judgment. The repetition serves to magnify their reward and create anticipation for the description of their Paradise that follows. It indicates that their station is so exalted and their felicity so great that it surpasses ordinary description, prompting wonder at the tremendous blessing Allah has prepared for those who obeyed Him in this life.

translation: And the companions of the left - what are the companions of the left?
interpretation: This verse introduces a category of people on the Day of Judgment who will receive their records in their left hands, signifying their rejection and ultimate loss. The rhetorical question 'what are the companions of the left?' is meant to evoke dread and emphasize the severity of their condition. It serves as a divine warning about the consequences of disbelief and disobedience, contrasting sharply with the companions of the right who achieve salvation. The repetition intensifies the gravity of their state and prepares the listener for a description of their punishment, urging reflection on one's deeds and spiritual direction in this life.

translation: And the foremost, the foremost
interpretation: This verse refers to those who are first and foremost in faith and righteous deeds - the pioneers who excel in responding to Allah's call and competing in good works. They represent the highest rank of believers who will be closest to Allah in Paradise, having distinguished themselves through their early acceptance of Islam, their sacrifices, and their unwavering commitment to the path of righteousness. These are individuals who race ahead in obedience and devotion, not merely following but leading in virtue.

translation: Those are the ones brought near [to Allah].
interpretation: This verse refers to the highest rank of believers in Paradise, those who have achieved the closest proximity to Allah through their exceptional faith, devotion, and righteous deeds. These muqarrabun (those brought near) represent an elite category of souls who surpass even the rightful companions of the right hand, enjoying the most intimate spiritual station and the greatest honors in the divine presence. Their nearness signifies not physical closeness but rather a special rank of spiritual favor, where they experience the fullest manifestation of divine mercy, witnessing and comprehension of divine attributes, and the ultimate satisfaction of being in the company of prophets and the most devoted servants of Allah.

translation: In gardens of pleasure.
interpretation: This phrase describes the ultimate reward of Paradise for the believers, emphasizing that the righteous will dwell eternally in gardens characterized by continuous bliss, comfort, and divine bounty. The use of 'Na'im' (pleasure/bliss) signifies not merely physical comfort but complete spiritual satisfaction and peace in the presence of Allah, where every desire is fulfilled and every hardship of worldly life is forgotten. It represents the culmination of faith and righteous deeds, where believers experience the fullness of God's mercy and generosity in an existence unmarred by suffering or sorrow.

translation: A company of the former peoples
interpretation: This phrase refers to a significant group from earlier generations or communities who will be among the foremost in Paradise. It emphasizes that righteousness and closeness to Allah is not limited to any particular era, and that many of those who preceded us in time also preceded us in faith and good deeds. The verse highlights Allah's justice in rewarding the faithful across all generations, showing that the path to divine nearness has always been open to those who sincerely seek it, regardless of when they lived in human history.

translation: And a few from the later peoples.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the rarity of true believers and those who attain the highest spiritual stations in later generations compared to earlier ones. It reflects that while the early communities of faith (particularly the companions of the prophets) produced many exemplary believers, subsequent generations would have fewer individuals reaching such elevated levels of devotion and righteousness. This serves as both a warning about spiritual decline over time and a recognition of the exceptional merit of those later believers who do achieve such stations despite living in ages of greater trial and distance from prophetic guidance.

translation: On thrones woven [with ornament]
interpretation: This verse describes the luxurious seating arrangements in Paradise, emphasizing the comfort and honor bestowed upon the believers in the Hereafter. The 'woven thrones' symbolize the meticulous craftsmanship and beauty of Paradise's furnishings, reflecting Allah's generosity and the elevated status granted to the righteous. It serves as both a literal description of Paradise's physical comforts and a metaphor for the dignity and tranquility that await those who fulfilled their covenant with Allah.

translation: Reclining on them, facing one another.
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the believers in Paradise, emphasizing the comfort, ease, and social harmony they will experience. The reclining posture signifies complete rest and leisure, freed from all worldly toil and hardship. The face-to-face arrangement indicates the absence of enmity, envy, or discord that often characterizes worldly relationships. Instead, the inhabitants of Paradise will enjoy pure companionship, mutual love, and intimate fellowship. This positioning reflects both physical comfort on luxurious furnishings and spiritual contentment in the company of the righteous, where all hearts are purified and all conversations are pleasant. It represents the perfect social order of the Hereafter, where human relationships are restored to their ideal state without the corruption of jealousy, competition, or malice.

translation: There will circulate among them young boys made eternal.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the blessings of Paradise, where eternal servants or attendants will serve the believers. These are pure, immortal beings created specifically for service in Paradise, reflecting the complete ease and honor bestowed upon the inhabitants of Jannah. Their eternal youth symbolizes the timelessness and perpetual perfection of Paradise, where everything is maintained in its most beautiful and perfect state without decay or change. The presence of such servants emphasizes that the believers will be treated with the utmost dignity and care, as honored guests of Allah, free from all burden and toil that characterizes worldly life.

translation: With goblets and ewers and a cup from a flowing spring
interpretation: This verse describes part of the divine hospitality awaiting the righteous in Paradise, emphasizing the pure and readily available nature of heavenly provisions. Unlike worldly wine that intoxicates and comes from questionable sources, the drink of Paradise flows from pure springs (ma'in) that never run dry or become contaminated. The variety of vessels mentioned - goblets (akwab), ewers (abariq), and cups (ka's) - suggests the complete and perfect service that will be provided, where every need is anticipated and met with elegance and abundance. This imagery conveys that the believers will be honored guests in their eternal abode, receiving service befitting their elevated status, and contrasts sharply with the temporary and imperfect pleasures of this world. The flowing spring symbolizes the endless and effortless nature of divine generosity, requiring no human labor or worry about depletion.

translation: They will not suffer headache from it, nor will they be intoxicated.
interpretation: This verse describes the nature of the wine or drink in Paradise, emphasizing its perfection and superiority over worldly pleasures. Unlike earthly intoxicants that cause harmful side effects such as hangovers, headaches, or loss of rational faculties, the heavenly drink purifies without impairing. This illustrates the broader principle that the pleasures of Paradise are free from the imperfections and negative consequences that accompany worldly enjoyments, representing the complete mercy and wisdom of Allah in rewarding the believers with delights that bring only joy and no harm.

translation: And fruit from whatever they select.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the blessings of Paradise, emphasizing the abundance and freedom of choice granted to its inhabitants. The use of 'yatakhayyarūn' (they select/choose) highlights that the believers in Paradise will have complete autonomy in selecting whatever fruits they desire, without restriction or scarcity. This reflects the perfect fulfillment of desires in the Hereafter, where the righteous are not limited by availability or access, but rather enjoy the fruits of their choice in unlimited variety and quality. It signifies divine generosity and the ultimate satisfaction of human preferences in a state of eternal bliss, contrasting with the limitations and constraints of worldly life.

translation: And the meat of fowl from whatever they desire.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the blessings of Paradise, emphasizing the divine generosity where believers are granted whatever they wish. The specific mention of fowl meat signifies that in Paradise, desires are fulfilled instantly and perfectly without the limitations of earthly life. It illustrates that Paradise is a realm where human wishes are honored and materialized, reflecting God's mercy and the reward for righteousness. The phrase 'whatever they desire' indicates complete freedom from want and the alignment of divine provision with human longing, demonstrating that Paradise satisfies both physical and spiritual appetites in ways that transcend worldly experience.

translation: And [for them are] fair women with large, [beautiful] eyes.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the rewards promised to the righteous believers in Paradise. The 'hur al-'ayn' (fair maidens with beautiful eyes) represent the spiritual and physical perfection of companionship in the afterlife, symbolizing the complete fulfillment and joy that awaits those who are faithful. Beyond the literal description, this reflects the Qur'anic method of communicating otherworldly realities through imagery comprehensible to human experience, emphasizing that Paradise contains delights that satisfy all dimensions of human nature—spiritual, emotional, and physical—in their most elevated and purified form.

translation: Like preserved pearls.
interpretation: This verse describes the extraordinary beauty and purity of the righteous inhabitants of Paradise, particularly the heavenly companions. The comparison to 'preserved pearls' emphasizes their pristine, unblemished nature—pearls that have been protected within their shells, untouched and unspoiled by external elements. This imagery conveys both physical perfection and spiritual purity, suggesting that the blessed in Paradise will possess a radiant, flawless beauty that has been divinely safeguarded, much like precious pearls hidden away from corruption or deterioration.

translation: A recompense for what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine principle of justice and accountability, indicating that every individual will receive consequences proportionate to their earthly actions. It underscores that human deeds are not forgotten or ignored, but rather carefully recorded and will be justly rewarded or punished in the Hereafter. The verse serves as both a warning to those who engage in wrongdoing and a reassurance to the righteous that their good works will be acknowledged and compensated by Allah, reflecting the Qur'anic concept that divine judgment is neither arbitrary nor unjust, but is precisely calibrated to one's conduct and intentions during their worldly life.

translation: They will not hear therein any ill speech or commission of sin.
interpretation: This verse describes the spiritual purity and elevated nature of Paradise, emphasizing that the environment of the Hereafter for the believers is fundamentally different from worldly life. The absence of 'laghw' (vain, meaningless talk) and 'ta'thim' (sinful speech or accusations of sin) indicates that Paradise is a realm purified from all forms of moral and spiritual pollution. This teaches that the blessed will exist in a state where harmful speech, gossip, lies, and all forms of verbal corruption that characterize much of human interaction in this world will be completely eliminated. It reflects the perfect harmony and peace of the afterlife, where interpersonal relationships are characterized solely by truth, goodness, and mutual respect, free from the ethical failings that burden earthly existence.

translation: Except the saying: 'Peace! Peace!'
interpretation: This verse describes the speech in Paradise, indicating that the inhabitants of Heaven will only hear peaceful, pleasant, and harmonious words. There will be no idle talk, offensive speech, or harmful conversation - only greetings of peace and safety. This reflects the complete spiritual serenity and absence of conflict in Paradise, where all communication serves to enhance tranquility and mutual respect among its inhabitants. The repetition of 'salama' (peace) emphasizes the abundance and continuity of this peaceful state, suggesting that peace permeates every aspect of existence in the Hereafter for the righteous.

translation: And the companions of the right - what are the companions of the right?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the elevated status and blessed fate of the righteous believers on the Day of Judgment. The rhetorical question 'what are the companions of the right?' serves to magnify their station and create anticipation for the description of their rewards that follows. The 'right' symbolizes honor, blessing, and favor in Islamic tradition, as the right side is associated with goodness and success. This verse indicates that these are people who will receive their record of deeds in their right hand, signifying their salvation and entry into Paradise. The repetition and questioning style underscores that their state is so magnificent and their reward so great that it surpasses ordinary description, inviting the listener to contemplate the immense blessings awaiting those who lived righteously and followed God's commands.

translation: Among thornless lote trees.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the blessings of Paradise, specifically mentioning the lote trees (sidr) that are 'makhḍūd' - stripped of their thorns. The interpretation is that Allah is illustrating the perfection and comfort of Paradise by contrasting its flora with their worldly counterparts. While lote trees on earth have thorns that can cause harm and discomfort, the lote trees of Paradise are purified of any imperfection or source of pain. This symbolizes how Paradise is free from all forms of suffering, annoyance, or deficiency that characterize worldly life. The mention of this specific detail serves to convey that every aspect of Paradise, even down to the trees, is designed for the complete pleasure and comfort of its inhabitants, representing Allah's perfect mercy and generosity toward the believers.

translation: And layered, clustered acacias (or banana trees with fruits piled one above another).
interpretation: This verse describes one of the pleasures of Paradise, specifically the abundant fruit-bearing trees that will be available to the righteous. The term 'talh' refers to trees laden with fruit arranged in layers or tiers, symbolizing the perfect order, beauty, and generosity of God's provision in the Hereafter. Unlike worldly trees that may have thorns or limited fruit, these trees represent divine bounty without any deficiency or harm, emphasizing that the inhabitants of Paradise will enjoy ease, comfort, and perpetual sustenance without toil or hardship.

translation: And shade extended.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the blessings of Paradise, referring to perpetual shade that provides comfort and relief to its inhabitants. Unlike worldly shade which shifts with the sun's movement, the shade in Paradise is permanent and unchanging, symbolizing the eternal nature of divine mercy and the complete absence of any discomfort or hardship. It represents Allah's perfect provision for the believers, where they will rest in constant ease without the fluctuations and limitations of earthly existence.

translation: And water poured forth
interpretation: This phrase refers to the seminal fluid that is emitted during reproduction, describing it as flowing water that is poured out, which serves as a reminder of the humble origins of human creation and Allah's power in creating life from such a simple substance

translation: And abundant fruit
interpretation: This phrase depicts one of the blessings of Paradise, emphasizing Allah's generous provision for the believers in the Hereafter. The abundant fruit symbolizes both physical sustenance and spiritual satisfaction, representing the completeness and inexhaustibility of divine bounty. Unlike worldly provisions that are limited and seasonal, the fruits of Paradise are described as plentiful and perpetually available, never diminishing or being forbidden, reflecting the eternal nature of divine reward and the fulfillment of every desire for those who attain it.

translation: Neither cut off nor forbidden.
interpretation: This phrase describes the fruits of Paradise, indicating that they are eternally available without seasonal interruption and accessible without any prohibition or restriction, contrasting with worldly fruits that have limited seasons and may sometimes be forbidden or inaccessible to people due to various circumstances.

translation: And carpets/furnishings raised high.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the luxuries of Paradise, where the believers will be honored with elevated, magnificent furnishings that symbolize their exalted spiritual status and the dignity they have attained through faith and righteous deeds. The raised carpets represent not merely physical comfort, but the elevation of the believers' rank in the sight of Allah, reflecting how their earthly struggles and submission to divine will have lifted them to a state of eternal honor and repose in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, We have created them (the maidens of Paradise) with a special creation
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute creative power and His ability to bring into existence beings with unique qualities beyond the natural order of worldly creation. It points to the divine prerogative to create with perfect attributes, demonstrating that the delights of Paradise are not bound by the limitations of earthly existence. The verse invites believers to reflect on Allah's boundless capability to fashion creations according to His perfect wisdom, and serves as a reminder that the rewards of the Hereafter transcend human imagination and earthly experience. It reinforces the concept that Paradise contains blessings that are fundamentally different from and superior to anything known in this world, all originating from Allah's will and creative command.

translation: And made them virgins
interpretation: This verse describes the spiritual transformation and renewal of the believers' spouses in Paradise, indicating that Allah will recreate them in a state of eternal youth, purity, and perfection, symbolizing the complete restoration and idealization of human companionship in the Hereafter, free from the effects of aging, sin, or worldly imperfections.

translation: Arabs, of equal age
interpretation: This phrase describes the companions of Paradise as being youthful, vibrant women who speak Arabic and are perfectly matched in age with their spouses, emphasizing the perfection and harmony of relationships in the Hereafter where believers will enjoy companionship free from the disparities and imperfections of worldly life

translation: For the companions of the right
interpretation: This phrase refers to the blessed souls who will receive their records of deeds in their right hands on the Day of Judgment, symbolizing their righteousness and salvation. The 'companions of the right' represent those who followed God's guidance, performed good deeds, and will be rewarded with Paradise. The right side in Islamic symbolism signifies honor, blessing, and favor, contrasting with the left which represents misfortune. This designation emphasizes divine mercy toward the faithful and the ultimate success of those who lived according to God's commands.

translation: A company of the former peoples
interpretation: This phrase refers to a large group or multitude from earlier generations or communities who will be among the blessed in Paradise. It emphasizes that divine favor and salvation are not restricted to later peoples, but that many from ancient times who believed and acted righteously will receive the same reward. The verse highlights the continuity of God's mercy across all eras of human history and affirms that righteousness has always been recognized and rewarded by Allah, regardless of the time period in which people lived.

translation: And a company of the later peoples.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the universal mercy and justice of Allah, indicating that Paradise and its blessings are not restricted to the early believers or any particular generation. It emphasizes that righteousness and divine reward transcend temporal boundaries, and that among the later generations of Muslims—those who come after the Prophet's time and the early companions—there will also be a significant group who will attain salvation and enter Paradise. This serves as encouragement for all subsequent generations of believers that they too have equal opportunity to earn Allah's pleasure and Paradise through faith and righteous deeds, regardless of when they lived in history.

translation: And the companions of the left - what are the companions of the left?
interpretation: This verse introduces a rhetorical question that emphasizes the gravity and wretchedness of those who will be on the left side on the Day of Judgment. The repetition serves to build suspense and draw attention to the dire fate awaiting this group, contrasting them with the companions of the right who achieve salvation. The 'left' symbolizes misfortune and rejection in Islamic eschatology, representing those whose deeds were weighed and found wanting, leading to their placement among the unfortunate ones destined for punishment. The interrogative form suggests that their condition is so terrible that it defies easy description, prompting reflection on the consequences of one's earthly choices.

translation: In scorching wind and scalding water.
interpretation: This verse describes the torment awaiting those who denied the truth in the Hereafter, depicting their punishment through two types of severe atmospheric and aquatic afflictions - the samoom being an intensely hot, poisonous wind that burns the skin and suffocates, while the hameem is boiling water that scalds. The pairing emphasizes the inescapable nature of divine retribution, where the disbelievers find no relief whether from the air they breathe or the water they encounter, symbolizing the comprehensive and unrelenting nature of punishment for those who rejected faith and divine guidance during their worldly lives.

translation: And a shade of black smoke.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the torments of Hell, specifically referring to the black, suffocating smoke that provides no relief or comfort to its inhabitants. Unlike beneficial shade that offers coolness and protection, this shade from Yahmum (black smoke) is oppressive and adds to the suffering. It represents the inversion of worldly comforts in the Hereafter for those who rejected faith - where they might have expected respite, they find only increased anguish. The imagery emphasizes that in Hell, even what appears to offer shelter becomes a source of torment, illustrating the completeness of punishment for those who chose disbelief over submission to Allah.

translation: Neither cool nor generous.
interpretation: This phrase appears to be referencing the description of Hellfire's shade in Surah Al-Mursalat (77:31), where it describes a shadow that provides no coolness or respite. The interpretation is that the torment of Hell offers no relief whatsoever - its shade fails to provide the comfort that shade normally gives, symbolizing the complete absence of mercy or benefit for those dwelling therein. It emphasizes the utter futility of seeking any form of comfort or escape in the Hereafter for those condemned, as even what appears to offer relief is devoid of any actual benefit or honor.

translation: Indeed, they were before that indulging in luxury.
interpretation: This verse indicates that excessive indulgence in worldly pleasures and luxurious living led these people away from righteousness and obedience to Allah. Their comfortable lifestyle made them heedless of spiritual development and moral accountability, causing them to become arrogant and resistant to divine guidance. The verse serves as a warning that material abundance without gratitude and moral discipline can be a trial that leads to one's downfall, as it did for previous nations who were destroyed due to their corruption stemming from their extravagant and self-indulgent ways.

translation: And they used to persist in the great sin.
interpretation: This verse condemns those who deliberately and stubbornly continued in grave sins without repentance or remorse. The emphasis on 'persistence' (yasirrūn) indicates a willful, habitual engagement in wrongdoing rather than occasional lapses. The 'great sin' (al-ḥinth al-ʿaẓīm) refers to major transgressions against divine commands, particularly associating partners with Allah or denying fundamental articles of faith. The verse highlights that the severity of sin is compounded not merely by committing it, but by one's obstinate refusal to abandon it despite knowing its wrongfulness, demonstrating a hardened heart that rejects guidance and accountability.

translation: And they used to say: 'When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?'
interpretation: This verse reflects the skepticism of the disbelievers regarding the resurrection and the afterlife. Their doubt stems from their inability to comprehend how physical bodies that have decomposed into dust and bones could be restored to life. This represents a challenge to divine power based on their limited human understanding and experience. The verse highlights the fundamental rejection of accountability in the Hereafter, which is rooted in materialistic thinking that cannot conceive of existence beyond the physical realm. It serves as a critique of those who judge divine capability by the standards of worldly observation, failing to recognize that the Creator who brought them into existence from nothing can certainly recreate them. This disbelief in resurrection ultimately leads to moral complacency, as the absence of belief in judgment removes the incentive for righteous living.

translation: Or our forefathers of old?
interpretation: This phrase represents a rhetorical question posed by disbelievers expressing skepticism about resurrection and the afterlife. It reflects their incredulity at the claim that not only they themselves will be brought back to life after death, but also their ancestors from distant generations past. The question reveals a deep-seated denial rooted in their inability to comprehend Allah's power to resurrect the dead, regardless of how long they have been deceased or how their bodies have decomposed. This objection stems from judging divine capability by human standards and material limitations, failing to recognize that the One who created them initially has absolute power to recreate them. The verse captures a common argument of deniers throughout history who view resurrection as impossibly remote, especially for those who died long ago.

translation: Say: 'Indeed, the former peoples and the later peoples...'
interpretation: This verse fragment introduces a universal declaration that transcends temporal boundaries, emphasizing that divine judgment and resurrection apply equally to all generations of humanity. The command to 'say' (qul) establishes prophetic authority in conveying a message of cosmic scope. By linking 'the former and the later peoples,' the verse abolishes any notion that some eras or generations might escape accountability, asserting instead that all of humanity—from Adam to the last person—shares a common destiny before God. This formulation serves to democratize the human condition, removing distinctions based on chronological existence and establishing that divine justice operates beyond the constraints of historical time, making every soul equally subject to resurrection and judgment regardless of when they lived.

translation: They will surely be gathered together for the appointment of a known Day.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the certainty of the Day of Judgment and the gathering of all humanity before Allah for accountability. The use of 'known Day' indicates that while humans may not know its exact timing, it is fixed and determined in Allah's knowledge. The verse serves as a reminder of divine justice and the inevitable reckoning that awaits every soul, encouraging believers to prepare through righteous deeds and warning the heedless to turn back to Allah before it is too late. The certainty expressed here reinforces that no one can escape this appointed time, regardless of their worldly status or power.

translation: Then indeed you, O those astray and denying,
interpretation: This verse serves as a direct address to those who have rejected divine guidance and denied the truth of revelation. The combination of being 'astray' (ḍāllūn) and 'denying' (mukadhdhibūn) indicates a dual condition: not only have these individuals lost their way from the straight path, but they have actively rejected the message when it was presented to them. This represents a more severe state than mere ignorance, as it involves willful rejection. The verse functions as an introduction to what follows, typically a description of the consequences that await such individuals in the Hereafter. The use of 'then' (thumma) suggests a sequential progression in the narrative, moving from previous descriptions to a new focus on this particular group and their fate.

translation: Indeed, you will be eating from the tree of Zaqqum
interpretation: This verse warns the disbelievers and wrongdoers of their punishment in Hell, where they will be compelled to consume from the tree of Zaqqum—a bitter, thorny tree that symbolizes the painful consequences of their rejection of faith and evil deeds. The imagery serves as a vivid reminder of divine justice, where those who chose spiritual corruption in this life will face its physical manifestation in the Hereafter. This emphasizes the principle of recompense and encourages believers to avoid the paths that lead to such severe punishment.

translation: Then indeed, you will be filling from it your bellies.
interpretation: This verse describes the torment of the people of Hell who will be forced to consume from the Tree of Zaqqum, filling their stomachs with its bitter, burning fruit as a form of divine punishment. It emphasizes the completeness of their suffering - they will not merely taste it, but will fill themselves entirely with this painful nourishment, illustrating how the consequences of their worldly choices will penetrate every aspect of their being in the Hereafter. The verse serves as a warning about the totality and inescapability of punishment for those who reject faith and commit evil deeds.

translation: Then drinking on top of it from scalding water
interpretation: This verse describes the punishment of the inhabitants of Hell who will consume the bitter fruit of the Zaqqum tree and then drink boiling water on top of it, intensifying their torment. The interpretation is that this represents the compounding nature of divine punishment for those who rejected faith - one affliction follows another without relief, symbolizing how the consequences of disbelief in the Hereafter are multiplied and unrelenting, with each element of punishment adding to rather than relieving the previous suffering.

translation: And you drink as the drinking of thirsty camels.
interpretation: This verse warns against excessive and uncontrolled consumption, whether literal or metaphorical, comparing such behavior to camels afflicted with an insatiable thirst that drink without restraint or benefit.
