This serves as both a warning to the heedless and a reminder that divine justice operates on perfect knowledge, emphasizing the importance of righteous conduct in this life in preparation for that inevitable reckoning.

translation: And when the sky is stripped away
interpretation: This verse describes one of the terrifying events of the Day of Judgment when the heavens will be peeled back or removed like a scroll being rolled up or a roof being torn off. It signifies the total dismantling of the cosmic order as humans know it, revealing what lies beyond the visible universe. This removal of the sky serves to expose the reality of the divine realm and demonstrates that the familiar natural world is merely temporary, collapsing before the eternal reality of God's dominion. The imagery emphasizes the absolute power of Allah over all creation and the inevitability of the Day of Reckoning when all earthly structures, including the heavens themselves, will be demolished.

translation: And when the Hellfire is set ablaze.
interpretation: This verse refers to the eschatological intensification of Hell's punishment on the Day of Judgment. The use of 'su'irat' (set ablaze/kindled) indicates that Hellfire will be stoked to its maximum intensity, prepared for those who rejected faith and engaged in wrongdoing. This serves as both a warning and a reminder that divine justice includes consequences for those who persist in evil, and that the preparation of Hell is part of the cosmic transformation occurring when the present world order comes to an end and the eternal realities are fully manifested.

translation: And when Paradise is brought near
interpretation: This verse describes a scene from the Day of Judgment when Paradise will be brought close to the righteous believers, signifying that the promised reward is now within their reach and imminent. The bringing near of Paradise serves as a manifestation of divine mercy and fulfillment of God's promise to those who lived righteously, creating a moment of profound anticipation before the believers enter their eternal abode, thus emphasizing that divine rewards are certain and that the distance between the righteous and their ultimate reward will be removed on that tremendous day.

translation: Every soul will know what it has brought [to account].
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the Day of Judgment when complete clarity and self-awareness will be granted to every individual regarding their deeds. The soul's knowledge here is not intellectual speculation but direct, undeniable witnessing of one's own actions—both good and evil—presented before them. It signifies that on that Day, all veils of forgetfulness, self-deception, and rationalization will be lifted, and each person will confront the full reality of what they prepared for the Hereafter during their worldly life. This serves as both a warning to the heedless and an encouragement to the righteous, reminding believers that ultimate justice requires complete transparency where nothing can be hidden or denied.

translation: So I swear by the retreating stars
interpretation: This verse introduces a divine oath by celestial bodies that possess two characteristics: they are 'khunnas' (الخنس) meaning they withdraw or retreat from sight, and they move in their orbits. Classical commentators understand this to refer to the five visible planets (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) which appear to move forward through the night sky, then retreat backward in retrograde motion, and disappear during daylight. The divine swearing by these phenomena emphasizes Allah's power over the precise cosmic order and serves to authenticate what follows in the subsequent verses, demonstrating that just as these celestial bodies follow immutable divine laws in their complex movements, so too are the revelations and warnings that follow absolutely certain and worthy of serious contemplation.

translation: The running [stars], the sweeping [ones]
interpretation: This phrase from Surah At-Takwir (81:16) refers to the planets in their orbital motion. The term 'al-jawari' denotes celestial bodies that move in courses, while 'al-kunnas' describes their apparent retrograde motion or their disappearance and reappearance, as planets seem to retreat and hide from view periodically. This verse demonstrates the Qur'an's acknowledgment of precise astronomical phenomena, reminding believers of Allah's intricate design of the cosmos and His mastery over the celestial order. The oath sworn by these planetary movements emphasizes the gravity and truthfulness of the revelation that follows, using observable cosmic realities as testimony to divine wisdom and the certainty of the Day of Judgment.

translation: And by the night when it recedes
interpretation: This verse is an oath by Allah invoking the night at the moment of its departure, when darkness begins to withdraw and the first light of dawn approaches. The divine oath emphasizes the cosmic rhythm and orderly transition between darkness and light as signs of Allah's power and wisdom. By swearing upon this specific moment of transformation, Allah draws attention to the precise natural phenomena that demonstrate His meticulous control over creation and serve as signs for those who reflect upon the universe's intricate design.

translation: And by the dawn when it breathes.
interpretation: This verse uses the metaphor of breathing to describe the dawn's gradual emergence, suggesting that just as breath is a sign of life, the dawn represents spiritual renewal and awakening. The personification of dawn as a living entity that breathes symbolizes the subtle, progressive nature of divine revelation and truth, which does not come suddenly but unfolds gently like the morning light dispelling darkness. It reflects how faith and understanding develop gradually in the human heart, and serves as a reminder that God's signs in nature point to His creative power and the cyclical nature of spiritual rebirth available to believers who reflect upon creation.

translation: Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine origin and authenticity of the Qur'an by affirming that it was conveyed through a noble and trustworthy messenger, referring to either the Angel Gabriel who brought the revelation from Allah to Prophet Muhammad, or to Prophet Muhammad himself who transmitted it to humanity. The use of 'noble' (karīm) underscores the elevated status, moral excellence, and reliability of the messenger, thereby establishing the credibility and sacred nature of the Qur'anic message and countering any doubts about its source or the integrity of its transmission.

translation: Possessor of power, secure in position with the Owner of the Throne.
interpretation: This verse describes the angel Gabriel, emphasizing his immense strength and honored, trusted status in the presence of Allah. His position of 'makīn' (secure, established) indicates that he holds a rank of utmost reliability and closeness to the Divine presence, being entrusted with carrying revelation to the prophets. The combination of power and secure position demonstrates that Gabriel's authority in conveying the message is both unquestionable in its strength and absolutely trustworthy in its source, as he occupies a station of permanent favor and access before the Lord of the Throne.

translation: Obeyed there, trustworthy.
interpretation: This verse describes the Angel Gabriel (Jibril), emphasizing his honored status in the heavenly realm where he is obeyed by other angels due to his rank, and highlighting his trustworthiness in conveying Allah's revelation to the prophets without any alteration or error. It establishes the credibility and authority of the source through which divine revelation comes to humanity, assuring believers that the message they receive through the Prophet Muhammad has been transmitted by a noble and reliable intermediary who faithfully delivers Allah's words exactly as commanded.

translation: And your companion is not insane.
interpretation: This verse defends the Prophet Muhammad against the accusations of madness made by the disbelievers of Makkah. It affirms his sound mental state and credibility as a messenger, establishing that his claim to prophethood and the revelations he received were not the product of delusion or insanity, but rather from divine inspiration. The verse serves to counter one of the common tactics used by opponents to discredit prophetic missions throughout history.

translation: And he certainly saw him on the clear horizon.
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Muhammad's vision of the angel Gabriel in his true celestial form during the initial revelation experience. The 'clear horizon' signifies the undeniable nature of this divine encounter, establishing the authenticity of the prophetic vision and refuting any claims that it was an illusion or fabrication. This sighting on the eastern horizon served as a powerful validation of Muhammad's prophethood, demonstrating that his message came from a legitimate heavenly source. The verse emphasizes the clarity and certainty of the experience, leaving no room for doubt about the supernatural origin of the Qur'anic revelation, and serves as a response to those who questioned the Prophet's truthfulness about his encounters with the divine messenger.

translation: And he is not a withholder concerning the unseen.
interpretation: This verse defends the Prophet Muhammad's character and mission, emphasizing that he does not withhold or conceal the divine revelation he receives. It affirms his trustworthiness as a messenger who faithfully conveys God's word without holding back any part of the unseen knowledge that has been revealed to him. The verse serves as a response to critics who accused him of fabricating or selectively sharing divine messages, establishing that he is generous and forthcoming with the truth he has been entrusted to deliver to humanity.

translation: And it is not the word of an outcast devil.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine origin of the Qur'an by negating any satanic influence in its revelation. It serves as a rebuttal to the claims of disbelievers who suggested that the Prophet Muhammad received his message from demonic sources. The verse establishes that the Qur'an's source is purely divine, coming from Allah through the Angel Gabriel, and is completely protected from any interference by Satan or evil forces. This authentication was crucial in establishing the credibility of the prophetic message and distinguishing true revelation from false inspiration or satanic whispers that might mislead people.

translation: So where are you going?
interpretation: This rhetorical question challenges humanity's misguided paths and choices in life, prompting reflection on the futility of turning away from divine guidance. It emphasizes that despite claims of autonomy and self-direction, humans ultimately have nowhere to turn except back to Allah, as all paths outside His guidance lead to confusion and loss. The verse serves as a wake-up call to recognize that true success and purpose can only be found by submitting to the divine will rather than following one's own desires or false ideologies.

translation: It is not but a reminder to the worlds.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the universal nature and purpose of the Qur'an as a divine reminder sent not merely to a specific community or time period, but to all of creation across generations and places. The use of 'reminder' (dhikr) indicates that the Qur'an's message is not introducing foreign concepts, but rather awakening within humanity the innate knowledge of truth and tawhid (divine unity) that exists within the human fitrah (primordial nature). This universality underscores both the comprehensive mercy of Allah and the shared responsibility of all humanity to heed this guidance, while also affirming that the Qur'an's relevance transcends cultural, temporal, and geographical boundaries.

translation: For whoever among you wills to take a straight course.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that divine guidance is available to all, but its actualization depends on the individual's sincere will and choice to pursue righteousness. It affirms human free will and moral responsibility—God provides the path of uprightness, but each person must actively choose to walk it. The verse underscores that faith and guidance are not imposed but require personal volition and commitment, highlighting the Islamic principle that humans are accountable for their choices in accepting or rejecting the straight path (al-sirat al-mustaqim) that leads to God's pleasure and ultimate salvation.

translation: And you do not will except that Allah wills - Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the fundamental Islamic concept of divine sovereignty and human will operating within Allah's supreme authority. It teaches that while humans possess the ability to choose and desire, their willing itself exists only within the framework of Allah's overarching will and permission. This does not negate human free will or moral responsibility, but rather places it in proper theological context - that human agency is derived from and dependent upon the Creator's sustaining power. The phrase 'Lord of the worlds' reinforces that this principle applies universally to all creation, reminding believers that true autonomy belongs only to Allah, and that recognizing this dependence should cultivate humility, reliance on Allah, and awareness that success in any endeavor ultimately requires divine facilitation alongside human effort.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the sky is cleft asunder.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the cosmic signs that will herald the Day of Resurrection, emphasizing the temporary nature of creation and Allah's absolute power over all existence. The splitting of the heavens signifies the complete dismantling of the current cosmic order, reminding believers that the seemingly solid and eternal structures of the universe are in fact fragile before their Creator, thus calling humans to reflect upon their ultimate return to Allah and to live with awareness of accountability in the Hereafter.

translation: And when the stars fall, dispersing.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the catastrophic cosmic events that will occur on the Day of Judgment, symbolizing the complete dissolution of the established natural order. The scattering of the stars represents the dismantling of the heavens and the cosmic system that humanity has relied upon for guidance, navigation, and the measurement of time. It serves to emphasize the absolute power of Allah over all creation and the temporary nature of the universe, reminding believers that everything except Allah is subject to destruction and that the Day of Resurrection will be marked by phenomena so tremendous that they shatter the very foundations of the physical world mankind knows.

translation: And when the seas are made to burst forth (or overflow).
interpretation: This verse describes an apocalyptic event on the Day of Judgment when Allah will cause the oceans to break their boundaries and surge forth violently, possibly merging together. This signifies the complete breakdown of the natural order that humanity has always known, demonstrating Allah's absolute power over creation and serving as one of the terrifying cosmic signs that will mark the end of the world. The bursting forth of the seas represents how all the stable systems that humans depend upon will be utterly transformed, reminding believers that the present world is temporary and that the Hour of Reckoning is inevitable and overwhelming.

translation: And when the graves are overturned.
interpretation: This verse describes a climactic event of the Day of Resurrection when the dead will be raised from their graves and brought forth for judgment. The overturning or scattering of graves symbolizes the complete upheaval of the earthly order and the transition from the temporal world to the eternal realm. It serves as a powerful reminder that death is not the end, but rather a passage to accountability before God. The imagery emphasizes that nothing of our deeds—whether hidden or apparent—will remain concealed, as even the graves that sealed our bodies will be burst open, revealing all souls for divine reckoning. This momentous event underscores the inevitability of resurrection and the fundamental Islamic belief in the afterlife, compelling believers to live with consciousness of their ultimate return to their Creator.

translation: Every soul will know what it has sent forward and what it has kept back.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the moment of ultimate accountability when each individual will have complete awareness of their deeds - both the righteous actions they performed and sent ahead to benefit them in the Hereafter, and the opportunities for good they delayed, neglected, or the harmful consequences they left behind. It reflects the comprehensive nature of divine judgment where nothing is hidden, and every person will witness the full record of their life's choices, including both their proactive virtuous deeds and their failures to act when they should have, as well as the lasting effects of their actions on others and themselves.

translation: O mankind, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?
interpretation: This verse poses a profound rhetorical question that serves as a wake-up call to human complacency and ingratitude. Allah is challenging the human being to reflect on what has caused them to become heedless or arrogant toward their Creator despite His continuous generosity and blessings. The question implies that there is no logical reason for such negligence - given that Allah is al-Kareem (the Generous), constantly bestowing favors, sustaining life, and showing mercy. The verse strikes at human presumption and false security, warning against being deceived by worldly life, Satan's whispers, or one's own desires into forgetting accountability to the One who created and honored them. It calls for deep self-examination about what barriers we erect between ourselves and proper worship and gratitude toward our infinitely Generous Lord.

translation: Who created you, then fashioned you, then proportioned you.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's role as the ultimate Designer who not only brings humans into existence but carefully shapes them with balance and harmony. The progression from creation (khalq) to fashioning (taswiyah) to proportioning ('adl) highlights the intentionality and precision in human formation. It serves as a reminder that the human form is not random but deliberately constructed with perfect equilibrium in its physical, mental, and spiritual dimensions. This should inspire gratitude and recognition of divine wisdom, prompting humans to reflect on their purpose and the One who fashioned them with such care and balance.

translation: In whatever form He willed, He assembled you.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute power and creative will in fashioning human beings. It refers to the divine design and assembly of human form in the womb, highlighting that our physical characteristics, features, and constitution are determined solely by Allah's will, not by chance or our own choice. The verse reminds believers of their complete dependence on their Creator and that the diversity in human appearance and forms reflects Allah's wisdom and capability. It serves as a call to recognize divine sovereignty over creation and to be humble before the One who shaped us according to His perfect knowledge and purpose.

translation: Nay, but you deny the Recompense.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who reject the concept of divine judgment and accountability in the Hereafter. The denial of the Day of Recompense (al-Din) reflects a fundamental rejection of moral accountability, which leads people to live without regard for divine consequences of their actions. This denial is not merely intellectual skepticism, but often stems from attachment to worldly life and unwillingness to accept that one's deeds will be judged. The verse serves as a rebuke, indicating that the rejection of accountability is the root cause of moral corruption and transgression, as people who deny ultimate justice feel emboldened to pursue their desires without restraint.

translation: And indeed, over you are guardians
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the concept of divine accountability by informing humanity that Allah has appointed angels to record and watch over all human deeds and actions. These guardian angels are witnesses to everything a person does, says, and even thinks, meticulously documenting good and evil deeds. This serves as both a warning against sin and an encouragement toward righteousness, as it reminds believers that they are never truly alone or unwatched, and that complete privacy from divine observation is impossible. The verse instills consciousness of God (taqwa) and moral responsibility, knowing that every action will be preserved as evidence for the Day of Judgment when all records will be presented and each person held accountable for their earthly life.

translation: Noble scribes (recording angels).
interpretation: This phrase refers to the angels appointed by Allah to record every deed, word, and thought of human beings. The description 'noble' (kirāman) emphasizes their honored status and trustworthy nature, while 'scribes' (kātibīn) indicates their function as meticulous recorders. This serves as a reminder that humans are under constant divine surveillance, which should inspire mindfulness in one's actions and accountability before God, knowing that nothing escapes documentation for the Day of Judgment.

translation: They know what you do.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes divine omniscience through angelic observation, reminding believers that their actions are constantly witnessed and recorded by the angels assigned to them. It serves as both a warning against sin and an encouragement toward righteousness, as nothing done in secret escapes divine knowledge. The verse cultivates consciousness of accountability and moral responsibility, knowing that all deeds—whether public or private—are documented and will be presented on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss.
interpretation: This verse establishes the fundamental principle that those who live righteously and fulfill their duties toward God and His creation will be rewarded with complete felicity in the Hereafter. The use of 'inna' (indeed) emphasizes the certainty of this promise, while 'al-abrar' (the righteous) refers to those characterized by comprehensive goodness in belief, speech, and action. The term 'na'im' (bliss) signifies not merely physical pleasures but a state of comprehensive well-being encompassing spiritual contentment, divine pleasure, and eternal joy that transcends worldly understanding. This represents the just recompense from God, whose wisdom ensures that virtue is ultimately rewarded, providing both encouragement for believers to persevere in righteousness and a manifestation of divine justice.

translation: And indeed, the wicked will be in Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse establishes the inevitable consequence of persistent wickedness and moral corruption. It emphasizes divine justice by contrasting the fate of the righteous with that of the fujjar—those who deliberately transgress divine boundaries and live in defiance of moral law. The use of 'indeed' (inna) stresses certainty, indicating that this is not merely a possibility but an assured outcome. The term 'jaheem' (Hellfire) specifically denotes an intensely blazing fire, suggesting that the punishment corresponds to the severity of persistent sinfulness. This serves as both a warning to redirect one's path toward righteousness and an affirmation that ultimate justice will be served, as no wrongdoing escapes divine accountability in the hereafter.

translation: They will enter it on the Day of Recompense.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the certainty and inevitability of divine judgment, where the wrongdoers or disbelievers will face the consequences of their actions on the Day of Judgment. The use of the present tense verb 'yaslawnaha' (they will enter/burn in it) indicates the absolute certainty of this future event in Allah's knowledge, making it as definite as if it were already occurring. The term 'yawm al-deen' (Day of Recompense) underscores that this is a day of perfect justice where every soul receives exactly what it has earned through its choices and deeds in worldly life, reflecting Allah's attribute of being the ultimate Judge who neither oppresses nor overlooks any deed.

translation: And they will not be absent from it.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the inescapable nature of divine punishment or accountability. It conveys that those destined for the consequences of their deeds will find no refuge or escape from what awaits them, underscoring the comprehensive and unavoidable nature of divine justice where no one can hide or be overlooked.

translation: And what can make you know what is the Day of Recompense?
interpretation: This rhetorical question emphasizes the incomprehensible magnitude and gravity of the Day of Judgment, indicating that its true reality is beyond human comprehension in this worldly life. The question serves to instill awe and mindfulness in the believer, reminding them that the consequences and events of that Day are so momentous that no mortal can fully grasp their weight until they witness it directly, thereby encouraging righteous conduct and accountability in preparation for that inevitable reckoning.

translation: Then what will make you understand what the Day of Recompense is?
interpretation: This rhetorical question emphasizes the incomprehensible magnitude and gravity of the Day of Judgment, highlighting that human understanding cannot fully grasp its reality or severity. It serves to instill awe and urgency in the listener, reminding believers that the consequences of that Day are beyond ordinary human experience and comprehension, thus encouraging righteous action and accountability in this life.

translation: A Day when no soul will possess [power to do] anything for another soul, and the command that Day is [entirely] with Allah.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of Allah on the Day of Judgment, stripping away all worldly intermediaries and dependencies. It teaches that the bonds of kinship, friendship, and patronage that people rely upon in this world will be severed, leaving each individual to stand alone before their Creator. The verse serves as both a warning against placing ultimate trust in created beings and a call to recognize that true authority belongs solely to Allah, particularly on that momentous Day when all pretenses of power and influence will be exposed as illusory, and when no intercession will avail except by His permission.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Woe to those who give less [than due], who defraud in measure and weight.
interpretation: This verse opens Surah Al-Mutaffifin with a stern warning against commercial dishonesty and ethical corruption in transactions. The divine threat of 'woe' (wayl) indicates severe consequences for those who cheat in their dealings by taking full measure when receiving but giving less when providing to others. Beyond its literal application to merchants and traders, this verse establishes a fundamental Islamic principle of justice and fairness in all human interactions. It warns against the spiritual disease of selfishness and double standards, where one demands full rights for oneself but fails to fulfill obligations toward others. The placement of this warning immediately after the basmala emphasizes the gravity of this sin in Allah's sight, as it combines theft, betrayal of trust, and oppression of others' rights. This teaching extends to all forms of giving less than what is due—whether in business, relationships, work, or worship—making it a comprehensive moral imperative for maintaining justice and integrity in society.

translation: Those who, when they take a measure from people, take in full.
interpretation: This verse condemns those who practice double standards in commercial transactions, demanding their full rights when receiving from others while denying others their full rights when giving to them. It highlights the moral corruption of self-serving behavior where one insists on complete justice for oneself but fails to reciprocate that justice to others. The verse exposes the hypocrisy of those who are meticulous about their own entitlements yet careless or exploitative when fulfilling obligations to others, establishing that true righteousness requires consistency and fairness in all dealings regardless of whether one is the receiver or the giver.

translation: And when they measure or weigh for them, they give less than due.
interpretation: This verse condemns the fraudulent merchants who cheat others by giving them less than what is rightfully theirs when measuring or weighing goods. It highlights a specific manifestation of injustice where people are meticulous in demanding their full rights when receiving, but become dishonest and deficient when giving to others. The verse exposes the hypocrisy and moral corruption of those who practice double standards in their transactions, treating themselves and others by different measures. It serves as a warning that such deceptive practices are a grave sin that undermines trust in society and violates the fundamental Islamic principle of fairness and justice in all dealings, particularly in commerce where the vulnerable can easily be exploited.

translation: Do they not think that they will be resurrected?
interpretation: This verse serves as a rhetorical question that challenges those who engage in fraudulent practices, particularly in commerce and dealings with others. It emphasizes the concept of divine accountability by reminding people that their actions in this worldly life are not without consequence. The verse implies that those who wrong others act as if there will be no Day of Judgment where they must answer for their deeds. It calls attention to the heedlessness of those who live without consciousness of the Resurrection and the final reckoning before Allah, suggesting that proper awareness of being raised and held accountable would prevent such unjust behavior and encourage righteousness and fairness in all transactions.

translation: For a great Day
interpretation: This phrase refers to the Day of Judgment (Yawm al-Qiyamah), described as 'great' due to its immense magnitude, terror, and significance as the ultimate day of reckoning when all of humanity will stand before Allah to account for their deeds, and when the final destinies of paradise or hellfire will be determined, making it the most consequential and awe-inspiring event in existence.

translation: The Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of all the worlds.
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Judgment as a moment of ultimate accountability where all human beings will stand in humble submission before their Creator. The phrase 'standing before the Lord' conveys both the physical resurrection and the spiritual state of exposure, where no secret remains hidden and every soul faces the consequences of their earthly deeds. The use of 'Lord of all the worlds' (Rabb al-'Alamin) emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty over all creation, reminding believers that the same Creator who sustained them in life will judge them with perfect justice. This standing represents a profound leveling of humanity—regardless of worldly status, wealth, or power—where each person stands alone before divine judgment, stripped of all pretenses and worldly distinctions.

translation: No! Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute certainty that the deeds of the wicked and immoral are recorded in a preserved register called Sijjin, which represents a place or state of constriction and punishment. The opening 'No!' serves as a strong refutation of any delusion the wrongdoers might harbor about escaping accountability. The verse establishes that divine justice maintains a meticulous record of human actions, and those who persist in corruption will find their deeds inscribed in a ledger that testifies against them on the Day of Judgment. Sijjin symbolizes both the written record of evil deeds and the ultimate destination of confinement for those whose lives were marked by transgression, contrasting sharply with the elevated register of the righteous mentioned elsewhere in the Qur'an.

translation: And what can make you know what is Sijjin?
interpretation: This rhetorical question emphasizes the severity and incomprehensibility of Sijjin, which is the register or record of the deeds of the wicked, or the place of their punishment. The interrogative form serves to magnify the gravity of the concept, indicating that Sijjin represents something so terrible and profound that human understanding cannot fully grasp its reality without divine revelation. It prepares the listener for understanding the dire consequences awaiting those whose records are inscribed therein, highlighting the serious fate of the wrongdoers and the precision of divine justice in recording every deed.

translation: A written record.
interpretation: This phrase refers to a preserved, documented book or record that is clearly inscribed and unchangeable. In Islamic eschatological context, it represents the complete accounting of human deeds maintained by Allah, which will be presented on the Day of Judgment. The term 'marqoom' (marked/inscribed) emphasizes the permanent, indelible nature of this record, indicating that nothing is forgotten or erased from the divine ledger. It serves as a reminder of ultimate accountability and the precision with which all actions are preserved in the divine knowledge.

translation: Woe on that Day to the deniers.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stern warning about the consequences of rejecting divine truth and prophetic messages. The repetitive use of this phrase throughout Surah Al-Mursalat emphasizes that those who deny God's signs, messengers, and the reality of the Day of Judgment will face severe regret and punishment. It underscores the principle of accountability, where intellectual arrogance and willful rejection of clear evidence lead to spiritual destruction. The phrase creates a rhythmic reminder that denial is not merely intellectual disagreement but a moral failing with eschatological consequences, urging believers to reflect on the certainty of divine justice and the importance of accepting truth when it is presented.

translation: Those who deny the Day of Judgment
interpretation: This verse characterizes a fundamental trait of disbelievers: their rejection of accountability in the Hereafter. The denial of the Day of Judgment (yawm al-din) represents not merely intellectual skepticism, but a moral position that undermines ethical responsibility. When people reject the reality of divine reckoning, they lose the ultimate framework for justice and moral obligation, often leading to transgression and oppression in worldly life. This denial is particularly grave because belief in the Hereafter is foundational to faith, serving as the basis for righteous conduct and restraint from evil. The verse implies that such denial is willful obstinacy rather than genuine ignorance, as the evidence for accountability is embedded in human conscience and divine revelation.

translation: And none denies it except every transgressor and sinner.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that rejection of divine truth is fundamentally linked to moral corruption. Those who deny God's revelations do so not due to intellectual barriers but because of their own moral transgressions and sins. The coupling of 'transgressor' (one who exceeds limits) and 'sinner' (one who accumulates wrongs) indicates that denial stems from a heart corrupted by wrongdoing, suggesting that ethical deviation precedes and enables theological rejection. The verse thus establishes that disbelief is not merely an intellectual position but a moral failure, as a pure heart naturally recognizes and accepts divine truth.

translation: When Our verses are recited to him, he says, 'Tales of the ancients.'
interpretation: This verse condemns the arrogant rejection of divine revelation by those who dismiss God's signs as mere myths or legends from past generations. It highlights a common pattern of disbelief where skeptics refuse to engage with the truth of the message, instead trivializing it as folklore or invented stories. This response reflects spiritual blindness and pride, as the rejecter refuses to recognize the divine origin of the Qur'an and instead attributes it to human fabrication. The verse serves as a warning against hardening one's heart to guidance and demonstrates how denial often manifests through dismissive labeling rather than sincere reflection on the content of revelation.

translation: No! Rather, the stain has covered their hearts of that which they used to earn.
interpretation: This verse indicates that persistent sinning and wrongdoing creates a spiritual rust or seal upon the heart that gradually diminishes one's capacity to perceive truth and respond to guidance. The accumulation of misdeeds is not merely a list of transgressions but has a transformative effect on the soul itself, hardening it and making it less receptive to divine light. This suggests that moral and spiritual corruption is both a cause and consequence of persistent disobedience, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where each sin makes the next easier and repentance more difficult, until the heart becomes veiled from recognizing its own condition.

translation: No! Indeed, from their Lord, that Day, they will be partitioned.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the severe spiritual consequence of disbelief and wrongdoing: complete separation from God's presence on the Day of Judgment. The divine veiling represents the ultimate punishment—being barred from witnessing God's countenance and experiencing His mercy. This deprivation is not merely physical distance but a state of spiritual exclusion, where the wicked are denied the blessed vision (ru'yah) that the righteous will enjoy. The emphatic negation 'kalla' (No!) reinforces that their worldly denial of accountability has led to this tragic barrier, suggesting that those who rejected God's signs in life will be rejected from His nearness in the Hereafter, experiencing the profound loss of being cut off from the source of all goodness and light.

translation: Then indeed, they will be burned in the Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the certainty and inevitability of divine punishment for those who rejected faith and engaged in wrongdoing. The phrase 'then indeed' (thumma innahum) conveys both sequence and absolute certainty, indicating that after judgment has been passed, the consequence is unavoidable. The term 'salū' (to be burned or roasted) describes an active, continuous state of suffering in the flames of Hell, not merely entering it but experiencing its full torment. This serves as a stark warning about accountability in the Hereafter and reinforces that divine justice will be fulfilled. The verse reminds believers of the serious consequences of disbelief and moral corruption, encouraging them to remain steadfast in faith and righteous conduct to avoid such a fate.

translation: Then it will be said, 'This is that which you used to deny.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the reality of Divine accountability and the moment of truth in the Hereafter. When faced with the consequences of their rejection, the disbelievers will be confronted with the very realities they dismissed in worldly life - whether Hell, resurrection, or judgment. The statement serves as both a rebuke and a closure to denial, highlighting that human rejection of truth does not nullify its existence. The use of demonstrative language ('this') indicates the tangible, undeniable nature of what they will witness, removing all room for doubt or excuse. It represents the ultimate vindication of prophetic warnings and the end of the opportunity for repentance, underscoring the Qur'anic theme that denial in this world leads to regretful recognition in the next.

translation: No indeed! The record of the righteous is surely in 'Illiyyun (the highest place).
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the elevated spiritual status and divine favor bestowed upon the righteous believers. The term 'Illiyyun suggests not merely a physical location but a state of supreme honor and proximity to Allah, indicating that the deeds and souls of the pious are preserved in the most exalted realm of existence. It serves as a contrast to the fate of the wicked and provides assurance that those who live righteously will be distinguished and rewarded with the highest stations in the hereafter, their records kept in a place of honor that reflects the nobility of their earthly conduct and sincere devotion.

translation: And what can make you know what 'Illiyyun is?
interpretation: This rhetorical question emphasizes the sublime and exalted nature of 'Illiyyun, which refers to the elevated register where the records of the righteous are kept. The question serves to magnify the incomprehensible honor and loftiness of the station prepared for the believers in Paradise, indicating that its reality surpasses human comprehension and that only Allah's knowledge fully encompasses its magnificence. It draws attention to the vast difference between worldly understanding and the divine realities of the Hereafter.

translation: A written record.
interpretation: This phrase refers to a book or record that is inscribed, marked, or made clearly manifest. In the Qur'anic context, it typically signifies a documented account that is preserved with precision, whether referring to the deeds of individuals recorded by angels, the divine decree written in the Preserved Tablet, or the Book given to the righteous on the Day of Judgment. The term 'marqūm' emphasizes the permanence, clarity, and official nature of what is recorded, indicating that nothing is left to chance or ambiguity in Allah's system of accountability and divine knowledge.

translation: Witnessed by those brought near (to Allah).
interpretation: This phrase indicates that the righteous deeds and records of the believers are witnessed and authenticated by the angels who are closest to Allah's throne, the highest rank of angels. Their witnessing serves as a divine testimony to the elevated spiritual status of these deeds, emphasizing that actions performed with sincere faith are not only recorded but are honored in the highest realm of heaven, in the presence of those who perpetually witness the divine presence. This suggests a hierarchy of spiritual witnessing where the most sacred matters are attended to by the most exalted beings in creation.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss.
interpretation: This verse affirms the ultimate reward awaiting those who lived righteously in accordance with God's guidance. The bliss mentioned encompasses both physical pleasures of Paradise and spiritual contentment that comes from divine proximity and satisfaction. It emphasizes that true piety and moral excellence lead to eternal felicity, contrasting the fate of the righteous with that of the wicked, and serves as both a promise to motivate believers toward virtue and a reminder that God's justice ensures every soul receives its due recompense in the hereafter.

translation: On thrones, observing.
interpretation: This verse describes the believers in Paradise who will be seated on couches or thrones in a position of honor and comfort, observing the fulfillment of God's justice. They witness either the punishment of the disbelievers or the manifestation of divine recompense, experiencing the satisfaction of seeing truth vindicated. Their elevated position symbolizes their high status and the reward they receive for their faith and righteous deeds in worldly life. The act of observing reflects their awareness and consciousness of God's perfect judgment, adding to their joy and contentment in the Hereafter.

translation: You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss.
interpretation: This verse describes the believers in Paradise, indicating that their inner state of joy and felicity will be outwardly manifest through their luminous, glowing faces. The physical appearance becomes a mirror of spiritual contentment, suggesting that in the afterlife, the barrier between inner reality and outer expression dissolves, and the blessed cannot conceal their happiness as it radiates naturally from their very being, making their state of grace immediately recognizable to any observer.

translation: They will be given to drink from a sealed nectar.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the rewards awaiting the righteous in Paradise, where they will be served a pure, divine drink that has been preserved and sealed to maintain its pristine quality and purity. The sealing signifies that this nectar is untouched, uncontaminated, and reserved exclusively for the blessed inhabitants of Paradise, symbolizing the honor, exclusivity, and supreme quality of the divine provisions that await those who have earned God's pleasure through their faith and righteous deeds in worldly life.

translation: Its conclusion is musk. So for this let the competitors compete.
interpretation: This verse encourages believers to strive and compete with one another in performing righteous deeds and seeking the rewards of Paradise, specifically the pure drink sealed with musk that awaits the righteous. It establishes that worldly competition should be redirected toward spiritual excellence and the pursuit of Allah's pleasure, making the eternal rewards of the Hereafter the true prize worth racing toward, rather than temporary material gains.

translation: And its mixture is of Tasnim.
interpretation: This verse describes the nature of the pure wine in Paradise, indicating that it will be mixed or flavored with Tasnim, which is the most exalted and finest drink in Paradise. The fact that this heavenly beverage is mixed with Tasnim signifies the supreme honor and elevated status bestowed upon those who receive it, as Tasnim represents the highest grade of celestial refreshment reserved for those nearest to Allah. The mixing suggests both enhancement of pleasure and a mark of divine generosity, where even the mixture itself comes from the most noble source.

translation: A spring from which those brought near [to Allah] drink.
interpretation: This verse describes a spiritual reward in Paradise reserved for the most devoted believers who have attained the highest stations of closeness to God. The spring represents not merely physical refreshment but the culmination of divine favor, where the elite among the righteous—those who excelled in faith, obedience, and spiritual intimacy with their Lord—enjoy exclusive access to divine gifts. It establishes a hierarchy in Paradise where proximity to Allah is reflected in the quality and exclusivity of blessings, suggesting that the intensity of one's devotion and nearness to God in this life determines the level of bliss in the hereafter. The drinking itself symbolizes full satisfaction and the quenching of all spiritual longing.

translation: Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed.
interpretation: This verse highlights the reversal of roles and the ultimate vindication of the faithful. In the worldly life, the disbelievers and sinners often mock and ridicule the believers for their faith, piety, and moral conduct. However, this verse serves as a reminder that such mockery is temporary and misguided. The criminals' laughter stems from their arrogance and false sense of superiority in worldly matters, failing to recognize the eternal consequences of their actions. The verse implies that on the Day of Judgment, the situation will be completely reversed - those who were mocked will be honored while the mockers will face humiliation and punishment. It teaches believers to remain steadfast despite worldly ridicule, as true success lies in the Hereafter, and warns the arrogant that their temporary worldly advantage and their derision of the faithful will ultimately lead to their own downfall.

translation: And when they passed by them, they would exchange derisive glances.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the arrogance and mockery of the disbelievers toward the believers in the worldly life. The act of winking and exchanging knowing glances represents a form of silent ridicule and contempt, where the mockers communicate their disdain without speaking. This behavior reflects the spiritual blindness of those who reject faith, as they fail to recognize the truth and instead make the righteous the object of their scorn. The verse serves as a reminder that the believers may face mockery and social persecution, but this temporary humiliation will be reversed in the Hereafter when the roles are reversed and the believers will be honored while the mockers face consequences for their arrogance.

translation: And when they returned to their people, they would return jesting.
interpretation: This verse describes the attitude of the disbelievers who would mock the believers and then return to their own communities in a state of amusement and self-satisfaction, treating their ridicule as entertainment. It reveals the spiritual blindness of those who take their rejection of faith lightly, making sport of sacred matters and deriving pleasure from their mockery. Their return 'jesting' indicates a heart hardened against truth, where instead of reflection or concern about the hereafter, they find comedy in their own disbelief and in mocking those who believe. This behavior demonstrates how arrogance and attachment to worldly life can make people callous to spiritual realities, turning what should be a matter of serious contemplation into a source of frivolous amusement among their peers.

translation: And when they saw them, they said, 'Indeed, these are truly astray.'
interpretation: This verse highlights the arrogance and delusion of the disbelievers who mock the believers, considering them misguided for following the truth. It reveals how those who reject faith often invert moral reality, perceiving guidance as error and their own misguidance as correctness. The verse serves as a reminder that worldly judgment can be severely flawed, and that true guidance is not determined by the opinion of the majority or the powerful, but by adherence to divine truth. It also foreshadows the reversal of fortunes in the Hereafter, where the mockers will discover their own profound error.

translation: And they were not sent as guardians over them.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that those who mock or disbelieve have no authority or divine mandate to monitor, judge, or control the affairs of the believers. It underscores the principle that humans are not appointed as overseers of others' faith and actions - that role belongs solely to God. The verse serves to remind believers not to be concerned with the ridicule or scrutiny of disbelievers, as these critics have no legitimate standing or responsibility over them. It also implies that on the Day of Judgment, these mockers will have no excuse for their behavior, as they were never given the duty to watch over or correct the believers, yet they took it upon themselves to ridicule them. This reinforces the Islamic concept of individual accountability before God alone, not before other humans who appoint themselves as judges.

translation: So today those who believed are laughing at the disbelievers
interpretation: This verse speaks to the reversal of circumstances between believers and disbelievers on the Day of Judgment. In the worldly life, the disbelievers used to mock and ridicule the believers for their faith, but in the Hereafter, the roles are reversed. The believers will experience joy and satisfaction as they witness the ultimate vindication of truth and the consequences faced by those who rejected faith. This serves as divine justice and compensation for the believers who endured mockery and persecution in their earthly lives, demonstrating that temporal power and scorn mean nothing before eternal reality.

translation: On thrones, observing.
interpretation: This verse describes the believers in Paradise who are seated in positions of honor and comfort, looking upon the blessings and delights of Paradise that Allah has bestowed upon them. The use of 'thrones' (ara'ik) symbolizes their elevated status and the comfort they enjoy, while 'observing' indicates they are witnessing the fulfillment of divine promises, the punishments of the disbelievers, or simply contemplating the magnificent bounties surrounding them. This scene reflects the ultimate reward of those who remained faithful - a state of dignified rest and satisfaction, where they can peacefully observe the justice of Allah's decree and the beauty of their eternal abode.

translation: Are the disbelievers rewarded [except] for what they used to do?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the principle of divine justice, rhetorically asserting that the recompense given to those who rejected faith is precisely commensurate with their actions in the worldly life. The verse implies that the punishment or consequences faced by disbelievers in the Hereafter are not arbitrary but are the direct result of their deliberate choices, their rejection of truth, and their deeds. It serves as a reminder that Allah's judgment is perfectly just, and that each person will receive exactly what their actions merit—the disbelievers are being repaid in full measure for what they earned through their denial and misdeeds, neither more nor less than what their conduct deserved.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the sky is split apart.
interpretation: This verse describes a cosmic event that will occur on the Day of Resurrection, signaling the complete dissolution of the current world order and the beginning of the Hereafter. The splitting of the sky represents the breakdown of the universe's structure as we know it, demonstrating Allah's absolute power over all creation and His ability to transform the heavens and earth at will. This dramatic imagery serves to awaken human consciousness to the reality of divine judgment and the temporary nature of worldly existence, urging believers to prepare for accountability before their Creator by living righteously in this world.

translation: And it has responded to its Lord, and this is its obligation.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the ultimate compliance and submission of all creation to God's will. The 'it' refers to something in creation - traditionally understood as either the earth or the heavens - which listens and responds to its Lord's command. The phrase 'and this is its obligation' (wa huqqat) indicates that this response is not optional but rather an inherent duty built into the nature of creation itself. The verse teaches that all elements of the universe are programmed to obey God's commands, and this obedience is both their natural state and their rightful purpose. This stands as a model for human beings, reminding them that just as the physical universe submits to divine decree without resistance, so too should conscious beings align their will with God's will, recognizing that such submission is not merely commanded but is the fulfillment of their true nature and purpose.

translation: And when the earth is stretched out
interpretation: This verse describes a cosmic transformation on the Day of Resurrection when the earth will be flattened and expanded, removing all its mountains, valleys, and irregularities to become a vast plain where all of humanity will be gathered for judgment. This leveling symbolizes the complete restructuring of the physical world and the end of its current form, preparing it to serve as the arena for divine accountability where nothing will be hidden and all deeds will be exposed.

translation: And it has cast out what is within it and emptied itself
interpretation: This verse describes the earth on the Day of Resurrection when it will expel all that it contains - the dead buried within it, treasures hidden in it, and secrets concealed beneath its surface. The earth will completely empty itself, holding nothing back, as it prepares to bear witness on the Day of Judgment. This signifies the total transformation of the natural order and the earth's submission to Allah's command, revealing everything for divine accountability and demonstrating that nothing can remain hidden from Allah's knowledge and justice.

translation: And it has responded to its Lord, and is obliged to do so.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the inherent nature of all creation to submit and respond to the will of Allah. It emphasizes that obedience to the Creator is not merely a choice but an existential reality embedded in the very fabric of existence. Everything in creation, whether willingly or unwillingly, ultimately fulfills its purpose as ordained by God, and this responsiveness is both a natural state and a duty. The verse highlights the cosmic order where all things inevitably return to and acknowledge their Lord, demonstrating that submission to divine command is the fundamental truth of existence.

translation: O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with [great] exertion and you will meet Him.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the fundamental reality of human existence as one of continuous striving and effort directed toward the ultimate meeting with Allah. Every human being, regardless of their path, is engaged in a journey that inevitably leads to their Creator. The term 'kadh' (laboring/striving) indicates that life is inherently filled with toil, struggle, and effort - whether in pursuit of worldly goals or spiritual advancement. The verse serves as both a reminder of accountability and an encouragement, asserting that all human endeavors, trials, and accomplishments are not in vain but are part of a purposeful journey culminating in the meeting with God, where one's deeds will be reckoned. This understanding should motivate believers to ensure their striving is directed toward what pleases Allah, as the meeting is certain and unavoidable.

translation: As for the one who is given his record in his right hand
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the righteous on the Day of Judgment, where receiving one's book of deeds in the right hand symbolizes success, honor, and salvation. It represents those who lived according to divine guidance and will be rewarded with Paradise. The right hand traditionally signifies blessing and favor in Islamic tradition, indicating that these individuals will face an easy reckoning and will be pleased with what they find in their record of deeds.

translation: Then he will be judged with an easy account.
interpretation: This verse promises that those who receive their record of deeds in their right hand on the Day of Judgment will experience a merciful and lenient reckoning. The 'easy account' refers to Allah's grace in overlooking minor sins and focusing on major good deeds, without strict interrogation or detailed questioning about every small matter. It contrasts with the severe accounting awaiting those who denied faith, indicating that believers who strived sincerely will find Allah's judgment to be one of mercy rather than harsh scrutiny, ultimately leading to their forgiveness and admission to Paradise.

translation: And he would return to his people in pride and joy.
interpretation: This verse describes the wrongdoer's misguided satisfaction with his worldly life and material success. He returns to his family and companions feeling pleased with himself, demonstrating his heedlessness of the Hereafter and his accountability before Allah. His joy is rooted in his attachment to temporal pleasures and the approval of his peers, reflecting a spiritual blindness where he mistakes worldly achievement for true success. This false sense of security and self-satisfaction ultimately leads to his downfall, as he neglects preparation for the eternal life and fails to recognize that his worldly contentment is fleeting and will be replaced with regret on the Day of Judgment.

translation: But as for he who is given his record behind his back
interpretation: This verse describes the state of those who will receive their book of deeds behind their backs on the Day of Judgment, symbolizing disgrace and humiliation. The manner of receiving one's record reflects one's fate: while the righteous receive theirs in their right hand with honor, the wicked receive theirs from behind their back, indicating their shame and the concealment of their evil deeds. This physical positioning represents their spiritual state of turning away from truth during their worldly life, and now facing the consequences with their backs turned to mercy. It serves as a warning that one's actions in this life determine not only the content of their record but also the humiliating or honorable manner in which they will face their accountability before Allah.

translation: Then he will call for destruction upon himself.
interpretation: This verse refers to the state of the disbeliever or wrongdoer on the Day of Judgment who, upon witnessing the punishment and realizing the gravity of their sins, will desperately wish for their own annihilation and call out for complete destruction rather than face the accountability and consequences of their deeds. It illustrates the profound regret and hopelessness that will overcome those who rejected faith, as death or non-existence will seem preferable to them than enduring divine justice and the reality of their errors.

translation: And he will burn in a blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse describes the inevitable punishment awaiting those who reject faith and do righteous deeds. The blazing Fire (sa'īr) represents divine justice being manifested, where the consequences of one's choices in the worldly life are fully realized. It emphasizes the reality of accountability in the Hereafter and serves as a warning to encourage people to turn toward righteousness and away from transgression while they still have the opportunity in this life.

translation: Indeed, he used to be among his people joyful.
interpretation: This verse criticizes the spiritual state of one who was excessively pleased with worldly life and his status among his people, forgetting the reality of the Hereafter and his accountability before God. His joy was misplaced because it was rooted in temporal matters and companionship with those who shared his heedlessness, rather than in devotion to God and preparation for eternal life. This serves as a warning against being deluded by worldly success and social approval, which can distract one from the true purpose of existence and the inevitable return to God for judgment.

translation: Indeed, he thought he would never return [to Allah].
interpretation: This verse addresses the human condition of heedlessness and false security. It refers to the disbeliever or the negligent person who lived with the mistaken assumption that there would be no resurrection, no accountability, and no return to their Lord for judgment. This false sense of permanence in worldly life led them to act without regard for divine consequences, indulging in sin and transgression. The verse serves as a warning that such a belief is fundamentally flawed, as every soul will inevitably return to Allah for reckoning. It highlights how denial of the afterlife corrupts human behavior and moral responsibility, making one live as though this temporal existence is all there is, thereby neglecting the preparation for eternal life.

translation: Yes, indeed his Lord is ever Seeing of him.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's complete and perfect knowledge of the individual's inner state, intentions, and actions. It serves as both a warning and a reassurance—a warning to those who think their deeds go unnoticed, and a reassurance to the righteous that God is fully aware of their struggles and circumstances. The term 'basīran' (Seeing) indicates not merely observation but comprehensive awareness coupled with wisdom, suggesting that divine knowledge encompasses both the outward actions and the hidden motivations of the heart, and that God will judge or reward accordingly with perfect justice and understanding.

translation: So I swear by the twilight glow.
interpretation: Allah is calling attention to the twilight—the reddish glow that appears after sunset—as a sign of His creative power and precise cosmic order. The oath by this natural phenomenon serves to emphasize the truthfulness of what follows, inviting reflection on the systematic transition from day to night as evidence of divine design and the certainty of resurrection and accountability that the subsequent verses address.

translation: By the night and what it enshrouds.
interpretation: This verse introduces a divine oath sworn by the night and everything it gathers, conceals, or draws together in its darkness. The oath emphasizes Allah's power in creation, using the night as a witness to His majesty. The phrase 'what it enshrouds' refers to the creatures, darkness, and stillness that the night collects and covers, highlighting the natural order and the transition from day's activity to night's rest. This serves to draw attention to the importance of what follows the oath, which typically relates to resurrection, accountability, or the truth of the Prophet's message. The night's encompassing nature symbolizes divine control over all creation and the inevitability of Allah's decree.

translation: And [by] the moon when it becomes full
interpretation: This is an oath by the full moon, which serves as a divine testimony to emphasize what follows. The moon's completion into fullness symbolizes perfection, order, and the precise system Allah has established in His creation. The cyclical nature of the moon—from crescent to full—demonstrates Allah's power over the universe and serves as a sign for reflection. Such oaths by celestial phenomena are meant to draw human attention to the magnificence of creation and to prepare the listener for an important truth that follows, reminding humanity of the Creator's wisdom and sovereignty over all natural phenomena.

translation: You will surely ride state after state.
interpretation: This verse indicates the inevitable progression of human existence through successive stages and transformations - from one condition to another, whether in this worldly life (from conception to birth to childhood to adulthood to old age to death) or in the afterlife (from death to resurrection to judgment). It emphasizes the dynamic nature of human experience and serves as a reminder that life is not static but rather a journey through various phases, each preparing for the next, ultimately leading to the final meeting with Allah. The verse can also be understood as addressing the certainty of resurrection and the stages humanity will traverse on the Day of Judgment.

translation: So what is [the matter] with them [that] they do not believe?
interpretation: This verse poses a rhetorical question expressing divine astonishment at human disbelief despite the clear signs and evidences presented. It implies that there is no rational justification for rejecting faith when the proofs of God's existence, His messengers, and the truth of revelation are manifest. The question serves to highlight the stubbornness and irrationality of those who reject belief, suggesting that their disbelief stems not from lack of evidence but from willful rejection, arrogance, or attachment to worldly desires. It calls believers to reflect on the clarity of faith's foundation while challenging disbelievers to examine their resistance to truth.

translation: And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate.
interpretation: This verse criticizes the spiritual negligence and stubborn refusal of the disbelievers to submit to Allah's words. The act of prostration (sujud) represents the ultimate expression of humility, surrender, and acknowledgment of divine authority. When they hear the Qur'an—which contains clear signs and commands—their failure to prostrate symbolizes their arrogance, hardness of heart, and rejection of the truth. This isn't merely about a physical action, but reflects a deeper spiritual defiance: they refuse to humble themselves before their Creator despite receiving His guidance. The verse exposes their inner state of pride and resistance, showing that their disbelief isn't due to lack of evidence, but rather a willful choice to remain heedless and rebellious against divine truth.

translation: Rather, those who disbelieve are in denial.
interpretation: This verse highlights the deliberate rejection of truth by the disbelievers. It indicates that their disbelief is not merely due to lack of evidence or understanding, but rather stems from a willful denial and rejection of the truth that has been made clear to them. The verse emphasizes that the disbelievers actively contradict and refuse to acknowledge the signs and revelations of Allah, despite their awareness of them. This suggests a hardening of hearts and a conscious choice to turn away from guidance, which is a more severe spiritual condition than simple ignorance or confusion.

translation: And Allah knows best what they conceal.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute and comprehensive knowledge of all hidden matters, particularly what people keep secret in their hearts and minds. It serves as both a warning to those who harbor evil intentions or deception, and a comfort to believers that no injustice or wrongdoing goes unnoticed by the Divine. The verse establishes that human attempts to conceal thoughts, plans, or actions are futile before Allah's all-encompassing awareness, reminding believers that accountability extends beyond outward actions to inner intentions and that divine justice accounts for everything hidden from human perception.

translation: So give them tidings of a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse serves as a warning and declaration of divine justice, indicating that those who persist in rejecting faith, committing injustice, or turning away from God's guidance will face severe consequences in the Hereafter. The use of 'tidings' or 'glad tidings' in the context of punishment is rhetorically powerful, as it ironically employs language typically used for good news to announce a grave outcome, emphasizing the certainty and inevitability of the punishment for those who deserve it. This verse underscores the principle of accountability before God and serves as a call to reflection and repentance before it is too late.

translation: Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds; for them is a reward uninterrupted.
interpretation: This verse establishes a crucial exception to a preceding statement about human loss or decline, emphasizing that salvation and divine reward are contingent upon two inseparable conditions: sincere faith in God and the manifestation of that faith through righteous action. The phrase 'reward uninterrupted' (ajr ghayru mamnun) signifies that God's recompense for the believers is neither finite, conditional on continued performance, nor accompanied by reproach or obligation that diminishes its value. It teaches that genuine faith must necessarily express itself in ethical conduct and good works, and that this combination merits an eternal, gracious reward from God that flows without cessation or diminishment, reflecting the perfect generosity of the Divine and the inherent dignity granted to those who align their beliefs with virtuous action.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the sky containing great stars (or constellations).
interpretation: This verse employs a divine oath by the celestial realm to emphasize a profound truth that follows. The reference to 'the sky with constellations' serves as a reminder of Allah's magnificent creation and cosmic order, inviting reflection on the precise arrangement of the heavens as evidence of divine wisdom and power. The oath draws human attention from earthly concerns to the vastness above, establishing that just as Allah has organized the heavens with perfect precision, so too does He govern all affairs with ultimate authority and knowledge, including the accountability of human deeds that this surah addresses.

translation: And [by] the promised Day
interpretation: This refers to the Day of Judgment, the Day of Resurrection when all of humanity will be gathered for accountability. It is called 'the promised day' because Allah has promised its occurrence throughout revelation, and it represents the fulfillment of divine justice where every soul will receive recompense for their deeds. The oath by this day emphasizes its tremendous significance and certainty, serving as a reminder that this temporal world will inevitably conclude with that appointed time when all matters will be settled and the ultimate truth will be manifest.

translation: By the witness and the witnessed.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment where the witness represents those who will testify (such as prophets, angels, and believers themselves) and the witnessed represents the assembled creation on that tremendous day when all will be held accountable for their deeds, emphasizing the certainty and solemnity of divine justice.

translation: Destroyed were the companions of the trench
interpretation: This verse refers to the persecution of believers who were thrown into fiery ditches by tyrant rulers for refusing to renounce their faith. It serves as a condemnation of religious persecution and oppression, while simultaneously affirming that such tyrannical acts will face divine retribution. The verse emphasizes that those who persecute believers for their faith will ultimately be destroyed or cursed by God, and it provides comfort to the oppressed by assuring them that their suffering is witnessed and will be avenged by divine justice. It also serves as a historical reminder of the trials faced by early monotheistic communities.

translation: The fire of fuel
interpretation: This phrase refers to a fire that is continuously fed and sustained, symbolizing either the eternal nature of hellfire that never extinguishes due to its constant fuel supply, or metaphorically representing intense tribulations and trials that are self-perpetuating. In the context of Surah Al-Buruj where this phrase appears, it specifically denotes the fire prepared by the tyrants for the believers, which ultimately becomes a testimony against the oppressors themselves and illustrates that those who kindle fires of persecution will face the eternal fire of divine justice.

translation: When they were seated by it
interpretation: This verse refers to the disbelievers who sat around the burning trench watching the believers being tortured and burned, highlighting their cruelty and direct involvement in persecution. It emphasizes their active, deliberate participation as witnesses and perpetrators of the atrocity, demonstrating the depths of human wickedness when faith is rejected and hearts become hardened against truth and mercy.

translation: And they were witnesses to what they were doing to the believers.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the conscious, deliberate nature of the persecution inflicted upon the believers. The persecutors were not acting in ignorance or absence, but were fully present and aware, witnessing their own cruel actions against the faithful. This highlights the severity of their sin - they cannot claim unawareness or unintentional harm. Their direct observation of their own oppression compounds their guilt before God, as they consciously chose evil while watching its effects unfold. It serves as a warning that all human actions, especially injustices against believers, are done in full consciousness and will be accounted for, as the perpetrators themselves bear witness to their own deeds.

translation: And they resented them not except for their belief in Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse reveals the fundamental irrationality of persecution against believers, demonstrating that the persecutors had no legitimate grievance against the faithful except their devotion to God alone. It exposes how the rejection of monotheism and submission to the Divine often stems not from any wrongdoing by believers, but from the persecutors' own spiritual obstinacy and inability to accept God's sovereignty. The verse emphasizes that true faith in God—characterized by His absolute power and perfect praiseworthiness—inevitably provokes hostility from those who resist submitting to Him, thus distinguishing between just and unjust causes of conflict and validating the righteousness of those who suffer solely for their faith.

translation: He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is Witness over all things.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute sovereignty over all creation and His complete awareness of everything that occurs within His dominion. The mention of His ownership of the heavens and earth establishes His supreme authority, while His being a witness over all things means nothing escapes His knowledge - neither actions, intentions, nor the hidden states of hearts. This serves as both a reminder of accountability and a source of comfort, as it affirms that the Just and All-Knowing Lord oversees all affairs, ensuring that no injustice goes unnoticed and no deed, good or bad, is lost or forgotten. It calls believers to live with consciousness of divine observation in all matters.

translation: Indeed, those who have tortured the believing men and believing women and then have not repented will have the punishment of Hell, and they will have the punishment of the Burning Fire.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's justice and mercy simultaneously. It warns those who persecute believers that they face severe consequences, yet leaves the door of repentance open. The double mention of punishment - both Hell and the Burning Fire - underscores the gravity of oppressing believers. However, the phrase 'then have not repented' reveals God's infinite mercy: no matter how grievous the sin of persecution, sincere repentance can avert punishment. This teaches that oppression of the faithful is among the most serious transgressions, as it combines injustice toward both Allah's servants and defiance of His authority, yet even such perpetrators are given the opportunity to turn back to God before facing accountability in the Hereafter.
